log: Pratt & Whitney commits to the Joint Venture
Rolls-Royce commits to the Joint Venture
P&W GTF2 (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture
RR UltraFan NB (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture
P&W-RR Joint Venture NB engine launched in 2035
Joint Venture engine ready 2036 (inherits a folded solo programme's schedule)

public_statements.boeing:
Back in 2025 I said we were turning the ship but hadn't turned it. I think we've turned it now. The balance sheet is repaired and staying repaired. The 737 line has built at 57 a month to plan for five straight years. The 777X and the MAX family are delivering. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here, and the job now is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. We'll do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. We've looked hard at it with the data in front of us, and the case isn't there yet. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we do go, we build it at rate the right way. With new engines in development at Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and CFM always at the table, we expect to give our customers a choice of engine, with durability proven before entry into service. When we launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year either. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

On production, the 737 stays at 57 a month and stays stable. Any step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We're keeping our trained people and our suppliers ready. Going slow has let us go faster, and stability is what lets us move when the time comes.

Our dates will be set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Every step to entry into service is gated on the maturity of its technologies and of the production system designed with it. Safety and quality come before schedule. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce will power it, and we will certify each engine as it matures, so that our customers have a choice and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. Its lines will keep running alongside the new aircraft, built to our customers' demand, for a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme remains funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Airbus has launched its new single-aisle and given its customers a choice of engine, and CFM is on it. We thank them for that. We don't have a birthright on any order, and we'll earn our place on that airplane every day.

So, together with our partners at Safran, we're committing to a new CFM engine for it, a step forward from today's LEAP, and we're offering it to both of our airframer customers. It's ready when testing says so, and not before 2041. We'll prove its durability in test, hot and harsh conditions included, before it enters service. Our customers ask that of us, and we ask it of ourselves. We're also working with Embraer, with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe.

RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

On capacity, we'll work with both airframers, together with Safran, on LEAP today and on what comes next. LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first.

Here's what we don't know: when the next airplane after this one launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The shortfalls were in our industrial performance: a manufacturing process issue in powder-metal parts, and shop and parts capacity that did not keep up, so engines did not get back to our customers fast enough. Engines flying in hotter, sandier conditions have also seen shorter time on wing than expected. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new-engine test hardware.

We control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch, and we are carrying it through for the customer that selected it. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. If the test data take longer, entry into service waits, and the testing does not. GTF2 is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Any partnership shares risk and investment; it never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules. On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward our share, so the commitment needs no new spending. The same durability rule applies to any Joint Venture engine. Rolls-Royce will speak for its own decisions, and the airframers for their own programmes.

The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So, plainly. UltraFan is in development for a new single-aisle on the full seven years: entry into service no earlier than 2037. Durability will be proven, and support and MRO will be in place through partner shops, before entry into service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our preference is partnership; it is not a need. Airbus has put Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney on the same aircraft, so we have moved first. Rolls-Royce has committed to the Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. There's no change of strategy. We have answered Boeing's invitation: UltraFan, on standard terms, with durability proven before entry into service. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.

boeing.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated)
boeing.detail: We continue to invite all three narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Selection will be on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. With P&W's GTF2 and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB now in development, our plan is to offer customers a choice of engine at launch (code 7: CFM plus GTF2 plus UltraFan NB). No fps date and no launch commitment.

boeing.move: Hold the 737 at 57 a month with KPI gates and stability first
boeing.detail: No rate step. KPIs are monitored monthly. 57 a month is the ceiling. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, treat CFM's concentrated sub-tier shortages as a watch item, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place. Any future step is gated one at a time on KPIs and FAA agreement.

boeing.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
boeing.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

airbus.move: Secure our own supply for the NGSA entry into service and ramp
airbus.detail: Continue the round-1 programme: the NGSA wing stays in-house (Wing of Tomorrow and the run-at-rate wing), with aerostructures through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites. Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts. The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist covers NGSA through its ramp. This serves our own ramp only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: Engine certification sequence and CFM long-term capacity agreements
airbus.detail: NGSA keeps three engine makers (code 7: CFM + P&W GTF2 + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB). CFM is certified first; GTF2 follows once its durability and full-life parts are proven, and UltraFan NB as it matures, as we did on the A320neo. The CFM long-term capacity agreements cover only our own A320neo and NGSA volumes from 2035, with no exclusivity and nothing above our own ramp. The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

airbus.move: Orderly A320neo family transition: Alt plan confirmed at the 2035 gate
airbus.detail: At the 2035 gate the operating head found no supply crunch, engine slip or quality event, so the Alt plan stands on its conditions. The steps are a ceiling, never above today's rate. NGSA has first claim on resources. Through the entry-into-service years we build to customer demand, not to the ceiling, and suppliers get that schedule now. The plan still reverts to base before EIS on any trigger. Its cost is budgeted from NGSA entry into service. No rate number is published.
Continue working with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

airbus.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2030s
airbus.detail: Continue apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe to staff NGSA certification, entry into service and ramp from our own pipeline. The programme does no targeted hiring from any rival's team [AX-0073, A-0330].

cfm.move: RISE stays funded as a technology programme with Safran: ground, durability and dust testing continue; no product launch and no entry-into-service date
cfm.detail: H5: no cancel and no programme dividend [CX-0174, CX-0398]. RISE becomes a product when an airframer wants it [CX-0469, CX-0205]. Continuing it as technology with Safran is joint practice. RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP [CX-0162]. The one RISE allowance stays unused.

cfm.move: LEAP durability kits and supply-base work (FLIGHT DECK) continue ahead of any new programme
cfm.detail: Safety, quality, delivery, cost [CX-0658]. We fix the supply base we have before we load it [CX-0613, CX-0540].

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture commitment with Rolls-Royce, on stated terms
pratt_whitney.detail: Pratt & Whitney puts its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the public record. The terms: (1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces. (2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233]. (3) Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' is answered by equal shares, its own modules and the equal-share rule. It is never answered with P&W technology or with cash beyond our $2B share; any cash credit would return to Finance as a capital item. (4) On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward P&W's share, so the commitment needs no new spending. (5) If the Joint Venture forms, the first engine to enter service is GTF2's tested configuration. Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block, after its own durability proof. (6) No Joint Venture engine enters service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decision. No date is given for the Joint Venture.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 proposal to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus on standard terms; no launch-style discounts
pratt_whitney.detail: This answers Boeing's public invitation to all three engine makers. GTF2 is ready six years from its 2030 launch, in 2036. Its durability will be proven before entry into service, which Boeing has made a contract condition. The offer is on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The same terms apply on NGSA. A rival's price does not move the offer. Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF fleet durability: Hot Section kit sold through MRO at value; fleet spares ahead of new-engine hardware
pratt_whitney.detail: The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0100]. Fleet spares are allocated ahead of GTF2 test hardware and ahead of GTF2 OE when they compete for the same parts [PX-0080]. The kit has no effect on the game board.

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture commitment to Pratt & Whitney
rolls_royce.detail: Rolls-Royce has committed to the Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney. This replaces the round-1 wording 'we commit when our partner does'. The terms are standard and win-win: shared risk and shared investment, crediting the technology Rolls-Royce brings [RX-0072, RX-0118]. There is no concession to Pratt & Whitney or to any airframer. No Joint Venture date is disclosed. The folded UltraFan keeps its own test programme through to entry into service.

Rolls-Royce offers UltraFan for a future Boeing single-aisle on standard terms, with no launch discount. Durability will be proven before entry into service, as a contract condition. Support and MRO through partner shops will be in place before entry into service, sized for a second airframe. No dates are given and no new spend is committed [RX-0058, RX-0081, RX-0283].

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan through partner shops (live since the NGSA selection)
rolls_royce.detail: The plan is a partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team, all in place before entry into service [RX-0283, RX-0287]. If a Joint Venture forms, the partner's shops add capacity after entry into service and never replace this plan before it. No dates are disclosed.
No concessions to buy narrowbody or widebody share. Terms are win-win, value is remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097].

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan technology and Trent time-on-wing work continue
rolls_royce.detail: UltraFan development runs at the full pace inside a flat R&D envelope [RX-0214]. The durability and time-on-wing programme on the installed Trent fleet continues: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000, and life-limited part extensions [RX-0123]. No widebody programme is launched.

boeing.move: Staged fps business case for the 2045 round (authority-to-offer work)
boeing.detail: Solo by default, since Pope's IP test finds Embraer adds no IP or capacity. The base case is the 10-year ramp: on this grid it beats the 7-year by $2.48-2.75B in every column and has the higher worst column. Renton comes only with Pope's MAX bridge plan, with code 7 and with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system together with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before building at rate (no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]). The case must show the item value in every column against the Board's two lines (no worse than -$1B anywhere, and above +$1B in the expected column) and Malave's slip leg as the baseline. It also sets out the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule: a 2035 launch settles at a long-run 42% (10-year) or 45% (7-year); a 2045 launch settles at 35% (7-year, EIS 2052) or 32% (10-year, EIS 2055). Sequence it under H4 against any 787 Re-engine. No date. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

boeing.move: Keep 787 Re-engine readiness warm (study only, no launch)
boeing.detail: Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. The study covers engine durability, a supplier gate on new parts (rate breaks only when supplier output is there, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]) and a certification plan with the type certificate before building at rate. No programme spend is committed. Re-test it in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), and sequence it against a 2045 fps under H4: a same-round 10-year fps sits at the 2-year limit, and a 7-year fps breaches it.

boeing.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers through any demand dip
boeing.detail: If MAX deliveries run below the 57-a-month slots, keep trained people and redeploy them to fps production-system work and the 787 rather than shed and rehire. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible [BX-1243, B-2330], so supplier readiness is never why a 2045 programme slips. This is the way we used the strike and the 2019 delay to prepare [BX-1258, BX-1225].

Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board, with headroom kept for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year). Nothing is said publicly.

airbus.move: NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
airbus.detail: Runs through EIS and the ramp. It covers wing and production-system maturity, engine readiness (GTF2 with one year of margin, UltraFan NB with none), certification status, and the A320 run-down under the Alt plan. Any quality finding goes to the Board at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AG-0038].

airbus.move: Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review
airbus.detail: The Committee confirms that neither the CFM capacity agreements (own volumes, no exclusivity) nor the skills programme (own pipeline, no targeted hiring) can be read as a Delay Tactics move [A-0299, AG-0022, A-0331].

airbus.move: Audit Committee cash gate each budget cycle through 2037
airbus.detail: Toepfer re-tests the $5.2B line and brings any of three triggers to the Board as abnormal risk: an NGSA bill above about $36.4B, any Alt spend falling before 2037, or a rate below about $1.07 per EUR. Net cash is flagged: on his proxy it runs to about zero by end-2036. So we add no new shareholder return before 2037, and any buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter with the NGSA peak shown. There is no equity raise and no dividend cut [AX-0104, AX-0102, AG-0058, AG-0059].

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine prepared for the 2045 gate (internal)
airbus.detail: It stays on hold. At the 2045 gate it comes back with five things: its own grid and peak cash (about $1.0B a year with no NGSA overlap); A350F and Spirit A350 absorption shown complete on the record; a widebody engine committed in time for its EIS (UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5); NGSA in service with no open quality finding; and a rule-3 check on any Boeing 787 Re-engine. No timing is disclosed [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253].

airbus.move: No Joint Venture request to Pratt & Whitney or Rolls-Royce
airbus.detail: We place no airframer demand for a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture on the record. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source, which would cut NGSA from three sources to two. If one forms anyway, the operating head reports what it does to the fitted sources.

cfm.move: Answer Airbus's request for long-term capacity agreements (A320neo and NGSA from 2035) through CFM, together with Safran
cfm.detail: Product and supply only, on standard terms. No price, no concession and no number reaches Airbus before Safran agrees, because narrowbody price and capacity are joint decisions [CX-0184, CX-0160]. We plan on the A320neo Alt-plan steps as a ceiling at or below today's rate, with NGSA having first claim. Spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]. On intent there's no daylight with Airbus [CX-0200]. Platform and capacity talks stay private [CX-0586].

cfm.move: Answer Boeing's request to confirm the LEAP-1B allocation at today's rate (57 a month), through CFM, together with Safran
cfm.detail: Confirm the allocation at the rate Boeing builds today, with no rate step, once Safran agrees. That's 1,368 engines a year, the rate CFM delivered in 2030-2034 with no slip on the record (Ali). It's a backlog we share [CX-0197]. Product and supply only, standard terms, no number before Safran agrees [CX-0184]. We won't get ahead of Boeing or the FAA on any future rate step [CX-0307].

cfm.move: Product-only reply to Boeing's sourcing invitation for its future single-aisle
cfm.detail: Offer the new CFM engine (the Ducted), with a LEAP derivative as the minimum (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. We accept proven durability before entry into service as a contract condition: it's our own standard. No price, terms or concession; any commercial term goes to Safran first [CX-0184]. No ready year earlier than 2041, and 2041 is a floor, not a promise (Ali's date ground).

cfm.move: Ducted hot-section durability plan, owned cross-functionally
cfm.detail: The plan is owned by the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team, with Safran [CX-0633, CX-0012]. Hot-and-harsh and dust testing (turn on, turn off) runs before any date moves. HPT dust testing starts with development, as on the RISE compact core [CX-0222]. Safety-critical parts get enhanced inspection in new-make and MRO. The hot section is built from LEAP durability hardware and RISE compact-core work, not a clean sheet (inference) [CX-0162]. 2041 is a floor: if testing moves it, it moves later, never earlier, and we say so. Ali owns two evidence gaps: the LEAP-1B kit outcome (with Boeing and the FAA) and RISE results after October 2025 (with Safran). Any test or field failure goes to the cross-functional team before any date moves.

cfm.move: Ducted long-lead supplier orders gated on floor data; LEAP durability kits and LEAP deliveries stay first
cfm.detail: Engineering and test start at launch. Long-lead supplier orders for the Ducted wait until floor data shows margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages [CX-0613]. LEAP kits and the LEAP rate come ahead of the new programme. Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order [CX-0658]. Lean before capital [CX-0540, CX-0653]; this follows doctrine because Ali's floor record ends in 2025.

cfm.move: Partner Embraer: terms worked through CFM with Safran
cfm.detail: A CFM engine for a third airframer, so it serves every airframer and fits joint practice (Safran consent assumed; inference). No Embraer number goes to the market or to an airframer until terms are agreed with Safran (Ghai's condition) [CX-0184].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 durability programme and evidence to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Eddy brings the plan and the data as they exist to the committee: Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme) at representative severe-environment conditions [PX-0084], and every life-limited part at full life at entry into service. Configuration freeze: if a Joint Venture forms, GTF2's final-year testing and tested configuration are untouched, and interface work stays off the certification path. If the data are late, entry into service moves and the testing does not. Any testing overrun beyond the $2B returns to Finance as a capital item. Eddy's watch item stands: an order or statement that gives an EIS date, claims durability as proven or compresses testing triggers his ground-1 veto.

pratt_whitney.move: Annual GTF2 whole-programme NPV review for the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: First review, from Mitchill's memo. The booked figure against the board's status quo is +0.48 (engine value +2.48, R&D -2.00). Against Do Nothing (GTF2 never launched and P&W off NGSA's code 7) it is +14.50 / +0.15 / +19.86 / +14.50 across S1 to S4: +13.15 at Mitchill's weights and +14.41 at the Board's. Against a $2B buyback (PV 0 at the 10% WACC) the margins are the same. Nominal payback is in 2041. This is repeated every year, as UTC's board did with the GTF.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture withdraw test written into the 2045 round, and GTF2 capacity qualified before rate
pratt_whitney.detail: (1) The 2045 withdraw test, Mitchill's wording. Order withdraw if the 2045 brief's withdraw row is no worse than hold in every column weighted at 0.2 or more, or if its weighted value against hold is at least 0. Also withdraw if a condition of the commitment has lapsed: (a) GTF2's spend no longer counts toward our share; (b) the gear and core are not P&W modules; (c) no live airframe not yet in service carries a code that includes Rolls-Royce, and Rolls-Royce has not committed on the record; (d) a technology credit is asked for in cash or in P&W technology. If Rolls-Royce's terms demand a gear or core licence, data access, or Rolls-Royce content in the first configuration, Eddy proposes withdraw at the first legal round. (2) Capacity: the dip from 816 engines (2036) to 579 (2037) is the window to qualify GTF2 parts capacity before the climb to 976 (2044). The ramp waits for qualification.

rolls_royce.move: Readiness reporting to the Board (not public)
rolls_royce.detail:
Every round, Watson reports to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee:
- the UltraFan NB ready year (2037) against NGSA's 2037 entry into service;
- his gates: partner-shop agreements from the 2030 trigger year, capacity qualified by 2036, support live before the first entry into service.
Testing never bends to an airframer's date. If maturity slips, we tell Airbus early [R-0970]. Gearbox, casting and forging capacity is placed with high-performing suppliers for a ramp to about 1,040 narrowbody engines a year.

rolls_royce.move: Review of the standing Joint Venture commitment at the 2045 round (not public)
rolls_royce.detail:
At the 2045 round the ExCo brings the Board one of two things:
- the Joint Venture formation, with its grid row; or
- `jv_with_pw: withdraw`, ordered in that same sealed round, if the formation row is below hold or no live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine in time.
McCabe's rule applies: if a fold of a ready Solo charges our $4B share on top of the $8B already spent, the withdraw is a firm plan, not a review.

If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, we bring the Board the full row for the Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB. Only one of them, A350 first. From 2037 each carries its bill plus the $5B strain for good, within a $3B premium cap ($1B for UltraFan WB).

bulletin_notes: Round 2 (2035) adjudicated. Public events: Pratt & Whitney commits to the Joint Venture; Rolls-Royce commits to the Joint Venture; P&W GTF2 (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture; RR UltraFan NB (Solo) folded into the Joint Venture; P&W-RR Joint Venture NB engine launched in 2035; Joint Venture engine ready 2036 (inherits a folded solo programme's schedule); CFM ducted engine launched in 2035; CFM-Embraer partnership launched in 2035.

Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, treat CFM's concentrated sub-tier shortages as a watch item, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place. Any future step is gated one at a time on KPIs and FAA agreement.

other_moves.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers through any demand dip
other_moves.detail: If MAX deliveries run below the 57-a-month slots, keep trained people and redeploy them to fps production-system work and the 787 rather than shed and rehire. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible [BX-1243, B-2330], so supplier readiness is never why a 2045 programme slips. This is the way we used the strike and the 2019 delay to prepare [BX-1258, BX-1225].

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board, with headroom kept for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year). Nothing is said publicly.

boeing.public_statement:
Back in 2025 I said we were turning the ship but hadn't turned it. I think we've turned it now. The balance sheet is repaired and staying repaired. The 737 line has built at 57 a month to plan for five straight years. The 777X and the MAX family are delivering. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here, and the job now is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. We'll do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. We've looked hard at it with the data in front of us, and the case isn't there yet. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we do go, we build it at rate the right way. With new engines in development at Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and CFM always at the table, we expect to give our customers a choice of engine, with durability proven before entry into service. When we launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year either. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

On production, the 737 stays at 57 a month and stays stable. Any step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We're keeping our trained people and our suppliers ready. Going slow has let us go faster, and stability is what lets us move when the time comes.

Our dates will be set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see. This is the frame's lean, confirmed by both memos.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. Pope's KPI gate is clean and her veto is not invoked. No Rate Increase is on the menu. CFM's sub-tier shortages are a watch item, not a live problem.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1303]
   - Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress on every 10-year row.
   - Technology: ready by EIS. GTF2 is ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037, CFM always.
   - Market: not ready on this grid. No fps row beats Do Nothing in any column.
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's slip leg, S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01, line -3.01):
   - Pass: Do Nothing, the Re-engine and the four 10-year rows.
   - Fail (binding): every 7-year and via-Embraer row.
   This round S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so the leg works as a level test.
   Pope's priors are unpriced but point the same way: a clean-sheet +3 years puts a 10-year fps at 2048; a derivative +2 years puts the Re-engine at 2042.
4. Is this doing less, better? [BX-1239] Yes. Do Nothing beats every fps row by $1.20B or more in every column. The only plans within ε of it in S1 (10-year + Re-engine rows) have worst columns $3.51-3.88B lower.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding buffer veto strikes every 7-year and via-Embraer row. None was ordered.
- Pope's H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is honoured: not ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto: no object this round.
- I decided the rest. No overrides.

fps: HOLD
- The best row, 10-year at Renton, gives up $1.20 / $1.46 / $1.20 / $1.22B (S1 to S4).
- My debt-first test needs a plan more than ε ahead of Do Nothing in S1. It is $2.20B short. The Board's -$1B per-item line fails in every column.
- An objective premium of $1.20B (S1) would sit inside my $2B cap. I won't use it: it would carry an item that fails my own test and the Board's line. 50/50 is the company's mission, not on my ranked list.
- Pope's discounting check shows the narrowing from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20 is mostly five years of discounting (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26). The case has moved later; it has not got better.
- Cost of waiting, said plainly. There is no 2040 round, so the earliest fps EIS becomes 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year). Under the lead-edge rule the long-run share falls from 42-45% (a 2035 launch) to 32-35% (a 2045 launch).
- The grid assumes nobody moves later, so it cannot price a 2045 launch. Malave confirms nothing in the brief puts a dollar figure on it. It is information for the 2045 case, not a reason to launch now. Airbus's 2037 date does not set ours [B-2313, B-2315].
- Ramp and route for 2045: the 10-year ramp, Solo. The 7-year fails the buffer and stress debt at new sites. Via Embraer sits $10.95-11.47B behind Solo with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty, and Pope finds it adds no IP or capacity.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call)
- Item value: +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4; -1.63 in S3. It passes Malave's buffer by $2.01B and debt holds at $0. In my expected column it is the best plan.
- Three grounds move me to hold:
  (a) The Board will veto it under its -$1B per-item line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine: Airbus says 'A350 family', and RR is waiting with a widebody UltraFan for 'a Re-engine on the table'. I have no override against the Board. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
  (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], has updated his read on the evidence: from 40-50% to about 30% (25-35%). That puts the weighted edge at +$0.92B ($0.74-1.10B). At the centre that is inside ε, so the higher worst column decides: Do Nothing -2.47 against -4.10. He also notes the +2.01 is a ceiling: it assumes Airbus never re-engines later.
  (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low. A launch now is a one-way door, since the EIS is 2040 and there is no round before it (H5).
- I'm not hiding what the hold costs. Pope shows 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay takes about 9.5% off its value. A 2045 Re-engine would meet a 2045 fps at H4's limit, so this hold may in practice close the programme.
- The cost is logged separately, as a Board-downside hold and not against the cap: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4; $1.63B saved in S3; $0.92B weighted at 30%.
- My reading of Airbus's probability is Low confidence on my record. I relied on Malave's read and on company doctrine (profile §7, the A330neo precedent [B-2446]).

SITE, CODE, RATE
- fps_site: new_site. Renton is worth 0.00 without a launch, and the full $3.0B capex saving needs only a choice 3 years before EIS.
- Engine code: null with the hold. At launch it will be code 7: three sources, all ready by EIS, an allowed pair against NGSA. That is doctrine and my public requirement; I have no record as Boeing CEO on engine choice.
- rate_737: hold, the only value. The ceiling stays at 57.

HARD RULES AND RED LINES
- H1: the 2030 ruling stands and is not re-made.
- H3, first half: lifted in 2030. Second half: in force. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the 787 Re-engine stays open but is held.
- H4: respected, with no development in flight.
- H5: nothing to cancel.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: soft total $0.
- H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- My own red lines are all respected: no concurrency, no fixed-price development, no FAA blame, no attribution of supplier problems to Airbus.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): -1.01 / -0.02 / -2.47 / -1.01.
- No Board items: fps, re787 and fps_site are each at their default, so every item value is 0.00.
- Expected column: S1. Risk case S4 is -1.01: 0.00 against Do Nothing, with $2.00B of headroom over -3.01. Buffer: pass.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547], and net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060. The grid holds the fps back, not the cash.
- Pope's gates: KPI clean; zero strain; engines ready by any EIS; no concurrency; Renton not chosen, with a bridge plan drafted for 2045.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine is logged as a Board-downside hold.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- the A350 probability (via Malave);
- engine code 7;
- the Renton bridge plan;
- the slip priors.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input on the Re-engine, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer: accepted to the cent. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows are struck. The 10-year rows pass, but at new sites with only $0.39B of headroom.
- Net debt: accepted from the metrics table. The debt penalty is already netted and not subtracted again.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass, accepted.
- Cash timing: accepted. The 10-year peaks at $8.44B in 2041, 92% of stress free cash flow. In cash, a same-round Re-engine falls entirely inside the fps spend.
- What moved me: his updated A350 read of about 30%, which he moved down on two of his own 2030 triggers. It puts the weighted edge just inside ε, so the higher worst column decides. That supports the Board's line rather than standing in for it.
- I log his offer: he would support the Re-engine on evidence that puts the A350 chance below 28%. That is the trigger to carry forward.
- His point that +2.01 is an undiscounted ceiling (it assumes no later A350 move) is noted.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I took her memo as gates and facts, not judgement.
- Accepted: the KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object; the 737 ceiling stays at 57. Strain is zero on the hold; a 2035 10-year + Re-engine pair sits at H4's limit, and a 7-year pair breaches it. Engines for code 7 are ready 5-9 years before EIS. Via Embraer fails the partner test. Re-engine readiness passes on the GEnx upgrade.
- Two of her findings sharpened the rationale. Her discounting check (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26) shows the fps case has moved later, not improved. And 2035 is the only zero-strain Re-engine slot against a 2045 fps, so I've said plainly that the hold may close it.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan and her 2045 readiness plan (workforce through the dip, fragile suppliers, production system proven at rate, one KPI-gated ask at a time) go into the other moves.
- Her statement that operations does not hold the Re-engine back is accepted. The hold rests on the market column S3 and the Board's line, not on readiness.

boeing.expected_scenario:
S1: rivals hold. Airbus keeps its Alt plan; per the bulletin it reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event, and none is on the record. No A350 Re-engine.
- S2 (Airbus back on its base plan) is the upside.
- S3 (an A350 Re-engine, about 30% on Malave's read) is the plausible downside.
- S4 (Delay Tactics) is the risk case. It equals S1 on every hold row.
The column values our plan; it does not set our dates [B-2313].
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (+1.00). I chose fps: hold + 787: hold (-1.01), $2.01B below it. That is a Board-downside hold: the Board's -$1B per-item line binds while S3 (-1.63) is not ruled out, and I have no override. It is logged separately and not against the cap. Weighted at Malave's 30% read of an A350 Re-engine, the gap is $0.92B, inside ε, where the higher worst column (-2.47 against -4.10) decides.
boeing.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0. Objective premium: $0.
- fps hold: no premium, because the grid prefers it. The best fps row (10-year at Renton) sits $1.20B below Do Nothing in S1 and $1.46B below in S2. Launching it for 50/50, incumbency or the engine enabler would be an objective premium of $1.20B. That is inside the cap, but it fails my debt-first test and the Board's -$1B line, so it is not taken.
- 787 Re-engine hold: a known cost, logged separately as a Board-downside hold, as the Board asked. It gives up $2.01B in S1, S2 and S4 and saves $1.63B in S3. Weighted at Malave's 30% (25-35%), the cost is $0.92B ($0.74-1.10B).
- What breaks the number: if the A350 does not re-engine, the hold gives up the full $2.01B. If it does, the hold saves $1.63B, and H3 closes the 787 Re-engine for good.
boeing.objective_note:
The objectives never change the payoff.
- Hold the 50/50 split: unmet on every hold plan. Preference share falls to 37% at NGSA's 2037 EIS and 20% from 2043. Not chased: the premium needed would breach the Board's line and my own debt-first test.
- Defend incumbency: unmet (worst year 20%). Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45 and recovers to 36.3% from 2047, when Airbus's capacity binds. This is the long-cycle stake the 2045 fps case must answer. Waiting costs share: 42-45% for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch. The grid does not price it.
- Balance sheet, repair and keep repaired (base and stress): met. Net debt is $0 from 2029 through 2050.
- Engine enabler, three makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, RR).
- Engine enabler, two or three sources on our narrowbody: unmet, since the MAX flies CFM only. It is answered at launch by code 7 and by the public, dateless engine-sourcing requirement.
boeing.predictions:
AIRBUS
- NGSA enters service in 2037 on schedule, and Airbus keeps the Alt plan (S1).
- An A350 Re-engine this round is about 30% (Malave's read). Airbus's engineering is on NGSA first, but its 'A350 family' wording and RR's waiting widebody UltraFan keep it open.
- No Delay Tactics effect: with no fps they would be 'naked' and draw a $48.32B fine, and S4 equals S1 on our hold.

ENGINE MAKERS

- CFM keeps the LEAP-1B on the MAX.
- No widebody UltraFan, since no Re-engine is on the table.

OUR RESULTS IF NOBODY MOVES AGAIN
- ΔPV: -1.01 (S1), -0.02 (S2), -2.47 (S3), -1.01 (S4).
- Net debt $0 in base and stress at every check year.
- NB preference share 37% in 2037 and 20% from 2043.

2045

- Re-test the 787 Re-engine only if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced under H4.

board_response.recommendation: Do not let Airbus set our dates; neither a launch nor a hold cites NGSA's EIS, the Alt-plan gate or any A350 move as its reason.
board_response.response: Taken. The fps hold rests on our own grid: no row beats Do Nothing, and the debt-first test fails. The public statement says our dates are set by our own readiness. The Re-engine hold rests on your downside line and on the market column S3, read from the bulletin, not on Airbus's timing. The expected column values the plan; it does not set our dates.

priorities: Safety and production readiness first. We approve no launch without Pope's KPI, engineering-capacity, supplier and strain results. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or certification problem, and the 737 holds at 57 a month. Her memo must still say so. If Renton is proposed, it must come with a MAX bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp [BG-0043, BG-0025, B-2236, BG-0069].

Proof before commitment on the fps: one well-founded launch, not a bet. This grid still gives no fps launch a business case. The best is launch_10yr at Renton with re787 hold. Its item value is -1.20 / -1.46 / -1.20 / -1.22 (S1-S4): $0.20B short of our -$1B line in its best column, and at least $2.20B short of the +$1B business-case line. One development at a time, and the 787 Re-engine on its downside. On its own it is worth +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4 but -1.63 in S3, an A350 Re-engine that the bulletin does not rule out. It breaches our -$1B line again, so it waits, logged as a Board-downside hold. With a 7-year fps it would also overlap by 5 years [BG-0066, B-2167, BG-0022].

board_guidance.risk_appetite: 4.5 of 5, unchanged since 2030. No Board item may lose more than $1B against its default in any plausible column, and all four columns count: the bulletin rules out no A350 Re-engine, and Delay Tactics are covert. The plan must sit within $2B of Do Nothing in the risk case S4 (line -3.01). At horizon 3 the fps gets no extra downside allowance for its long-term position. The balance sheet is repaired on the brief, so this round the binding limit is the per-item downside line, not the rating.

recommendations.text: Hold the fps this round and give no fps date in the public statement. Keep the staged case (authority to offer first) for 2045: the 10-year ramp, Renton with a MAX bridge plan, and the item value in every column against our two lines (no worse than -$1B anywhere, and above +$1B in the expected column). The case has narrowed: the best fps item value was -2.08 in 2030 and is -1.20 now. For 2045, also set out what waiting costs under the public lead-edge rule. A 10-year fps launched in 2035 settles at a long-run 42% share. Launched in 2045, it settles at 35% (7-year) or 32% (10-year). That is information for the 2045 decision, not a reason to launch now: at horizon 3 we grant the fps no extra downside.

The objectives (50/50 split, incumbency, the dual-source engine enabler) are unmet on every hold plan, and Do Nothing's preference share falls to 20% from 2043. Log any objective premium with its reason against the $2B cap. Note that our -$1B per-item line binds first: a 10-year fps brought on a $1.20-1.46B objective premium would draw our veto. We acknowledge the long-cycle stake. It must be answered with a case that clears our tests.

787 Re-engine: hold it, and log its known cost separately as a Board-downside hold, not against the cap. The hold gives up $2.01B in S1, S2 and S4 and saves $1.63B in S3. Its edge has narrowed since 2030 (+3.30 / -2.48 then, +2.01 / -1.63 now). Re-test it in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), and sequence it against the fps under H4: a same-round 10-year fps overlaps it by 2 years (the limit) and a 7-year fps by 5. We will approve it on a grid where its worst plausible column is at or above -$1B.

Show the submitted plan's risk-case column S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01; line -3.01), with Malave's buffer number, his 'Fundable when the 777X turns' result and the base and stress net-debt line from the brief's metrics table. The grid already nets the debt penalty, so do not subtract it again.

Pope's memo is our production and safety test. It should state the KPI gate (no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem in the brief), engineering capacity, supplier readiness and two-front strain for any launch. If Renton is chosen, it should give the MAX bridge plan so the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp, and confirm there is no production-certification concurrency.

Engines: keep the public engine-sourcing requirement dateless, with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. At any launch, name a code whose makers are ready by EIS. On the record, code 7 gives three sources (CFM, plus GTF2 ready 2036 and UltraFan NB ready 2037), and it is an allowed pair against NGSA's code 7.

Cash: net debt has been $0 since 2029, and base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board. Keep headroom for the staged fps: $60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year. Make no dividend or buyback signal in the public statement.

Do not let Airbus set our dates. NGSA's EIS in 2037, its Alt-plan gate and any A350 move are read from the bulletin only. Neither a launch nor a hold should cite them as its reason; decide on our market, technology and balance-sheet readiness.

frame.question:
2035 is our last decision year before 2045, because there is no 2040 round. NGSA is in development for a 2037 EIS, and the new engines are on the record: GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, and CFM is always available. The balance sheet is repaired and the KPIs are stable. So is this the round to start the next airplane, the 787 Re-engine, both, or neither?

On this grid no fps row beats Do Nothing in any column. The best one, the 10-year ramp at Renton, is $1.20-1.46B behind. The Re-engine is worth +$2.01B in three columns and -$1.63B if Airbus re-engines the A350.

frame.situation:
Round 2, decision year 2035. We launched nothing in 2030. We are on today's products: the 737 MAX at 57 a month (684 a year) and the 787.

**Public record**
- Airbus launched NGSA in 2030 for an EIS in 2037, with engine code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR).
- Airbus is on its Alt plan: A320 lines kept longer through the NGSA ramp. The plan is re-checked at the 2035 gate and reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. None of the three is on the record.
- P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037) launched on NGSA's selection. The GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- No A350 Re-engine has been launched, so H3's second half has not closed the 787 Re-engine.
- Airbus says its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. RR says there will be no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. Both are signals, not a rule-out.

**Market on Do Nothing**
- Delivered share was 40.1% in 2030-34. Our firm backlog was all delivered by 2033. The waiting backlog falls from 1,319 (2033) to 763 (2035) and reaches zero by 2038.
- From NGSA's EIS, our preference share falls 3 pp a year: 37% in 2037, and 20% from 2043.
- Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45. It recovers to 36.3% from 2047, because Airbus's capacity of about 1,200 a year binds and its flexible customers take our free slots.
- That is why Do Nothing loses only $1.01B in S1: narrowbody operating profit is -3.64, offset by +2.63 from supply and demand.

**Balance sheet**
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and stays there to 2060 in both base and stress.
- Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year. On Do Nothing, profit runs $0.13-0.78B a year below the game baseline in 2037-45.
- How the surplus is used is the Board's decision.

**Objectives**
- Balance-sheet lines: all met.
- 50/50 split and incumbency: not met (worst year 20%).
- Engine enabler: three narrowbody makers in the market in 2045 and 2050 is met. Two or three sources on our own narrowbody is not met (the MAX flies CFM only). Every 10-year Solo row shows 3 sources in 2050.

**KPIs.** The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The MAX delivered to plan. The Rate Increase is not on the menu (it was a 2030-only order).

**Item values against Do Nothing (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)**
- 787 Re-engine alone: +2.01 / +2.01 / -1.63 / +2.01. In 2030 it was +3.30 / -2.48, so its edge is narrowing.
- fps 10-year at Renton: -1.20 / -1.46 / -1.20 / -1.22. At new sites: -1.58 / -1.82 / -1.58 / -1.61.
- fps 7-year: -3.68 to -4.48.
- fps via Embraer, hold rows: -12.16 to -12.78.
- Renton adds +0.36 to +0.39 on the 10-year ramp and +0.42 to +0.58 on the 7-year, and only alongside a launch.
- Best plan by column: the Re-engine alone in S1, S2 and S4 (+1.00, +1.99, +1.00); Do Nothing in S3 (-2.47).

**Board guidance.** It does not bind, but its veto binds after my decision.
- It would veto every fps launch. The 10-year fails its -$1B per-item line in every column and its +$1B business-case test. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows also fail Malave's buffer.
- It would veto the 787 Re-engine: S3 at -1.63 breaks its -$1B line, and the bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine.
- It would approve a hold on both, and new_site. It would take Renton only with a launch it approves and a MAX bridge plan, and it wants code 7 at any launch.
- It wants to see:
  - S4 against Do Nothing;
  - Malave's buffer and 'Fundable when the 777X turns' results;
  - net debt in base and stress;
  - Pope's gates;
  - H3's second half confirmed;
  - every premium logged;
  - the cost of waiting set out for 2045.

These are Board risks for our package, not red lines.
levers_in_play: fps: hold / launch_7yr / launch_10yr / launch_via_embraer. The 7-year enters service in 2042 at $65.00B. The 10-year enters service in 2045 at $60.32B. Via Embraer enters service in 2045 at $100B on our board. There is no 2040 round: a hold means the next chance is 2045, with EIS in 2052 or 2055.

- Renton avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex, in full if chosen at least three years before EIS.
- It is worth +0.36 to +0.39 on the 10-year ramp and +0.42 to +0.58 on the 7-year, and only alongside a launch.
- It winds down Renton's three MAX lines (47 of the 57 a month) as the fps ramps. Only the Everett North Line carries on, at up to 15 a month.

(7,7) is an allowed pair against NGSA. It does not change our payoff; it decides the engine enabler. This is an inference with Low confidence, since I have no statement as Boeing CEO on engine choice. Code 7 keeps CFM, and it is what we told the market in 2030.

- The 10-year ramp beats the 7-year by $2.48-2.75B in every column.

F. Rows to close, not to choose: fps launch_via_embraer.
- Item value: -12.16 to -13.96.
- It sits $10.95-11.47B below the Solo 10-year in every column.
- Buffer: fails. S4 runs -12.36 to -13.58.
- Undiscounted debt penalty: $52.5B. Stress-case net debt fails in most rows.
red_lines: H1 (no fps in Round 1): I lifted it in my 2030 ruling because its grounds had lapsed. The 777X is delivering, the MAX 7/10 are certified and net debt has been $0 since 2029 [BX-0550, BX-0547, BX-1305]. The Board does not need the ruling again, and none is made.

H3, first half: lifted in 2030. H3, second half, stays in force: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. That is not on the record, so the Re-engine is still open this round. If the A350 re-engines this round, it closes for good.

H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus, and none under a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. No rate order is possible this round.

Mine: no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments [BX-1247, B-2326]. Both conditions are met (my 2030 ruling), so this is not a bar this round.

frame.asks_cfo:
Jay, you're my independent check on these estimates [BX-1316]. Run the buffer test as the baseline, not as a sensitivity [BX-0553].

1. **Buffer test.** Compare risk case S4 with Do Nothing (-1.01); the line is -3.01. My read:
   - Pass: Do Nothing -1.01; Re-engine +1.00; 10-year -2.62; 10-year at Renton -2.23; 10-year + Re-engine -1.28; 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -0.90.
   - Fail: every 7-year row (-4.02 to -5.37; 7-year at Renton + Re-engine sits 3.01 below Do Nothing, past the $2B line) and every via-Embraer row (-12.36 to -13.58).
   Confirm or correct.

2. **The Re-engine.** It is +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4, and -1.63 in S3. Weighted at p, the chance of an A350 Re-engine this round, its edge is 2.01 - 3.64p: above zero below p = 55%, above ε below p = 28%.
   - Your 2030 read was 40-50%, from doctrine. You said you would change it on a sign that Airbus was putting its engineering into NGSA first, or that Airbus or RR were moving away from a widebody engine.
   - The bulletin now shows:
     - NGSA in development to 2037;
     - Airbus saying its widebody focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F;
     - RR saying no widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table;
     - no A350 Re-engine in 2030, although doctrine expected an early one.
   - Give me your updated p. Say whether anything rules S3 out; unless something does, the Board's line binds.
   - Tell me what waiting costs:
     - the edge fell from +3.30 to +2.01 in five years;
     - a 2045 Re-engine would enter service in 2050;
     - H3 closes it for good if the A350 moves first;
     - a 2045 fps would put it up against H4.

3. **Debt.** The grid already nets the debt penalty, so don't subtract it again. Undiscounted, for scale only: 10-year fps $19.1B, 7-year $22.0B, via Embraer $52.5B, Re-engine $0.6B. Confirm from the metrics table:
   - Do Nothing, the Re-engine and every 10-year row hold at $0 in base and stress;
   - stress fails on the 7-year new-site rows ($0.6-0.8B), the 7-year + Re-engine rows ($2.2-3.5B) and most via-Embraer rows.

4. **Cash timing of each bill.**
   - 10-year fps: $60.32B over 2035-45, booked in 2045. Year 1 at 5% is about $3.0B; the peak at 14% is about $8.4B around year 7, roughly 61% of base free cash flow.
   - 7-year fps: $65.00B over 2035-42.
   - Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, booked in 2040.
   - Strain, undiscounted: $1.2B for 10-year + Re-engine, $3.0B for 7-year + Re-engine.
   - Renton avoids about $3.0B of capex.
   Do any two bills land together?

5. **'Fundable when the 777X turns'.** Confirm the result: the 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547], and net debt is $0.

6. **Expected column.** I lean S1. Airbus's Alt plan reverts only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event, and none is on the record. S2 is the upside, S3 the plausible downside and S4 the risk case. Confirm or correct.

7. **Cost of waiting on the fps.** There is no 2040 round. Under the public lead-edge rule, a 2035 launch settles at a long-run 42% (10-year, EIS 2045) or 45% (7-year, EIS 2042). A 2045 launch settles at 35% (7-year) or 32% (10-year). The grid assumes nobody moves after this round, so it cannot price a 2045 launch. Tell me whether anything in the brief puts a dollar figure on it. If nothing does, it is information for 2045, not a reason to launch now.

8. **Premiums.** If we hold the fps: launching the 10-year at Renton anyway would need an objective premium of $1.20B in S1 ($1.46B in S2). That is inside my $2B cap, but it fails both the Board's -$1B line and my own debt-first test. If you favour holding the Re-engine, tell me whether that is a soft premium or a Board-downside hold to log separately.

The Re-engine passes my buffer. This is advice, not a veto.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
787 Re-engine: I would back re787: launch if the public record gives me grounds to put the chance of an A350 Re-engine this round below about 28%, so that its edge (2.01 - 3.64p) clears ε. Examples:
- Airbus commits its widebody engineering to the A350F and NGSA with no new engine;
- RR turns to a Trent upgrade rather than holding UltraFan WB for a re-engine;
- the Board accepts that S3 is not plausible, or relaxes its -$1B per-item line for a derivative carrying a $0.6B penalty.
It already clears my buffer by $2.01B, and a 2035 start clears any 2045 fps window, so in that case I would support it, not merely concur. An A350 Re-engine on the record closes it for good (H3).

fps: I would back a launch on any row that sits within $2B of Do Nothing in S4 and more than ε above it in the expected column. There is none on this grid. In 2045 I would take whichever ramp passes the slip leg with the higher worst column.

Balance sheet: if the chosen row's stress-case net debt rose above $0, I would hold whatever drives it.

A live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem would only confirm hold.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the buffer as the baseline: S4 no worse than -3.01, $2B under Do Nothing's -1.01. Your list is right. Every 7-year and via-Embraer row fails, $1.01B to $10.57B past the line, and that veto binds. One note: S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so this round the slip leg is really a level test.

fps: the 10-year rows clear my buffer, but none beats Do Nothing in any column; the best, at Renton, gives up $1.20-1.46B. It is fundable: the 777X turned in 2029 and net debt holds at zero in base and stress. The grid holds it back, not the cash. Nothing in the brief prices a 2045 launch, and the one dollar trend on record runs the other way: -2.08 in 2030, -1.20 now.

787 Re-engine: it clears my buffer by $2.01B and debt stays at zero, so no veto. The signals I named in 2030 have partly come in: Airbus's engineering goes to NGSA first, its widebody focus to the A350 and A350F. RR is waiting, not walking away, and nothing rules S3 out. My read moves from 40-50% to about 30%. That puts the edge at +$0.92B, just inside ε, where I take the higher worst column: -2.47 over -4.10. And the +2.01 holds only barring a later A350 Re-engine too.

So, Do Nothing: a higher confidence plan. Log the Re-engine as a Board-downside hold: $2.01B given up, $1.63B saved in S3. We're bullish on 2045.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record [BX-1331], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S4 (Airbus Delay Tactics) against the nominal S1 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. The doctrine slip priors are not priced on the board.
tests.numbers: MAX: 684 a year (57 a month) delivered exactly to the public plan in 2030-34. Risk case S4 against S1: Do Nothing -1.01 / -1.01 and the Re-engine alone +1.00 / +1.00. 100% of their value survives Delay Tactics, which act only from fps EIS. The fps rows lose little to S4: 10-year 0.02-0.03, 7-year 0.10-0.26, via Embraer 0.02-0.03. The board prices no slip. Sensitivity (inference: discounting at the 10.5% WACC only, with no cost overrun): each year of later EIS takes about 9.5% off a programme's value. The Re-engine's fall from +3.30 (2030 grid, EIS 2035) to +2.01 (EIS 2040) is five years of discounting: 3.30 / 1.105^5 = 2.00. On the derivative slip prior (+2 years, range +1 to +4; doctrine), a 2035 Re-engine loses about $0.36B (to +1.65), or $0.66B at +4 years (to +1.35). It stays positive in S1, S2 and S4. fps, on the clean-sheet prior (+3 years, range +2 to +5): the 7-year's nominal 2042 becomes 2045 central, so it has no headroom; the 10-year's 2045 becomes 2048. The best fps item narrowed from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20, and -2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26, so the narrowing is mostly discounting: the case has moved later, not improved (inference).

tests.name: KPI gate (doctrine; my veto) - answers the CEO's ask 1
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month or less, at least 6 months apart, after 2-3 stable months, each agreed with the FAA. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no live quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem. The MAX delivered 684 a year in each of 2030-34, exactly the public plan of 57 a month. No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), so my veto has nothing to act on and is not invoked. Watch item, not a live problem: CFM's public note that 80% of its shortages came from 9 suppliers at 15 sites bears on the LEAP-1B, our sole MAX engine. Our line has not felt it. On Do Nothing the MAX runs below its 684 slots from 2037: 552 (81%), then 409-468 a year in 2038-42 (60-68%, about 34-39 a month), 521 in 2045, 618 in 2046 and 684 in 2047. The climb from about 43 to 57 a month in 2045-47 (+8, then +5.5 a month in a year) fits doctrine pacing of at most +10 a month a year. Each step will still need stable KPIs and FAA agreement in 2045-47, which the board does not model (inference).

tests.name: Two-front strain / engineering capacity (doctrine) - answers ask 2
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps window EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine window EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (both on hold): 0 years, $0, and no development in flight.

A 2035 Re-engine (window 2035-40):
- with a 2035 10-year fps (2038-45): 2 years, $1.2B, at the limit with no slack;
- with a 2035 7-year fps (2035-42): 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach.

On the board the Re-engine item falls from +2.01 alone to +1.33/+1.34 beside a 10-year fps in S1, S2 and S4, and to -2.30/-2.31 in S3. That is $0.68B for the overlap: strain plus the steeper debt penalty. On the derivative slip prior (+2 years, EIS 2042), the real overlap with a 10-year fps is 4 years ($2.4B at the board's rate), past H4.

Sequencing:
- A 2035 Re-engine clears any 2045 fps (7-year 2045-52, 10-year 2048-55) by 0 years.
- A Re-engine held to 2045 (2045-50) meets a 2045 fps at 2 years (10-year, the limit) or 5 years (7-year, a breach).
- A 2050 Re-engine (2050-55) meets a 2045 7-year by 2 years and a 10-year by 5.

So 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year (inference)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the workforce and suppliers in the brief? State the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers:
No fps this round.

A 2035 launch:
- 7-year: EIS 2042, central 2045 on the clean-sheet prior (+3, range +2 to +5);
- 10-year: EIS 2045, central 2048.

Stress-case net debt:

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP (record [BX-1330, BX-1333], applied to airplanes by inference) - answers ask 4
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds IP or capacity Boeing lacks, within $1B of Solo.

tests.name: Engine and supplier readiness (doctrine; supplier readiness is a hard gate) - answers ask 3
tests.threshold: Each named engine maker ready by EIS, with durability proven before EIS. Supplier output meets the rate before each rate break. A sole source is a risk to reduce.
tests.numbers:
The engine code is null with the hold.

At a launch, code 7:
- GTF2 ready 2036 and UltraFan NB ready 2037 (public record), and CFM always available;
- that is 5-9 years of margin before a 2042 or 2045 EIS, and 15-19 years before a 2052 or 2055 EIS from a 2045 launch;

Code 7 cuts our single-source exposure. Today 100% of MAX engines are CFM: LEAP-1B, about 1,368 engines a year at 684 aircraft. CFM also serves the A320neo (kept longer on Airbus's Alt plan) and NGSA. Durability proven before EIS should be a contract condition [BX-1298].

Re-engine:
