tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2035 launch, EIS 2040 (doctrine) - answers ask 6
tests.threshold: Engineering free, Charleston capacity, engine maker and durability, supplier gate, and the type certificate before building at rate (no production-certification concurrency).
tests.numbers:
My 2030 results are re-confirmed:
- Engineering: nothing is in development, so a 2035 launch is the one development.
- Charleston: the footprint covers 787 rates in the teens. The 787 builds 100 a year (8.3 a month). A lone Re-engine, gaining 1 pp a year from 58.8%, reaches about 108 a year (9.0 a month) in 2045, 134 (11.2) in 2060 and 145 (12.0) at the 85% cap, all inside the teens.
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- Supplier gate on new parts: a condition at the rate break.
- Certification: the type certificate comes before building at rate.
- Central EIS on the derivative prior: 2042.

H3's second half has not closed it: no A350 Re-engine is on the record. Operations does not hold the Re-engine back. Its open question is the market column S3 (-1.63), and that is not an operations test.

tests.name: Renton or new site, with the MAX bridge plan (inference) - answers ask 5
tests.threshold: Renton only alongside a launch, with a MAX bridge plan so that the Renton wind-down follows the fps's actual ramp; otherwise new_site.
tests.numbers:
With the fps on hold, Renton changes nothing (item value 0.00), so keep new_site. There is no reason to set it before a launch: the site can change in any round before EIS, and the full ~$3.0B capex saving needs only a choice at least 3 years before EIS. Alongside a launch Renton is worth +0.36 to +0.39 (10-year) or +0.42 to +0.58 (7-year).

The risk it carries: Renton's three lines are 47 of the 57 a month. If the fps slips (clean-sheet prior +3 years) after Renton is converted, the MAX falls to the Everett North Line, at up to 15 a month (180 a year). That is a gap of up to 504 aircraft a year against 684.

Bridge plan, when Renton is chosen:
1. No Renton line converts before the fps type certificate (no concurrency).
2. Each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps line has held its rate for 2-3 stable months on KPIs.
3. One Renton MAX line stays warm until the fps reaches about 50 a month, about 4 years after EIS.
4. The LEAP-1B allocation and MAX suppliers are sized to the actual wind-down, not the planned one.
5. The Everett North Line carries the MAX tail, at up to 15 a month.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand (inference, one remark [BX-1329])
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column; otherwise not applicable.
tests.numbers:
There are no Rate Increase rows on this grid (it was a 2030-only order). Demand for more MAX capacity is not visible:
- the waiting backlog falls from 763 (2035) to 419 (2036) and 138 (2037), and is 0 from 2038;
- deliveries run 132-275 a year below the 684 slots in 2037-46.

Read the other way, the test says: add no MAX capacity, and keep 57 a month as the ceiling. Charleston already covers a Re-engine's widebody demand (above).

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record [BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326], applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option: when the bill lands, and what it does to cash and net debt, as numbers rather than adjectives.
tests.numbers:
Base free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in stress).

- Do Nothing: no bill. Profit runs $0.13-0.78B a year below the game baseline in 2037-45. Net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060.
- Re-engine: $5B over 2035-40, about $1.0B a year (7% of base free cash flow, 11% of stress), booked in 2040, with a $0.6B undiscounted debt penalty. It returns about $400M of PV per $1B of bill in S1, S2 and S4, and costs about $330M per $1B in S3. Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2035-45. Year 1 is about $3.0B (22% of base free cash flow); the peak is about $8.4B in year 7 (61% of base, 92% of stress). It costs $20M (Renton) to $26M (new site) of PV per $1B. Net debt $0 in base and stress.
- 10-year fps with the Re-engine: the two bills land together in 2035-40, plus $1.2B of strain over the 2 overlap years. That is roughly $8-9.5B a year at the 2038-40 peak, about 60-70% of base free cash flow (inference from the standard curve). Net debt is still $0.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2035-42, about $9.3B a year (67% of base, 101% of stress). It costs $57M of PV per $1B at Renton. Stress fails at new sites ($0.6-0.8B).
- Via Embraer: a peak of about $14.0B (102% of base, 152% of stress). It costs $122M of PV per $1B. Stress fails in 14 of 16 cells.

Renton avoids ~$3.0B of capex, and only with a launch.

tests.name: 2045 readiness: workforce, production system, supplier base, Renton bridge (doctrine and inference) - answers ask 7
tests.threshold: What has to happen over 2035-45 so that a 2045 launch is ready on day one, the way the strike and the 2019 delay were used to prepare?
tests.numbers:
There is no order this round; this is the plan.

1. Workforce: on Do Nothing the MAX dip (409-468 a year in 2038-42 against 684 slots) idles about a third of MAX capacity. Keep the trained workforce and redeploy it to fps production-system work and the 787, rather than shed it and rehire for 2045. The board does not price this (inference).
2. Production system: design the fps line with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before building at rate.
3. Supplier base: fund fragile suppliers through the dip. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation at 57 a month for the 2045-47 climb back. Hold engine proposals from all three makers, with durability proven before EIS, and plan on code 7.
4. Renton bridge: written by 2045 and decided with the launch, as above.
5. Sequencing: the 2045-47 MAX climb from about 43 to 57 a month and any 2045 fps launch land together. Plan one KPI-gated ask at a time.
6. If the Re-engine is still held in 2045, it meets that fps under H4 (2 years with a 10-year fps, 5 with a 7-year).

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase (KPI veto NOT invoked)
vetoes.ground: No Rate Increase is on the menu (it was a 2030-only order), and the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem: the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. The KPI doctrine therefore has neither a ground nor an object this round. It would bind against any future rate step ordered while such a problem is live. The 2045-47 climb back to 57 a month should be gated step by step on KPIs and the supply of LEAP-1B engines.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto: 5 years of overlap (fps 2035-42, Re-engine 2035-40) and $3.0B of strain undiscounted, past the 2-year limit. The CEO must strike it. The same breach applies in 2045 to a 7-year fps launched in the same round as a held Re-engine.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_10yr with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: H4 advice, not a breach on the board: 2 years of overlap (2038-40) and $1.2B of strain, at the limit with no slack. On the +2-year derivative slip prior the real overlap is 4 years. Next to the fps, the Re-engine item falls from +2.01 to +1.33 (S1). The row sits $1.88-2.13B below the Re-engine alone in every column and $3.51B below Do Nothing in S3.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: IP advice, not binding: on the board the partner brings no IP, capacity or strain relief. It has the same EIS as the Solo 10-year, sits $10.95-11.47B below it in every column and carries a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty. Stress-case net debt fails in 14 of 16 cells.

vetoes.plan: fps_site: renton without a launch, or with a launch but no MAX bridge plan
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding. Without a launch Renton changes nothing (0.00). With a launch it needs the bridge plan in my memo: an fps slip after conversion leaves the MAX on the Everett North Line at up to 180 a year, a gap of up to 504 aircraft a year against 684.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
KPI gate: if a quality escape, FAA scrutiny or supply-chain shortfall were reported before the orders are sealed, the gate would fail. That includes CFM's concentrated LEAP shortages reaching our line, or a LEAP-1B allocation short of 57 a month. My veto would then bind on any rate step, and I would also fail the Re-engine's supplier gate.

787 Re-engine: I would recommend launch, with operations ready for a 2035 launch and a 2040 EIS, if Malave's updated read puts the chance of an A350 Re-engine well below 28% on the bulletin's evidence and the Board accepts that S3 is not plausible this round. Two things support that: 2035 is the only zero-strain slot against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay costs about 9.5% of its value. I would move further against it on evidence of a shortfall on its new parts, a GEnx-upgrade durability gap at EIS, or a certification plan that needs production-certification concurrency.

fps: I would back a launch only on a grid where the Solo 10-year clears the Board's lines. Even then I would back only the 10-year ramp (it has headroom for the +3-year clean-sheet prior), with code 7, durability before EIS and a Renton bridge plan.

Via Embraer: only if a partner brought IP or capacity Boeing lacks at a cost within $1B of Solo. On this grid it is $10.95B or more short.
ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes, so the KPI, supplier and strain gates run on operations doctrine, marked as such.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery (record, applied by inference). The MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, so the KPI gate is clean (doctrine). No Rate Increase is on the menu; my veto has nothing to act on. The real job is the dip: on Do Nothing, MAX deliveries fall to 409-468 a year in 2038-42, 60-68% of our slots, and climb back to 684 by 2047. We hold the trained workforce and fund fragile suppliers through it.

Second, engineering capacity (doctrine). Holding both: zero strain. A 2035 Re-engine clears any 2045 fps by zero years. Held to 2045, it meets that fps at H4's 2-year limit, or breaks it with a 7-year ramp. Beside a 10-year fps today it sits at the limit and its value falls from +2.01 to +1.33.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth (record). Every $1B of Re-engine bill returns about $400 million in three columns and costs about $330 million in S3. Each year of later entry takes 9.5% off its value: +3.30 became +2.01 on five years of discounting alone. Embraer brings no IP or capacity we lack, at $10.95-11.47B more than Solo.

Orders: fps hold, new_site, no code; Re-engine hold. Its S3 risk is the Board's to carry. Operations does not hold it back.

other_moves.move: Staged fps business case for the 2045 round (authority-to-offer work)
other_moves.detail: Solo by default, since Pope's IP test finds Embraer adds no IP or capacity. The base case is the 10-year ramp: on this grid it beats the 7-year by $2.48-2.75B in every column and has the higher worst column. Renton comes only with Pope's MAX bridge plan, with code 7 and with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition. Design the production system together with the airplane and prove it at rate before authority to offer. The type certificate comes before building at rate (no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]). The case must show the item value in every column against the Board's two lines (no worse than -$1B anywhere, and above +$1B in the expected column) and Malave's slip leg as the baseline. It also sets out the cost of waiting under the public lead-edge rule: a 2035 launch settles at a long-run 42% (10-year) or 45% (7-year); a 2045 launch settles at 35% (7-year, EIS 2052) or 32% (10-year, EIS 2055). Sequence it under H4 against any 787 Re-engine. No date. No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Engine-sourcing requirement for our next single-aisle (updated)
other_moves.detail: We continue to invite all three narrowbody engine makers (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce) to bring proposals for a future Boeing single-aisle. Selection will be on value among engines actually launched, with durability proven before entry into service as a contract condition. With P&W's GTF2 and Rolls-Royce's UltraFan NB now in development, our plan is to offer customers a choice of engine at launch (code 7: CFM plus GTF2 plus UltraFan NB). No fps date and no launch commitment.

other_moves.move: Keep 787 Re-engine readiness warm (study only, no launch)
other_moves.detail: Engine basis: the GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033. The study covers engine durability, a supplier gate on new parts (rate breaks only when supplier output is there, as on the 787 heat exchangers [B-2308]) and a certification plan with the type certificate before building at rate. No programme spend is committed. Re-test it in 2045 only if the A350 has not re-engined (H3, second half), and sequence it against a 2045 fps under H4: a same-round 10-year fps sits at the 2-year limit, and a 7-year fps breaches it.

other_moves.move: Hold the 737 at 57 a month with KPI gates and stability first
other_moves.detail: No rate step. KPIs are monitored monthly. 57 a month is the ceiling. Confirm the LEAP-1B allocation with CFM at today's rate, treat CFM's concentrated sub-tier shortages as a watch item, and keep the FAA-agreed process in place. Any future step is gated one at a time on KPIs and FAA agreement.

other_moves.move: Keep the trained workforce and fragile suppliers through any demand dip
other_moves.detail: If MAX deliveries run below the 57-a-month slots, keep trained people and redeploy them to fps production-system work and the 787 rather than shed and rehire. Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot, with embedded staff, buffers and second sources where possible [BX-1243, B-2330], so supplier readiness is never why a 2045 programme slips. This is the way we used the strike and the 2019 delay to prepare [BX-1258, BX-1225].

other_moves.move: 787 capacity in Charleston as customers need it
other_moves.detail: Continue the Charleston footprint for 787 rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]. This is capacity growth, not a new programme.

other_moves.move: No shareholder-return signal
other_moves.detail: Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress. Allocating the surplus is reserved to the Board, with headroom kept for a staged fps ($60.32B on the 10-year ramp, about $8.4B in its peak year). Nothing is said publicly.

decision.public_statement:
Back in 2025 I said we were turning the ship but hadn't turned it. I think we've turned it now. The balance sheet is repaired and staying repaired. The 737 line has built at 57 a month to plan for five straight years. The 777X and the MAX family are delivering. A lot of people did hard work the right way to get here, and the job now is to keep it steady.

We are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date. We'll do a new airplane when the market, the technology and Boeing are all ready. We've looked hard at it with the data in front of us, and the case isn't there yet. The work goes on in stages. We're designing the production system together with the airplane, so that when we do go, we build it at rate the right way. With new engines in development at Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, and CFM always at the table, we expect to give our customers a choice of engine, with durability proven before entry into service. When we launch, it will be on a conservative plan with headroom in it, and we will not take on fixed-price development risk.

We're not launching a 787 Re-engine this year either. The 787 remains the most efficient airplane in its class, and we'll keep adding capacity in Charleston as our customers need it.

On production, the 737 stays at 57 a month and stays stable. Any step comes when the KPIs say so, with no subjectivity. We're keeping our trained people and our suppliers ready. Going slow has let us go faster, and stability is what lets us move when the time comes.

Our dates will be set by our own readiness. It is so much more important that we do this right than fast. I'd much rather be a month late than a month early. The financials will follow our production performance, and we'll keep earning our customers' trust in every transaction.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every lever. fps hold (new_site, engine code null), rate_737 hold, re787 hold. Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board. The package below answers what it asked to see. This is the frame's lean, confirmed by both memos.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes. The brief reports no quality, FAA, supply-chain or certification problem, and the MAX delivered 684 a year to plan in 2030-34. Pope's KPI gate is clean and her veto is not invoked. No Rate Increase is on the menu. CFM's sub-tier shortages are a watch item, not a live problem.
2. Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1303]
   - Balance sheet: ready. Net debt has been $0 since 2029 and holds in base and stress on every 10-year row.
   - Technology: ready by EIS. GTF2 is ready in 2036, UltraFan NB in 2037, CFM always.
   - Market: not ready on this grid. No fps row beats Do Nothing in any column.
3. What if certification takes longer? Malave's slip leg, S4 against Do Nothing (-1.01, line -3.01):
   - Pass: Do Nothing, the Re-engine and the four 10-year rows.
   - Fail (binding): every 7-year and via-Embraer row.
   This round S4 sits within $0.26B of S1 on every row, so the leg works as a level test.
   Pope's priors are unpriced but point the same way: a clean-sheet +3 years puts a 10-year fps at 2048; a derivative +2 years puts the Re-engine at 2042.
4. Is this doing less, better? [BX-1239] Yes. Do Nothing beats every fps row by $1.20B or more in every column. The only plans within ε of it in S1 (10-year + Re-engine rows) have worst columns $3.51-3.88B lower.

TEAM RULE
- Malave's binding buffer veto strikes every 7-year and via-Embraer row. None was ordered.
- Pope's H4 flag on 7-year + Re-engine is honoured: not ordered.
- Pope's KPI veto: no object this round.
- I decided the rest. No overrides.

fps: HOLD
- The best row, 10-year at Renton, gives up $1.20 / $1.46 / $1.20 / $1.22B (S1 to S4).
- My debt-first test needs a plan more than ε ahead of Do Nothing in S1. It is $2.20B short. The Board's -$1B per-item line fails in every column.
- An objective premium of $1.20B (S1) would sit inside my $2B cap. I won't use it: it would carry an item that fails my own test and the Board's line. 50/50 is the company's mission, not on my ranked list.
- Pope's discounting check shows the narrowing from -2.08 (2030) to -1.20 is mostly five years of discounting (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26). The case has moved later; it has not got better.
- Cost of waiting, said plainly. There is no 2040 round, so the earliest fps EIS becomes 2052 (7-year) or 2055 (10-year). Under the lead-edge rule the long-run share falls from 42-45% (a 2035 launch) to 32-35% (a 2045 launch).
- The grid assumes nobody moves later, so it cannot price a 2045 launch. Malave confirms nothing in the brief puts a dollar figure on it. It is information for the 2045 case, not a reason to launch now. Airbus's 2037 date does not set ours [B-2313, B-2315].
- Ramp and route for 2045: the 10-year ramp, Solo. The 7-year fails the buffer and stress debt at new sites. Via Embraer sits $10.95-11.47B behind Solo with a $52.5B undiscounted debt penalty, and Pope finds it adds no IP or capacity.

787 RE-ENGINE: HOLD (the hard call)
- Item value: +2.01 in S1, S2 and S4; -1.63 in S3. It passes Malave's buffer by $2.01B and debt holds at $0. In my expected column it is the best plan.
- Three grounds move me to hold:
  (a) The Board will veto it under its -$1B per-item line, which counts every plausible column. The bulletin does not rule out an A350 Re-engine: Airbus says 'A350 family', and RR is waiting with a widebody UltraFan for 'a Re-engine on the table'. I have no override against the Board. Bringing an item I know will be vetoed is not proof before commitment [BG-0021].
  (b) Malave, my independent check [BX-1316], has updated his read on the evidence: from 40-50% to about 30% (25-35%). That puts the weighted edge at +$0.92B ($0.74-1.10B). At the centre that is inside ε, so the higher worst column decides: Do Nothing -2.47 against -4.10. He also notes the +2.01 is a ceiling: it assumes Airbus never re-engines later.
  (c) My appetite for technology and launch risk is low. A launch now is a one-way door, since the EIS is 2040 and there is no round before it (H5).
- I'm not hiding what the hold costs. Pope shows 2035 is the only Re-engine slot with zero strain against any 2045 fps, and each year of delay takes about 9.5% off its value. A 2045 Re-engine would meet a 2045 fps at H4's limit, so this hold may in practice close the programme.
- The cost is logged separately, as a Board-downside hold and not against the cap: $2.01B given up in S1, S2 and S4; $1.63B saved in S3; $0.92B weighted at 30%.
- My reading of Airbus's probability is Low confidence on my record. I relied on Malave's read and on company doctrine (profile §7, the A330neo precedent [B-2446]).

SITE, CODE, RATE
- fps_site: new_site. Renton is worth 0.00 without a launch, and the full $3.0B capex saving needs only a choice 3 years before EIS.
- Engine code: null with the hold. At launch it will be code 7: three sources, all ready by EIS, an allowed pair against NGSA. That is doctrine and my public requirement; I have no record as Boeing CEO on engine choice.
- rate_737: hold, the only value. The ceiling stays at 57.

HARD RULES AND RED LINES
- H1: the 2030 ruling stands and is not re-made.
- H3, first half: lifted in 2030. Second half: in force. No A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the 787 Re-engine stays open but is held.
- H4: respected, with no development in flight.
- H5: nothing to cancel.
- H6: no rate order.
- H8: soft total $0.
- H2 cannot bind. H7 has no trigger. The FAA-process gate passes [BX-1309].
- My own red lines are all respected: no concurrency, no fixed-price development, no FAA blame, no attribution of supplier problems to Airbus.

BOARD PACKAGE
- Submitted row (Do Nothing): -1.01 / -0.02 / -2.47 / -1.01.
- No Board items: fps, re787 and fps_site are each at their default, so every item value is 0.00.
- Expected column: S1. Risk case S4 is -1.01: 0.00 against Do Nothing, with $2.00B of headroom over -3.01. Buffer: pass.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass. The 777X has been cash-positive since 2029 [BX-0547], and net debt is $0 in base and stress to 2060. The grid holds the fps back, not the cash.
- Pope's gates: KPI clean; zero strain; engines ready by any EIS; no concurrency; Renton not chosen, with a bridge plan drafted for 2045.
- Premiums: soft $0 and objective $0. The Re-engine is logged as a Board-downside hold.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE:
- the A350 probability (via Malave);
- engine code 7;
- the Renton bridge plan;
- the slip priors.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Malave's memo was the decisive input on the Re-engine, weighed as my independent check [BX-1316]. His buffer veto binds; his other views are advice from a thin seat (one call, Low confidence).
- Buffer: accepted to the cent. The 7-year and via-Embraer rows are struck. The 10-year rows pass, but at new sites with only $0.39B of headroom.
- Net debt: accepted from the metrics table. The debt penalty is already netted and not subtracted again.
- Fundable when the 777X turns: pass, accepted.
- Cash timing: accepted. The 10-year peaks at $8.44B in 2041, 92% of stress free cash flow. In cash, a same-round Re-engine falls entirely inside the fps spend.
- What moved me: his updated A350 read of about 30%, which he moved down on two of his own 2030 triggers. It puts the weighted edge just inside ε, so the higher worst column decides. That supports the Board's line rather than standing in for it.
- I log his offer: he would support the Re-engine on evidence that puts the A350 chance below 28%. That is the trigger to carry forward.
- His point that +2.01 is an undiscounted ceiling (it assumes no later A350 move) is noted.
memo_weighing.ops:
Pope's seat runs on [NOW] operations doctrine with no airplane-business evidence (Very low confidence), so I took her memo as gates and facts, not judgement.
- Accepted: the KPI gate is clean and her veto has no object; the 737 ceiling stays at 57. Strain is zero on the hold; a 2035 10-year + Re-engine pair sits at H4's limit, and a 7-year pair breaches it. Engines for code 7 are ready 5-9 years before EIS. Via Embraer fails the partner test. Re-engine readiness passes on the GEnx upgrade.
- Two of her findings sharpened the rationale. Her discounting check (-2.08 / 1.105^5 = -1.26) shows the fps case has moved later, not improved. And 2035 is the only zero-strain Re-engine slot against a 2045 fps, so I've said plainly that the hold may close it.
- Her five-step Renton bridge plan and her 2045 readiness plan (workforce through the dip, fragile suppliers, production system proven at rate, one KPI-gated ask at a time) go into the other moves.
- Her statement that operations does not hold the Re-engine back is accepted. The hold rests on the market column S3 and the Board's line, not on readiness.

decision.expected_scenario:
S1: rivals hold. Airbus keeps its Alt plan; per the bulletin it reverts to base only on a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event, and none is on the record. No A350 Re-engine.
- S2 (Airbus back on its base plan) is the upside.
- S3 (an A350 Re-engine, about 30% on Malave's read) is the plausible downside.
- S4 (Delay Tactics) is the risk case. It equals S1 on every hold row.
The column values our plan; it does not set our dates [B-2313].
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: In S1 the best plan is fps: hold + 787 Re-engine (+1.00). I chose fps: hold + 787: hold (-1.01), $2.01B below it. That is a Board-downside hold: the Board's -$1B per-item line binds while S3 (-1.63) is not ruled out, and I have no override. It is logged separately and not against the cap. Weighted at Malave's 30% read of an A350 Re-engine, the gap is $0.92B, inside ε, where the higher worst column (-2.47 against -4.10) decides.
decision.premium_reason:
Soft doctrine premium against the $2B cap: $0. Objective premium: $0.
- fps hold: no premium, because the grid prefers it. The best fps row (10-year at Renton) sits $1.20B below Do Nothing in S1 and $1.46B below in S2. Launching it for 50/50, incumbency or the engine enabler would be an objective premium of $1.20B. That is inside the cap, but it fails my debt-first test and the Board's -$1B line, so it is not taken.
- 787 Re-engine hold: a known cost, logged separately as a Board-downside hold, as the Board asked. It gives up $2.01B in S1, S2 and S4 and saves $1.63B in S3. Weighted at Malave's 30% (25-35%), the cost is $0.92B ($0.74-1.10B).
- What breaks the number: if the A350 does not re-engine, the hold gives up the full $2.01B. If it does, the hold saves $1.63B, and H3 closes the 787 Re-engine for good.
decision.objective_note:
The objectives never change the payoff.
- Hold the 50/50 split: unmet on every hold plan. Preference share falls to 37% at NGSA's 2037 EIS and 20% from 2043. Not chased: the premium needed would breach the Board's line and my own debt-first test.
- Defend incumbency: unmet (worst year 20%). Delivered share falls to 26.6-29.9% in 2041-45 and recovers to 36.3% from 2047, when Airbus's capacity binds. This is the long-cycle stake the 2045 fps case must answer. Waiting costs share: 42-45% for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch. The grid does not price it.
- Balance sheet, repair and keep repaired (base and stress): met. Net debt is $0 from 2029 through 2050.
- Engine enabler, three makers in the market: met (CFM, P&W, RR).
- Engine enabler, two or three sources on our narrowbody: unmet, since the MAX flies CFM only. It is answered at launch by code 7 and by the public, dateless engine-sourcing requirement.
decision.predictions:
AIRBUS
- NGSA enters service in 2037 on schedule, and Airbus keeps the Alt plan (S1).
- An A350 Re-engine this round is about 30% (Malave's read). Airbus's engineering is on NGSA first, but its 'A350 family' wording and RR's waiting widebody UltraFan keep it open.
- No Delay Tactics effect: with no fps they would be 'naked' and draw a $48.32B fine, and S4 equals S1 on our hold.

ENGINE MAKERS
- GTF2 ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037, both fitted to NGSA.
- CFM keeps the LEAP-1B on the MAX.
- No widebody UltraFan, since no Re-engine is on the table.

OUR RESULTS IF NOBODY MOVES AGAIN
- ΔPV: -1.01 (S1), -0.02 (S2), -2.47 (S3), -1.01 (S4).
- Net debt $0 in base and stress at every check year.
- NB preference share 37% in 2037 and 20% from 2043.
- MAX deliveries 409-468 a year in 2038-42, back to 684 from 2047.
- WB share 58.8%.

2045
- Bring the staged fps case: Solo, the 10-year ramp, Renton with a bridge plan, code 7, against the Board's two lines and Malave's slip leg.
- Re-test the 787 Re-engine only if the A350 has not re-engined, sequenced under H4.

board_response.recommendation: Hold the fps with no date; keep the staged 2045 case (authority to offer first) with the 10-year ramp, Renton with a MAX bridge plan, item values against both lines, and the cost of waiting under the lead-edge rule set out as information.
board_response.response: Taken. fps: hold, new_site, no date in the public statement. The staged 2045 case is a private other move: Solo, the 10-year ramp, Renton only with Pope's five-step bridge plan, code 7, item values in every column against your -$1B and +$1B lines, and Malave's slip leg as the baseline. The cost of waiting is set out: 42-45% long-run for a 2035 launch against 32-35% for a 2045 launch, unpriced on this grid. It is information for 2045, not a reason to launch. I also note Pope's finding that the narrowing from -2.08 to -1.20 is mostly discounting.

board_response.recommendation: Log any objective premium against the $2B cap; the -$1B per-item line binds first; answer the long-cycle stake with a case that clears the tests.
board_response.response: Taken. Objective premium $0, soft premium $0. Launching the 10-year at Renton would have needed $1.20B (S1) to $1.46B (S2). airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Every step to entry into service is gated on the maturity of its technologies and of the production system designed with it. Safety and quality come before schedule. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce will power it, and we will certify each engine as it matures, so that our customers have a choice and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. Its lines will keep running alongside the new aircraft, built to our customers' demand, for a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme remains funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION: hold course on every lever, on our own clock.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (NGSA continues to EIS 2037), `ngsa_engine_code: 7`, `a320_plan: alt`, `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`.
- All five are this round's defaults. So there are no Board items and no override, and the game's single override stays unspent.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: the orders contradict none (Wagner, ask 7). No supply crunch, engine slip or quality event is on the record.
2. Ramp: the A320 builds 85 a month to EIS. The Alt plan stands, and in 2037-38 we build to orders: 725 and 796 delivered against capacity of about 1,006 and 807.
3. Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA holds 2037 with no slip, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Margin to 2037 is zero; a one-year slip lands in 2038, still inside "the second half of the 2030s".
4. Board: the default is its best passing plan in every column.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted (red lines and pillars):
- Every Delay Tactics row. Under rule 4, fps is not public, so any move carries the naked fine. One move is -15.68 in S1/S6 with a best gain of +0.59 (S4); `both` is two moves, at -16.13/-16.14. `bottleneck` and `both` also fail the integrity pillar. The team's stricter condition stays in force: I do not set it aside.
- Every NGSA cancel row (rule 7). Continuing leads by 26.69 / 25.85 / 25.85 / 24.95 / 25.85 / 26.70 / 25.85 $B.

Tested against Toepfer's and Wagner's tests:
- Alt + A350 Re-engine fails Toepfer twice: peak cash ($6.67B a year in 2035-36 against $5.2B) and robustness (-1.21 in S6/S7; +0.76 equal-weighted). Wagner passes it at the limit, with flags.
- Base + hold fails Toepfer's robustness: no trigger is recorded, and it is -2.69 in S1/S6, beyond the Board's -$2B.
- Base + Re-engine fails cash and robustness (-3.90 / -3.12 in S6/S7). It is dominated.
- The only survivor is the default.

Best grid plan against the survivor:
- Alt + A350 Re-engine scores +14.32 on my weights and +15.26 in S1. The default scores +13.05 and +13.71.
- On my weights the default is $1.27B behind (1.55 in S1), so it is not within $1B. I decide on the tests, not on the doctrine default.
- On Toepfer's equal weights the gap is +0.76, within $1B. There every tie-break favours hold: less concurrency and strain, a later capex start, fewer Board items.

Override considered and declined:
- The margin, +1.27 on my weights (+1.55 in S1), clears the $1B bar in the expected column.
- But on a Qualified Majority item the Board also requires the plan to be ahead in the worst plausible column, and it is -1.21 in S6/S7.
- `rea350: launch` is on the Board's would-veto list, and I hold no override against the Board. Spending the game's only override on an item that reverts to hold buys nothing.

Beyond the arithmetic, five reasons:
1. Cash: 128% of one year's FCF, while Toepfer's proxy runs net cash to about zero by end-2036.
2. Zero margin on three fronts at once: the overlap, NGSA EIS and UltraFan NB.
3. A one-year NGSA slip turns the 2-year overlap into a rule-6 breach.
4. No widebody engine is launched for it. UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5, and Rolls-Royce will not launch until a Re-engine is on the table. Supply certainty is the test I apply to every target.
5. The company's 2033-35 window closes with this round. I say so openly: the 2045 gate (about $1.0B a year, no overlap) needs its own grid, A350F status and a rule-3 check.

Other levers:
- A320 plan: Alt stands. Wagner records no trigger; base would cost 1.36 to 2.69 $B. On any safety, quality, crunch or engine-slip record before EIS I revert at once [AX-0056].
- Engine code 7 is Wagner's supply recommendation: 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040-2050. If UltraFan NB misses 2037 it falls back to CFM + GTF2, and it forms no barred pair. We do not ask for a Joint Venture.
- Own clock: Boeing held in 2030. No Boeing move, actual or expected, re-times or cancels NGSA (rules 2 and 7).

SCENARIO TABLE (my weight; default row; Re-engine row, rejected)
- S1 hold, 35%: +13.71; +15.26
- S2 10-year fps, 30%: +12.87; +14.41
- S3 10-year fps at Renton, 5%: +12.87; +14.41
- S4 7-year fps, 10%: +11.80; +13.35
- S5 fps via Embraer, 10%: +12.87; +14.41
- S6 787 Re-engine, 5%: +13.23; +12.02
- S7 10-year fps + 787 Re-engine, 5%: +12.38; +11.17

Summary: the default is +13.05 weighted and +12.82 equal-weighted, with S4 (+11.80) its worst plausible column. The Re-engine row's worst column is S7 (+11.17).

BOARD GATE
No Board items. For the record, the default row:
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass. Peak $5.07B against $5.2B, headroom $0.13B; bill unmoved ($36.3B = NGSA $35.52B + Alt $0.75B); no trigger hit; robustness passes.
- Wagner: pass on every test.
- Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.87 / +12.87 / +11.80 / +12.87 / +13.23 / +12.38.

Not tabled: `rea350: launch`.
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: fail (cash, robustness).
- Wagner: pass at the limit, with flags.
- Item value: +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.21.

FLAGS I CARRY
- Toepfer's net-cash proxy: no new return before 2037; any buyback goes to the Board.
- Overrun and exchange-rate triggers: a bill above $36.4B; a rate below $1.07 per EUR.
- Engine margins: UltraFan NB has none; GTF2 must prove durability.
- 2037 EIS-year dip: operating profit $5.6B, 725 deliveries. Guidance in ranges, attributed to the transition.
- A 787 Re-engine would close the A350 Re-engine at 2045 (rule 3).

   - If a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture forms, its engine counts as one and we drop to 2 sources. Should we keep from asking for one?
   - Certify CFM first and the others as they mature.
4. A350 Re-engine test.
   - Give A350F and Spirit A350 work-package absorption status.
   - Can engineering carry a 2-year overlap in 2035-36 (your limit) with NGSA in its final development phase? What happens on a one-year NGSA slip, when the overlap becomes 3 years?
   - If the Board's 2045 gate (entry into service 2050) is the right next look, what would you need to see then?
5. Ramp. Confirm the A320 at 85 a month to entry into service, and that CFM and P&W supply covers both lines in the overlap.
6. Supply and integrity. Confirm that the CFM capacity agreements cover only our own A320neo and NGSA volumes, with no exclusivity. Confirm that the skills pipeline involves no targeted hiring from a rival's fps team. Both should be ready for the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review.
7. Five pillars. Flag any order or public line we plan that contradicts them.
frame.initial_lean:
I lean to holding course on every lever, on our own clock. Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security come first, and NGSA is two years from entry into service.

ORDERS
`ngsa: hold`, `ngsa_engine_code: 7`, `a320_plan: alt`, `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`. All five are defaults, so there are no Board items. I will show the Board the default row and record that the single override stays unspent.

- Default row: +13.71 / +12.87 / +12.87 / +11.80 / +12.87 / +13.23 / +12.38.
- Worst column S4 +11.80; equal-weighted +12.82; +13.05 on my weights.

| Column | Weight |
|---|---:|

Why these weights: Boeing's own words point to a hold or a 10-year or Embraer fps. It gives no date, develops in stages, wants a conservative plan with headroom, and calls Charleston "capacity growth, not a new programme". The Board reads it the same way.

THE A350 RE-ENGINE
This is the real question of the round, and I will not pretend the grid settles it.
- It is worth +1.54/+1.55 in five columns and +1.27 on my weights, so the default is not within $1B on my weights.
- It falls on cash, not on value. NGSA plus the Re-engine runs at about $6.67B a year in 2035-36 against the $5.2B line, which fails Thomas's test.
- No override can carry it. It trails the default by $1.21B in S6/S7, the worst columns, and I hold no override against the Board, which would veto it.
- The 2-year overlap sits at Lars's limit and becomes a rule-6 breach on a one-year NGSA slip.
- The company's 2033-35 window closes with this round. A 2045 launch would be outside that window and need its own grid, peak cash, A350F status and a check on any 787 Re-engine (rule 3). I will say so to the Board, not hide it.
- I would table it only if Thomas shows the line holds and Lars's absorption and overlap tests pass. I do not expect either.

A320 PLAN
Alt stands unless Lars records a crunch, an engine slip or a quality event. Reverting to base costs 1.36 to 2.69 $B, which I accept at once on a safety or quality record [AX-0056].

DELAY TACTICS
Off. fps is not public, and one move is -15.68 against a best gain of +0.59. The stricter team condition stays in force, and the integrity pillar decides it.

NGSA
Never cancelled for a Boeing move.

OBJECTIVE
The briefing goal is met today. S4 may cost 60/40 in 2050, but no allowed order buys it back, and I pay no premium.

PUBLIC LINE
Five pillars first; a "disciplined and controlled" ramp [AX-0010]. The next single-aisle stays on track for the second half of the 2030s, its engines chosen for supply certainty. An orderly A320neo transition. Focus on the A350 family and the A350F, with no Re-engine timing. Zero-for-zero, financial flexibility, no Delay Tactics.

2035 cash gate, for the Audit Committee.

Recommendation: hold course on every lever. NGSA continues to EIS 2037 on code 7 (Lars's call; I defer), Alt stands, the A350 Re-engine stays on hold, no Delay Tactics. No Board items.

Peak cash: pass. NGSA is $35.52B / 7 = $5.07B a year in 2035-36 against one year's FCF of about $5.2B (EUR 4,753m at $1.10): headroom $0.13B. The bill has not moved: the $36.3B booked in 2037 is NGSA $35.52B plus the Alt plan's $0.75B, budgeted from 2037. Neither trigger is hit: a bill above $36.4B or a rate below $1.07 per EUR.

FCF path: the record gives none for 2030-34. Operating profit held at $7.6B, as in the status quo, so on my proxy NGSA took 97% of FCF each year. No equity raise or dividend cut is needed, but net cash does not hold at $13.4B: at today's dividend it runs to about zero by end-2036 (inference). It rebuilds from 2037, when programme spend stops though profit dips to $5.6B. I would add no new return before 2037; the 2029 outlook counts as upside only.

A350 Re-engine now: $5.07B + $1.00B + $0.60B = $6.67B a year, $1.47B over the line; -1.21 in S6/S7, +0.76 equal-weighted. Binding soft veto; it fails the Board's worst-column override test. No 2035 form passes; at the 2045 gate it runs at $1.0B a year, no overlap.

Delay Tactics and NGSA cancellation: red lines. Base only on a trigger Lars records.

- NGSA capacity on the brief: 8 / 27 / 93 / 293 / 551 / 798 / 959 / 1,098 / 1,194 aircraft in 2037-45 (about 46 a month in 2041, 80 in 2043, 100 in 2045).
- Confirmed: NGSA goes onto the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review through EIS and the ramp.

tests.name: A320 Alt plan re-check (ask 2)
tests.threshold: Alt stands unless a supply crunch, an engine slip or a quality event is recorded. Conditions: the steps are a ceiling, NGSA has first claim on resources, and the plan reverts to base before EIS on any trigger
tests.numbers:
No trigger: the brief reports no supply crunch, no engine slip and no quality event. Alt stands. I record no trigger, so base has no operating ground (it is -1.36 to -2.69 against Alt).
- Ceiling: A320 capacity on the brief is 998 / 780 / 734 / 550 / 504 / 297 / 168 / 168 / 25 in 2037-45, about 83 / 65 / 61 / 46 / 42 / 25 / 14 / 14 / 2 a month, never above 85. NGSA capacity is filled first every year.

- That is a step-down from 85 to about 60 a month in the EIS year. CFM and P&W get that schedule now, and nothing is built to stock.
- From 2039 we are capacity-bound again.
- Conditions unchanged; the plan can still revert until EIS 2037.

tests.name: A320 ramp shield and engine supply for both lines (ask 5)
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with an open A320 ramp commitment
tests.numbers:
There is no open ramp commitment: the end-2027 date is long past, and the A320 has built 85 a month (1,020 a year) since 2026 and does so through 2036. No ramp problem is reported. The A350 Re-engine is a widebody programme and takes no A320 slots.
- Engines cover both lines in the overlap. Airbus narrowbody engine demand is 2,040 in 2036, then 1,450 / 1,592 / 1,654 / 1,686 in 2037-40.
- At the 60/40 split the A320neo needs about 860 / 923 / 881 / 660 CFM and 574 / 615 / 587 / 440 P&W. NGSA needs 16 / 54 / 186 / 586 across three makers.
- Demand passes 2036's level only from 2041 (2,110) and peaks at 2,532 in 2044, by which time GTF2 and UltraFan NB have been in NGSA service for years.

tests.name: Supply crunch
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply-chain crunch: no new concurrency
tests.numbers: None is reported, and the board has no injects. Our capacity limit (waiting backlog 1,978 in 2033, 901 in 2035, 416 in 2036) is the factory ceiling, not a supplier crunch. The test is not triggered for the default or for the Re-engine case.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip (ask 3)
tests.threshold: If reported: re-time NGSA so EIS stays at or after the technology-ready year; never cancel
tests.numbers: None is reported. GTF2 is ready 2036 (1 year of margin to EIS 2037); UltraFan NB is ready 2037 (no margin). On this board a maker that is not ready by EIS is dropped rather than delaying NGSA, so rule 8 cannot bind and CFM keeps EIS whole. Watch items: P&W's own condition (no entry into service until durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life) and its stated GTF time-on-wing record; UltraFan NB's zero margin.

tests.name: Engine supply: code 7 (recommendation, not a veto ground; ask 3)
tests.threshold: CFM plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7); code 7 when it is unclear which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS
tests.numbers:
Code 7 fits CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB: 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on every NGSA-hold row.
- If UltraFan NB misses 2037, Rolls-Royce drops and code 7 flies CFM + GTF2 (2 sources, still dual), the same as code 6, so 7 loses nothing and keeps the third. If GTF2 slipped, 7 still gives CFM + UltraFan NB.
- Codes 5 and 6 drop a maker for certain; code 3 is CFM alone. Code 7 forms no barred pair with Boeing's 3 or 7.
- Joint Venture: its engine counts as one source and the solo programmes fold into it, so NGSA drops from 3 sources to 2. P&W will consider one only on an airframer's demand on the record, so we should not ask for one.
- Certification: CFM first, the only maker always ready; GTF2 once its durability and full-life parts are proven; UltraFan NB as it matures. On the A320neo we also certified the makers one after the other.

tests.name: Supply and integrity of the other moves (ask 6)

tests.numbers: CFM long-term capacity agreements: our own A320neo and NGSA volumes from 2035 only (2,040 engines in 2036, 1,450-1,686 a year in 2037-40), with no exclusivity and nothing above our own ramp. The public move states supply certainty, not leverage. Own supply: the wing in-house, Aubert & Duval titanium and forgings, and the raw-materials watchlist, for our ramp only. Skills: apprenticeships, graduates and universities in Europe, with no targeted hiring from any rival team. Both are ready for the Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review.

tests.numbers: The default orders (ngsa hold, code 7, a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none) contradict no pillar, and no quality event is on the record. Public line: windows, not dates ('second half of the 2030s' survives a slip to 2038 or 2039). No A350 Re-engine timing, no rate number for the 2037 step-down, no Delay Tactics.

tests.numbers: Continuing beats cancelling by 26.69 / 25.85 / 25.85 / 24.95 / 25.85 / 26.70 / 25.85 $B (S1-S7). Cancelling writes off about $25.37B (Board figure) and drops NGSA to 2 engine sources (2 makers in S1/S6). No slip or failed case is on the record to re-time.

vetoes.ground:
Flag only, no operating veto. My capacity, absorption, supply-crunch and ramp-shield tests pass, at the limit: 2-year overlap, $1.2B strain, one launch. Grid against the default: +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.21.

Flags:
- The margin is zero on three things at once: the overlap, NGSA EIS 2037 and UltraFan NB readiness.
- No widebody engine is launched for it. UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5, and Rolls-Royce launches it only once a Re-engine is on the table.
- If a one-year NGSA slip is recorded before the order, the overlap becomes 3 years ($1.8B). That is a binding rule-6 red line, because S6/S7 are not $1B ahead.

Peak cash ($6.67B against $5.2B) is the CFO's test and the Board's veto, not mine.

ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived (Very low confidence): nothing of mine is on record, so I apply company doctrine.

NGSA at the 2035 gate: pass. EIS 2037 holds, no slip, two years above the 2035 floor and no margin to 2037. A one-year slip lands in 2038, inside our public window. The record holds no wing or production-system measurement; I report the proxy. NGSA goes onto the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review through EIS and the ramp.

Engines: GTF2 is ready 2036, one year of margin; UltraFan NB 2037, none. If UltraFan NB slips, Rolls-Royce drops and code 7 flies CFM plus GTF2, so keep 7. Do not ask for a Joint Venture: it cuts us to two sources. Certify CFM first.

Alt plan: no crunch, no engine slip, no quality event, so Alt stands, on its conditions. In 2037 we build to orders: about 60 a month on the A320, 725 delivered against 1,006 of capacity. CFM and P&W get that schedule now. Engine demand stays below 2036's 2,040 through 2040.

A350 Re-engine: my tests pass, at the limit: two years of overlap, $1.2B strain, absorption passed on the game proxy. No veto from me. But every margin is zero at once. A one-year NGSA slip makes it three years and $1.8B, a rule-6 breach. No widebody engine is launched for it: UltraFan WB needs six years against its five. Cash is Thomas's test. I recommend hold; look again in 2045.

Binding vetoes: any Delay Tactics, any NGSA cancel.

other_moves.move: Secure our own supply for the NGSA entry into service and ramp
other_moves.detail: Continue the round-1 programme: the NGSA wing stays in-house (Wing of Tomorrow and the run-at-rate wing), with aerostructures through Airbus Atlantic, Airbus Aerostructures and the ex-Spirit sites. Titanium and forgings come through the Aubert & Duval co-ownership and additive (DED) parts. The critical raw-materials and rare-earths watchlist covers NGSA through its ramp. This serves our own ramp only and makes no claim on any rival's capacity [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

other_moves.move: Engine certification sequence and CFM long-term capacity agreements
other_moves.detail: NGSA keeps three engine makers (code 7: CFM + P&W GTF2 + Rolls-Royce UltraFan NB). CFM is certified first; GTF2 follows once its durability and full-life parts are proven, and UltraFan NB as it matures, as we did on the A320neo. The CFM long-term capacity agreements cover only our own A320neo and NGSA volumes from 2035, with no exclusivity and nothing above our own ramp. The aim is supply certainty, not leverage [AX-0054, A-0243, A-0360].

other_moves.move: Orderly A320neo family transition: Alt plan confirmed at the 2035 gate
other_moves.detail: At the 2035 gate the operating head found no supply crunch, engine slip or quality event, so the Alt plan stands on its conditions. The steps are a ceiling, never above today's rate. NGSA has first claim on resources. Through the entry-into-service years we build to customer demand, not to the ceiling, and suppliers get that schedule now. The plan still reverts to base before EIS on any trigger. Its cost is budgeted from NGSA entry into service. No rate number is published.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy
other_moves.detail: Continue working with the European and US industry associations, Boeing included, to keep civil aerospace on a tariff-free, zero-for-zero footing [AX-0088, AX-0046].

other_moves.move: Skills for the Airbus of the 2030s
other_moves.detail: Continue apprenticeship, graduate and university programmes in Europe to staff NGSA certification, entry into service and ramp from our own pipeline. The programme does no targeted hiring from any rival's team [AX-0073, A-0330].

other_moves.move: NGSA on the full Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
other_moves.detail: Runs through EIS and the ramp. It covers wing and production-system maturity, engine readiness (GTF2 with one year of margin, UltraFan NB with none), certification status, and the A320 run-down under the Alt plan. Any quality finding goes to the Board at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, AG-0038].

other_moves.move: Ethics, Compliance and Sustainability Committee review
other_moves.detail: The Committee confirms that neither the CFM capacity agreements (own volumes, no exclusivity) nor the skills programme (own pipeline, no targeted hiring) can be read as a Delay Tactics move [A-0299, AG-0022, A-0331].

other_moves.move: Audit Committee cash gate each budget cycle through 2037
other_moves.detail: Toepfer re-tests the $5.2B line and brings any of three triggers to the Board as abnormal risk: an NGSA bill above about $36.4B, any Alt spend falling before 2037, or a rate below about $1.07 per EUR. Net cash is flagged: on his proxy it runs to about zero by end-2036. So we add no new shareholder return before 2037, and any buyback comes to the Board as a reserved matter with the NGSA peak shown. There is no equity raise and no dividend cut [AX-0104, AX-0102, AG-0058, AG-0059].

other_moves.move: A350 Re-engine prepared for the 2045 gate (internal)
other_moves.detail: It stays on hold. At the 2045 gate it comes back with five things: its own grid and peak cash (about $1.0B a year with no NGSA overlap); A350F and Spirit A350 absorption shown complete on the record; a widebody engine committed in time for its EIS (UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5); NGSA in service with no open quality finding; and a rule-3 check on any Boeing 787 Re-engine. No timing is disclosed [AX-0019, AX-0082, A-0253].

other_moves.move: No Joint Venture request to Pratt & Whitney or Rolls-Royce
other_moves.detail: We place no airframer demand for a P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture on the record. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source, which would cut NGSA from three sources to two. If one forms anyway, the operating head reports what it does to the fitted sources.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft is in its final phase of development and remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. Every step to entry into service is gated on the maturity of its technologies and of the production system designed with it. Safety and quality come before schedule. CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce will power it, and we will certify each engine as it matures, so that our customers have a choice and our ramp-up has secure supply. The A320neo family remains the backbone of our single-aisle offer. Its lines will keep running alongside the new aircraft, built to our customers' demand, for a long and orderly transition. On widebodies our focus stays on the A350 family and the A350F. We will continue a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and we continue to secure key work packages, materials and skills in Europe for our own industrial system. The programme remains funded from operating cash flow within our financial framework, preserving our financial flexibility and our shareholder return policy. With our industry partners on both sides of the Atlantic, we continue to support a zero-for-zero tariff regime for civil aerospace.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: hold course on every lever, on our own clock.
- Orders: `ngsa: hold` (NGSA continues to EIS 2037), `ngsa_engine_code: 7`, `a320_plan: alt`, `rea350: hold`, `delay_tactics: none`.
- All five are this round's defaults. So there are no Board items and no override, and the game's single override stays unspent.

THE ROUND AGAINST MY PAID OBJECTIVES, IN ORDER
1. Five pillars: the orders contradict none (Wagner, ask 7). No supply crunch, engine slip or quality event is on the record.
2. Ramp: the A320 builds 85 a month to EIS. The Alt plan stands, and in 2037-38 we build to orders: 725 and 796 delivered against capacity of about 1,006 and 807.
3. Airbus of the 2030s: NGSA holds 2037 with no slip, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Margin to 2037 is zero; a one-year slip lands in 2038, still inside "the second half of the 2030s".
4. Board: the default is its best passing plan in every column.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
Deleted (red lines and pillars):
- Every Delay Tactics row. Under rule 4, fps is not public, so any move carries the naked fine. One move is -15.68 in S1/S6 with a best gain of +0.59 (S4); `both` is two moves, at -16.13/-16.14. `bottleneck` and `both` also fail the integrity pillar. The team's stricter condition stays in force: I do not set it aside.
- Every NGSA cancel row (rule 7). Continuing leads by 26.69 / 25.85 / 25.85 / 24.95 / 25.85 / 26.70 / 25.85 $B.

Tested against Toepfer's and Wagner's tests:
- Alt + A350 Re-engine fails Toepfer twice: peak cash ($6.67B a year in 2035-36 against $5.2B) and robustness (-1.21 in S6/S7; +0.76 equal-weighted). Wagner passes it at the limit, with flags.
- Base + hold fails Toepfer's robustness: no trigger is recorded, and it is -2.69 in S1/S6, beyond the Board's -$2B.
- Base + Re-engine fails cash and robustness (-3.90 / -3.12 in S6/S7). It is dominated.
- The only survivor is the default.

Best grid plan against the survivor:
- Alt + A350 Re-engine scores +14.32 on my weights and +15.26 in S1. The default scores +13.05 and +13.71.
- On my weights the default is $1.27B behind (1.55 in S1), so it is not within $1B. I decide on the tests, not on the doctrine default.
- On Toepfer's equal weights the gap is +0.76, within $1B. There every tie-break favours hold: less concurrency and strain, a later capex start, fewer Board items.

Override considered and declined:
- The margin, +1.27 on my weights (+1.55 in S1), clears the $1B bar in the expected column.
- But on a Qualified Majority item the Board also requires the plan to be ahead in the worst plausible column, and it is -1.21 in S6/S7.
- `rea350: launch` is on the Board's would-veto list, and I hold no override against the Board. Spending the game's only override on an item that reverts to hold buys nothing.

Beyond the arithmetic, five reasons:
1. Cash: 128% of one year's FCF, while Toepfer's proxy runs net cash to about zero by end-2036.
2. Zero margin on three fronts at once: the overlap, NGSA EIS and UltraFan NB.
3. A one-year NGSA slip turns the 2-year overlap into a rule-6 breach.
4. No widebody engine is launched for it. UltraFan WB needs 6 years against the Re-engine's 5, and Rolls-Royce will not launch until a Re-engine is on the table. Supply certainty is the test I apply to every target.
5. The company's 2033-35 window closes with this round. I say so openly: the 2045 gate (about $1.0B a year, no overlap) needs its own grid, A350F status and a rule-3 check.

Other levers:
- A320 plan: Alt stands. Wagner records no trigger; base would cost 1.36 to 2.69 $B. On any safety, quality, crunch or engine-slip record before EIS I revert at once [AX-0056].
- Engine code 7 is Wagner's supply recommendation: 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040-2050. If UltraFan NB misses 2037 it falls back to CFM + GTF2, and it forms no barred pair. We do not ask for a Joint Venture.
- Own clock: Boeing held in 2030. No Boeing move, actual or expected, re-times or cancels NGSA (rules 2 and 7).

SCENARIO TABLE (my weight; default row; Re-engine row, rejected)
- S1 hold, 35%: +13.71; +15.26
- S2 10-year fps, 30%: +12.87; +14.41
- S3 10-year fps at Renton, 5%: +12.87; +14.41
- S4 7-year fps, 10%: +11.80; +13.35
- S5 fps via Embraer, 10%: +12.87; +14.41
- S6 787 Re-engine, 5%: +13.23; +12.02
- S7 10-year fps + 787 Re-engine, 5%: +12.38; +11.17

Summary: the default is +13.05 weighted and +12.82 equal-weighted, with S4 (+11.80) its worst plausible column. The Re-engine row's worst column is S7 (+11.17).

BOARD GATE
No Board items. For the record, the default row:
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: pass. Peak $5.07B against $5.2B, headroom $0.13B; bill unmoved ($36.3B = NGSA $35.52B + Alt $0.75B); no trigger hit; robustness passes.
- Wagner: pass on every test.
- Grid ΔPV: +13.71 / +12.87 / +12.87 / +11.80 / +12.87 / +13.23 / +12.38.

Not tabled: `rea350: launch`.
- Five pillars: pass.
- Toepfer: fail (cash, robustness).
- Wagner: pass at the limit, with flags.
- Item value: +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.54 / -1.21 / -1.21.

FLAGS I CARRY
- Toepfer's net-cash proxy: no new return before 2037; any buyback goes to the Board.
- Overrun and exchange-rate triggers: a bill above $36.4B; a rate below $1.07 per EUR.
- Engine margins: UltraFan NB has none; GTF2 must prove durability.
- 2037 EIS-year dip: operating profit $5.6B, 725 deliveries. Guidance in ranges, attributed to the transition.
- A 787 Re-engine would close the A350 Re-engine at 2045 (rule 3).

It is not a survivor:

decision.premium_reason:
I pay no doctrine premium. The chosen plan is the highest-grid survivor of the red-line deletions and both colleagues' tests.

The $1.27B weighted gap ($1.55B in S1) to the Alt + A350 Re-engine row is not a premium. It is the cost of a binding soft veto on cash and robustness that I cannot override within the Board's rule, and of the Board's own veto.

The doctrine's two premium purposes do not arise this round:
- No 787 Re-engine is on the record.
- No second Delay Tactics move is in question.

Delay Tactics and NGSA cancel rows are deleted as red lines, which are never traded for PV.
decision.objective_note:
Briefing goal: "Defend 60/40 edge; Protect A320 family", with the stable-engine-supply enabler. It is scored by the GM, and I trade no PV for it.

Status on today's state: all four tests are met.
- Worst narrowbody preference year: 72.0% (2040); 80% in 2045 and 2050.
- A320: 60.0% before NGSA enters service.
- 3 sources and 3 makers in 2040-2050.

My reading of rules.md (approximate), from NGSA EIS 2037:
- S1 and S6 (NGSA alone, +3 pp a year): met.
- S2, S3, S5 and S7 (fps EIS about 2045, 8-year lead, long-run split 58/42 in our favour): about 64% in 2040, 68-69% in 2045 and 63-64% in 2050. Met.
- S4 (7-year fps, EIS 2042, 5-year lead, long-run split 55/45): about 64% in 2040 and 62-63% in 2045, falling to about 57-58% in 2050. Lost in 2050.

Protect the A320 family is now locked in: Boeing's Rate Increase lapsed and preference held 60% to EIS.

Enabler: code 7 holds 3 sources and 3 makers on every NGSA-hold row. A P&W-Rolls-Royce Joint Venture would cut us to 2 sources, so we do not ask for one.

No allowed order restores S4's 2050 share. Delay Tactics are deleted and the Re-engine is widebody, so I pay no premium.

cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Airbus has launched its new single-aisle and given its customers a choice of engine, and CFM is on it. We thank them for that. We don't have a birthright on any order, and we'll earn our place on that airplane every day.

So, together with our partners at Safran, we're committing to a new CFM engine for it, a step forward from today's LEAP, and we're offering it to both of our airframer customers. It's ready when testing says so, and not before 2041. We'll prove its durability in test, hot and harsh conditions included, before it enters service. Our customers ask that of us, and we ask it of ourselves. We're also working with Embraer, with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe.

RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

On capacity, we'll work with both airframers, together with Safran, on LEAP today and on what comes next. LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first.

Here's what we don't know: when the next airplane after this one launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The record moved in 2030. NGSA launched for entry into service in 2037 on code 7, and two rival new narrowbody engines (GTF2, ready 2036, and UltraFan NB, ready 2037) are launched and selected next to us. On the hold path our narrowbody share falls from 76% to 43.4% in 2045, and hold is already -22.89. We don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564]. We win by defending the seat the record gives us, paid for in the columns the record supports, without betting the balance sheet. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
- ducted: launch.
- partner_embraer: launch.
- open_fan, lobby_emissions and genx: hold.
This is option B, the package. Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own. No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609].
- Package row: -21.53 / -39.48 / -25.59, against hold at -22.89 / -33.48 / -29.64.
- Item: +1.36 / -6.00 / +4.05. The grid charges the full $6B bill ($4B of R&D plus the $2B strain next to the live GEnx).
- With NGSA on the record, S1 shows the launch's own effect: +1.36. Rahul's correction stands: all of that S1 gain is Partner Embraer's (+1.80 / 0.00 / +2.49). The Ducted alone is -0.44 / -6.00 / +1.56, so it's both or neither.
- Cost in S2: the whole $6B bill and no more. Airbus would have to walk away from its own stated aim of "supply certainty, not leverage".
- The bill is committed today. The next round, 2045, comes after the 2041 ready year, so there's no cancel. I carry that risk because it's bounded at the bill and S2 is the column the record argues against.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column S1, the record. Weights: S1 60 / S2 10 / S3 30.
- I moved 10 points from S3 to S1, off my frame's 50/10/40 and onto Rahul's reading. Boeing launched nothing, gave no date, and says it would "much rather be a month late than a month early". I defer to the airframer on dates [CX-0205].
- Weighted values (hold / Ducted alone / package):
  - 60/10/30: -25.97 / -26.37 / -24.54. Package item +1.43.
  - My frame's 50/10/40: item +1.70.
  - Equal weights: item -0.20.
  - Record only, 90/10/0: item +0.62.
- S2 break-evens. At my 2:1 ratio of S1 to S3: 27.3% for the item to stay at zero or better, 15.2% for it to clear $1B. With S1 = S3: 31.1% and 19.6%. The Ducted alone needs S2 below 8.5% (S1 = S3), or 3.6% at 2:1.
- The record puts S2 at 10%, for three reasons: Airbus chose code 7, it says it certifies CFM first, and it seeks capacity agreements with us from 2035. It isn't zero: 2035 is the one round Airbus can switch before 2037.
- The package clears my $1B ε by 0.43, so no tie-break is needed. At a 50/20/30 stress blend it falls inside ε (+0.69). That is the line I watch.

3. No birthright [CX-0564, CX-0587]. I read S2 as hard as S3. In S2 the package loses its bill. In S3, Boeing selects all three makers, and P&W and RR take part of the 737 slot CFM holds alone today. There the package is +4.05, the best plan.

4. H3 (Ducted only as a defence). The trigger is on the public record: GTF2 and UltraFan NB were launched in 2030 and selected on NGSA. The column where a rival takes CFM's slot is S3, where the item is +4.05, more than $1B ahead; S1 is a three-way split too. The Ducted is a defensive LEAP-class step with less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain [CX-0183]. It is never offered or described as the next generation.

5. My 20% line [CX-0217]: rebutted, not struck. It binds RISE, the next-generation engine, and RISE stays the engine of more than 20%. The Ducted answers the line by never being offered as the next engine.

6. Durability line [CX-0208]: held. Ali reports no order trades durability. 2041 is a floor that moves later if tests say so. LEAP kits stay ahead of the new programme.

7. Ali's date test.
- Ducted ready 2041, which is launch + 6. Partner Embraer counts from 2042, on that engine. No value rests on an earlier year.
- The statement says "not before 2041" as a floor, and gives no Open Fan date.
- His recorded veto on Partner Embraer riding on an Open Fan (2042 on a 2045 engine) doesn't apply: there's no Open Fan order.

8. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- Three projects (the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the live GEnx) carry one $2B strain, and the grid pays for it net.
- The floor margin is not shown. Ali's floor data ends in 2025. The rate delivered (2,592 engines a year) is on the record; the margin is not.
- So I follow doctrine (lean before capital) [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Engineering and test start now. Long-lead supplier orders wait for floor data. Kits and the LEAP rate stay first.

9. H2 and the Open Fan. NGSA enters service in 2037, eight years before any Open Fan could be ready, so every Open Fan row carries the wait.
- Alone: -20.59 / -10.00 / -24.26.
- In the four-item plan: -20.02 / -9.00 / -23.83 against the package, or $20.06B at my weights.
- That is beyond the $2.0B cap and the $15B RISE allowance. Hold, no cancel (H5). RISE stays whole as technology [CX-0214, CX-0174].
- Lobby serves only an Open Fan, so hold.

10. Premium: $0. The package is the best grid plan in S1, in S3 and at my weights. Game total: $0 of $4.0B. RISE allowance unused.

SAFRAN GATE (H7, the CFM parity rule)
- Ducted: a defence on an airframe where rivals are now selected next to CFM, offered to both airframers. That's how CFM serves every critical platform [CX-0185, CX-0587], so consent is assumed as joint practice (inference).
- Partner Embraer: a CFM engine for a third airframer, which serves every airframer. Consent assumed (inference). No Embraer number goes out before terms are agreed with Safran.
- Airbus's capacity-agreement request and Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation go through CFM with Safran, on product and supply only, standard terms, with no number before Safran agrees [CX-0184, CX-0160].
- GEnx is GE alone and is on hold.

THE BOARD'S CONDITIONS
- Weights given (60/10/30), with the expected column S1, not S2.
- Weighted item +1.43, at or above zero; +4.05 in S3, more than $1B.
- Bounded downside: the worst column (S2, -6.00) equals the bill.
- The three safety items, from Ali:
  - LEAP-1B kit outcome: not in our record. The 2030-2035 record shows no quality event, but that is an absence, not a test. Ali owns the gap with Boeing and the FAA.
  - Hot-section plan: owned by the cross-functional supply-chain, engineering and quality team, with Safran. It holds 2041 or later, with hot-and-harsh and dust testing before any date moves.
  - RISE: more than 200 hours of wind tunnel, more than 350 tests and HPT dust testing from October 2025; nothing later. Ali owns that gap with Safran.
- No safety or durability flag is raised. Absence of failure isn't clearance, so any test or field failure goes to the cross-functional team before any date moves [CX-0012, CX-0009].
- My 20% line is rebutted, and no binding objection stands.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE three things: Partner Embraer (Embraer isn't in my record), the supply-load gate (Ali's floor record ends in 2025), and the S2 weight (no precedent).

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND
- Airbus signals a code change or withdraws its capacity request, raising S2 above about 15% at my ratio.
- A test or field failure in the hot section.
- Floor data showing the supply base can't carry LEAP and the kits alongside the Ducted.
- Safran declining.
If Partner Embraer falls, the Ducted falls with it. It ain't that hard [CX-0653].

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

The NGSA question is settled. Airbus launched in 2030 for entry in 2037 and chose all three engine makers (code 7). Two rival new narrowbody engines are now launched and selected next to us. So the question is no longer whether we're on the next Airbus. It's how much of that installed base we keep once three engines share it, and what we're holding when Boeing moves [CX-0422, CX-0493].

On the hold path our narrowbody share falls from 76% to 43.4% in 2045, and the hold row is already -22.89 against the status quo. We don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564], and the record now says so in writing.

This round comes down to one call. Do we spend $6B on a defensive LEAP-class step? That's a $4B Ducted, ready 2041, plus the $2B strain it triggers next to the live GEnx, with Partner Embraer riding on it from 2042. On the grid that package is +1.36 in S1 (the record as it stands) and +4.05 in S3 (Boeing launches with all three engines). It loses exactly its $6B bill in S2 (Airbus drops us from NGSA). Or do we hold, which wins only in S2?

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630]. We win by defending the seat the record gives us, paid for in the columns the record supports, without betting the balance sheet. RISE stays whole as technology. The Open Fan stays off the table because the airframer has set the date, and it isn't 2045 [CX-0205].
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2035 bulletin)
- NGSA: launched 2030, entry into service (EIS) 2037. Airbus runs the Alt plan, keeping the A320neo lines longer.
- NGSA engine selection is code 7: CFM, P&W and RR. Airbus says it will certify CFM first. It seeks long-term capacity agreements with CFM covering the A320neo and NGSA from 2035, and calls the aim "supply certainty, not leverage".
- Rival new narrowbody engines: GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (launched 2030, ready 2037). Both are selected on NGSA.
- No Joint Venture is on the record. RR commits only when P&W does, and P&W is not committing.
- Boeing: no fps launch, no date, no launch commitment.
  - It invites all three makers to propose. It will select among engines actually launched, with durability proven before EIS as a contract condition: code 3 by default, code 7 if P&W and RR can be ready by EIS.
  - It asks CFM to confirm the LEAP-1B allocation at today's rate (57 a month).
  - Its fps plan is new sites.
- Our GEnx upgrade: launched 2030, ready 2033. It counts from 2042, since no widebody Re-engine is on the record.
- Observed CFM engine share, 2030-2034: narrowbody 76.1%, widebody 42.0%.

OUR POSITION (if nobody moves): ΔPV -22.89, yield 85.69%.
- Narrowbody share path: 77.0% (2037), 65.0% (2040), 55.8% (2041), 43.4% (2045, the worst year), 48.0% from 2047. Widebody 44.8% from 2042.
- CFM narrowbody engines fall from 2,592 a year to 2036, to between 1,454 and 1,966 a year in 2037-2045, as NGSA ramps with three makers.
- Objective, narrowbody share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: NOT MET (worst year 43.4%).
- Objective, Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: NOT MET. 2035 is the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050, and NGSA's 2037 entry means any Open Fan launched now waits (H2).

DATES
- A Ducted launched now is ready in 2041: four years after NGSA's 2037 entry, and four years before a 10-year fps would enter service in 2045 (S3).
- Partner Embraer launched now counts from 2042, on that 2041 Ducted.
