- On the record: NGSA launched in 2030 on code 7; GTF2 and UltraFan NB launched in 2030 and selected on it. The hard-rule-3 trigger is met on the record.
- S1 is itself a column where rivals take CFM's slot. NGSA splits three ways where the A320neo gives CFM 60%, which is why hold's narrowbody share falls from 76.1% to 43.4% in 2045.
- S3 (+4.05) rests on an fps that has not been launched. It counts only through the carve-out: P&W and RR take part of the slot the 737 gives CFM alone.

Which values rest on agreed volumes: none is signed.
- S1 rests on a selection that is on the record.
- Airbus's request for capacity agreements is not yet agreed and goes through CFM with Safran.
- S3 rests on no agreed volume.

The package passes on S1 alone. Its margin above $1B does depend on S3: on the record alone it is +0.62.

tests.name: Volumes first: Partner Embraer (Ask 4)
tests.threshold: Same test. Its value must not rest on a selection or volume that is not on the record (inference).
tests.numbers:
On this board Partner Embraer is +5 pp on the new types where CFM is fitted; the rules shift engine share only on the fps and NGSA. The grid confirms it with 0.00 in S2, where CFM has no new type.
- Its S1 +1.80 rests on the NGSA code-7 selection on the record, the same volume as the Ducted. It does not rest on Embraer airframes.
- Its S3 +2.49 rests on the fps, through the carve-out.

It passes as mapped. One real-world condition, on disclosure rather than capital: no Embraer partnership is on the record and no Embraer volume is agreed, so no Embraer number goes to the market or an airframer until terms are agreed through CFM with Safran.

What would make it fail: a GM ruling that its value rests on an Embraer airframe not on the record, or its first counting year moving past 2042 (Ali's ground).

tests.name: No overcapitalization: payout, rating, the 2-3% band and the strain (Ask 5)
tests.threshold: New R&D plus strain committed this round, spread over its development years, must fit in the cash left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow (about $2.55B a year). The 2-3% capex band is advice in this run (inference: analogy and threshold).
tests.numbers:
- New spend: $4B/6 + $2B/6 = $0.67B + $0.33B = $1.00B a year over 2035-2040. Partner Embraer adds none.
- Room: 30% of $8.5B = $2.55B, which leaves $1.55B of headroom.
- Band: 2-3% of about $44B of revenue (the Board's figure, not in my brief) is $0.88-1.32B, and $1.00B sits inside it.
- Payout: 70% of $8.5B = $5.95B stays whole. New spend is about 11.8% of free cash flow.
- Rating: I see no risk to the A-range anchor [CX-0252]. The loss is bounded at $6B over six years.
- Strain: confirmed as booked. The Ducted alone is -6.00 in S2, which is $4B + $2B, and the GEnx is the only other live project.
- For comparison, any Open Fan would add $0.80B a year ($8B/10).

tests.name: Terms: standard terms, no concession, no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran (Ask 5)
tests.threshold: No public statement or other move that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or that talks CFM narrowbody price without Safran.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (Ask 6)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium of at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game. One RISE allowance of up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (advice)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores.
tests.numbers:
The package's worst column is S2 at -39.48: 14.94 below my blend (-24.54) and 14.53 below Culp's (-24.95). The item's worst is -6.00, the bill.

Not in the columns:
1. Irreversibility. S2 is decided this round, and the next round (2045) falls after the 2041 ready year, so there is no cancel.
2. Boeing moves other than a 10-year, code-7 fps: a 7-year fps (entry 2042), a launch via Embraer, or a 2045 launch that would also find the Ducted ready. That is upside S1 doesn't count.
3. A P&W-RR Joint Venture. It is not on the record and would take 10 pp from CFM.
4. Supply. The Ducted comes in from 2041 as CFM narrowbody volume steps down from 2,592 to 1,454-1,966 engines a year. The board prices only the $2B strain. The floor is Ali's ground, and my LEAP volume dates have slipped on suppliers before (2,000 LEAPs promised for 2024, now guided for 2026).
5. Widebody re-engines or a rival widebody upgrade.
6. Airframer delivery slowdowns, tariffs or a recession [CX-0961].

tests.name: Dated profit sequence (advice)
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill years, ready year and first year of share gain, inside the board's horizon (narrowbody to 2056; widebody to 2061 per the brief) (inference).
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: bill 2035-2040 ($4B R&D plus $2B strain); ready 2041 (Ali's ground). First share gain in 2041 on NGSA in S1 and S3, plus the fps from 2045 in S3. That is 16 years of narrowbody count to 2056.
- Partner Embraer: no bill; counts 2042-2056 (15 years).
- GEnx: live; counts 2042-2061.
- Open Fan: bill 2035-2044; ready 2045; no share gain on the board, and the wait penalty runs from NGSA's 2037 entry.

A PV grid can't date the year of cumulative break-even, and I won't invent one.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan that stacks two or more projects (the $2B strain). GEnx passes only net of the strain it adds. GE9X losses are not live (inference).
tests.numbers: Flag raised. The package runs three projects (the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the live GEnx) on one $2B strain. The grid prices the strain, and net of it the package is +1.36 in S1 and +1.43 at my weights, so it passes. The $2B is the only supply cost the board prices; the floor load is Ali's ground. GEnx is on hold, so there is no GEnx item. GE9X losses are not live: I expected them past peak a year after its 2026 entry.

tests.name: Guide low (advice) (Ask 7)
tests.threshold: Recommend a low expected PV at the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed (inference).
tests.numbers:
Book -26.0.
- That is 1.46 below the package at my weights (-24.54) and 1.05 below Culp's (-24.95).
- It books the package as if S2 carried about 19% at my S1:S3 ratio, near the 20% line. The stress blend of 50/20/30 gives -26.34.
- It takes no credit for the Boeing upside or Partner Embraer's S3 value until the capacity agreements are signed and an fps is on the record.

Culp's plan to book below -24.95 points the right way; -26.0 is my number.

vetoes.plan: C, if ordered: ducted launch without partner_embraer (this also covers the package if Partner Embraer is struck)
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding ground 1 (pays for itself). The item is -0.44/-6.00/+1.56:
- -0.40 at my weights (S1 60 / S2 10 / S3 30);
- -0.20 at Culp's (50/10/40);
- -1.63 at equal weights.
It loses in S1, the record column. The hard-rule-3 route needs S2 below 8.5% (S1 = S3) or 3.6% (my ratio), and the record does not give that.

The veto lifts if Culp either:
- answers with evidence from the record that puts S2 below those lines; or
- declares the gap (0.40 at my weights, 0.20 at his) as a doctrine premium within the $2.0B cap.

Note: my veto right is an inference. teams.md §1 shows my tests, not a formal decision right, and the GM reads a failed test as binding unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: D, if ordered: open_fan launch in any form (alone, with lobby_emissions, with partner_embraer, or inside the four-item plan)
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding grounds 1 and 2.
- Ground 1: the item is negative in every column. Alone it is -20.59/-10.00/-24.26 against a $10B bill; inside the four-item plan it is -20.02/-9.00/-23.83 against the package. It loses more than its bill in S1 and S3.
- Ground 2: its cost against the best non-RISE plan is $20.02B (S1), $23.83B (S3) and $20.06B at my weights. That is above the $2.0B round cap and the $15B RISE allowance.

RISE stays funded as technology. This is a veto on the launch, not on the R&D (H5).

Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: lobby_emissions launch without an Open Fan that passes
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding ground 1. It has no effect on the board on its own: -1.00 next to the package, or -3.00 with strain next to the GEnx alone (inference; not a grid row).

Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: partner_embraer launch without the Ducted (alone, or on an Open Fan)
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding ground 1. It needs a new CFM engine. On an Open Fan it is 0.00 against hold in every column (OF+PE equals OF), so it does not beat hold, and the Open Fan under it fails. It would also count from 2042 on an engine not ready until 2045 (Ali's ground).

Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: A, if chosen with S3 as the expected column: hold everything
vetoes.ground:
Capex, binding ground 2 (premium above the cap, hard rule 9). Holding with S3 as the expected column gives up $4.05B against the package, above the $2.0B round cap.

Holding at my weights gives up $1.43B, and at Culp's $1.70B. Those are within the round cap, but either must be declared: it would use 36-43% of the $4.0B game cap.

Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement, answer to the airframers' capacity requests, or other move that carries launch-era pricing, a price concession, or CFM narrowbody price without Safran
vetoes.ground:
Terms, binding ground 3. Culp's draft does not engage it. The answers to Airbus's capacity-agreement request and Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation must stay on product and supply, on standard terms, with no number to an airframer before Safran agrees. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision.

Note: my veto right is an inference (teams.md §1); it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: B, the package as recommended (advice)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, not a veto ground:
- It is both or neither: if Partner Embraer is struck, hold the Ducted.
- Book expected PV low, at -26.0.
- No Embraer volume goes out until it is agreed through CFM with Safran.
- Stacking flag: three projects on one $2B strain, while the supply-floor evidence is Ali's.
- The $6B cannot be cancelled before the 2041 ready year.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Things that would turn me against the package:
1. A credible reading from the record that puts S2 at 15% or more at my S1:S3 ratio (20% with S1 = S3). The package then sits inside the $1B ε, and I would advise hold on the tie-break. At 27% (31% with S1 = S3) it fails pays-for-itself, and I would veto it.
2. Airbus withdrawing its capacity-agreement request, or signalling a code change before NGSA's 2037 entry. Either would raise S2.
3. Partner Embraer struck: Safran declines, Ali's date ground fails it, or the GM rules that its value rests on Embraer airframes not on the record. Then the Ducted alone (-0.40 at my weights) fails, and my veto applies.
4. Floor evidence from Ali that LEAP and a Ducted can't run together at a cost inside the $2B strain. I would re-price it.

Things that would strengthen it:
1. A Boeing fps launch on code 7 on the record. S3 then becomes a record column (+4.05), and I would book higher.
2. Signed capacity agreements with Airbus, through CFM with Safran. That is the volume commitment that lets me raise the booking from -26.0.

Things that would make me re-test:
1. A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment on the record, which takes 10 pp from CFM.
2. A widebody re-engine.

On an unresolved durability flag (Ali's ground, not mine): holding then costs $1.43B at my weights ($1.70B at Culp's). That is within the round cap, and it must be declared.
cfo.memo:
Larry, there's nothing to hide, and the record has moved. Your rows are right: the package is +1.36 in S1, -6.00 in S2, +4.05 in S3. But the S1 positive is Partner Embraer's. The Ducted alone is -0.44 in S1 and -0.40 at my weights, so it's both or neither.

My weights: S1 60, S2 10, S3 30. S1 is the record. S2 is low because Airbus chose code 7, certifies us first and wants our capacity. Not zero: this is the one round Airbus can switch. S3 gets less than your 40. Boeing has no launch and no date, and we don't raise on early signals. The package is +1.43 at my weights and +1.70 at yours; both clear the $1B. On the record alone it's +0.62, so part of that margin is Boeing's.

Volumes: S1 rests on NGSA's selection, on the record. On this board Partner Embraer is five points on the new types where we're fitted, zero in S2, so it rests on that same volume. It passes. No Embraer number goes out until it's agreed, with Safran.

Capex: about $1.0B a year against $2.55B of room. Payout stays at 70%-plus; no rating risk.

What the case leaves out: S2 at -39.48, 15 below our blend, and no round to cancel in before 2041. But the good news is the loss stops at the bill.

Premium: $0. The Open Fan costs $20-24B: no. Book it low, -26.0, and raise it once the capacity agreements are signed.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): Ducted launched in 2035 (options B and C)
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than launch + 6. An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails
tests.numbers: Launch 2035, ready 2041 = 2035 + 6. Package item (Ducted + Partner Embraer minus hold) +1.36 / -6.00 / +4.05; Ducted alone -0.44 / -6.00 / +1.56 (S1/S2/S3). I recomputed both from the grid rows: -21.53, -23.33 and -22.89 in S1; -39.48 and -33.48 in S2; -25.59, -28.08 and -29.64 in S3. By the rules the board books the +10 pp 'from the year it is ready', so the value rests on 2041 and no earlier year. 2041 is the board's development time, not a test result, because no ducted product has been tested. I hold it as a floor and accept no earlier year.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): Partner Embraer on the Ducted (option B)
tests.threshold: Counts 7 years after launch, and only on a CFM engine that is ready by then
tests.numbers: Launch 2035, counts from 2042 = 2035 + 7, on a Ducted ready in 2041, so the engine is ready one year before the partner counts. Item (package minus Ducted alone): +1.80 / 0.00 / +2.49.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): Partner Embraer on an Open Fan, with or without Lobby (not in Culp's options; recorded)
tests.threshold: Counts 7 years after launch, and only on a CFM engine that is ready by then (inference: my test standard applied)
tests.numbers: It would count from 2042 on an engine ready in 2045 at the earliest, three years too early. Without Lobby the grid credits nothing: Open Fan + Partner Embraer minus Open Fan = 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00. With Lobby it credits value: Open Fan + Partner Embraer + Lobby (-42.81 / -44.48 / -52.59) minus Open Fan + Lobby (-44.48 / -44.48 / -54.90) = +1.67 / 0.00 / +2.31. That value depends on a CFM engine three years before any test could back it. The frame's 0.00 holds only without Lobby. In the four-item plan Partner Embraer rides on the 2041 Ducted (+2.30 / 0.00 / +3.18 against Ducted + Open Fan + Lobby), so its date passes there.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): Open Fan launched in 2035 (option D)
tests.threshold: Ready no earlier than launch + 10 and not before 2045
tests.numbers: Launch 2035: max(2035 + 10, 2045) = 2045. The grid's Open Fan rows are booked on 2045 and no earlier year, so the date passes. Readiness against the airframe fails (see below). Confirmed for Culp's ask 1: an Open Fan cannot be ready by NGSA's 2037 entry, so H2 holds.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (veto: dates): GEnx (hold; the 2030 upgrade is live)
tests.threshold: Counts 3 years after launch, not before 2035, and not before the first re-engined widebody (2042 if none)
tests.numbers: Launched 2030, ready 2033 = 2030 + 3. No widebody Re-engine is on the record, so it counts from 2042 (widebody share 44.8% from 2042 on the hold path). No value rests on an earlier year. It still counts as a live project for strain.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (veto: dates): Culp's draft public statement and other moves
tests.threshold: Every date must be one a test can back: no Ducted year before 2041, no promise of a year, no Open Fan entry date at all, no demo year
tests.numbers: 'It's ready when testing says so, and not before 2041' is a floor equal to launch + 6, not a promise. PASS. 'RISE stays our technology programme with Safran, with no date on it': no Open Fan entry date and no demo year. PASS. The answers to Airbus's capacity request and Boeing's sourcing invitation are product and supply only, and must carry no Ducted year before 2041 and no year as a promise. What the dates stand on: the board's development times. Our RISE test record ends in October 2025: more than 200 hours of wind tunnel, more than 350 tests with an early durability focus, HPT-blade dust testing from October 2025, and noise tests with Airbus. The fly demo slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade', so every date is a floor.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Ducted
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted that is ready late still earns +10 pp from its ready year, so a late date does not fail it
tests.numbers: Ready 2041. That is 4 years after NGSA's 2037 entry (S1 and S3), and the grid already counts only from 2041. It is 4 years before a 10-year fps entering in 2045 (S3). In S2 CFM is off NGSA, and with no fps there is no new airframe to serve, so the item is -6.00, exactly the bill. On Boeing's condition that durability be proven before entry into service (Culp's ask 1): 2041-2045 gives four years of NGSA fleet time before a 2045 fps entry, on top of ground test before 2041. That is a window for field data, not a guarantee. Whether it is enough is a test result, and I will not answer it by analysis. LEAP's hot-and-harsh gap was found in the field (about 4,800 cycles against 7,000-8,000 for the CFM56), so hot-and-harsh and dust turn on, turn off goes into ground test before 2041, not after.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe (advice): Open Fan
tests.threshold: Ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service, or the board takes 35 pp of NB share (20 pp with Lobby)
tests.numbers: Ready 2045 against NGSA's 2037 entry, 8 years late in every column. Item against hold: -20.59 / -10.00 / -24.26; with Lobby -21.59 / -11.00 / -25.26; inside the four-item plan against the package, -20.02 / -9.00 / -23.83. H2 from the readiness side: hold, with RISE whole as technology.

tests.name: Physics (advice): wording check and Culp's 20% line (ask 4)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. Never call a Ducted the next generation, since it gets less than half the gain
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data. The draft calls the Ducted 'a new CFM engine ... a step forward from today's LEAP', not the next generation, and makes no fuel-burn claim. Confirmed: a ducted engine has 'less than half the fuel burn improvements' of an open fan, and 20% is 'practically impossible' without one. The Ducted is a defensive LEAP-class step (hard rule 3, doctrine), never the next generation. RISE stays the engine of more than 20%. Culp's 20% line binds RISE, and the Ducted answers it by never being offered as the next engine.

tests.name: Durability first (advice)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule
tests.numbers: The frame claims no durability is traded, so the test applies. No order trades it, provided 2041 stays a floor that moves later if testing says so, and LEAP kits stay ahead of the new programme. Yardsticks: CFM56 at about 17,000 cycles (benign) and 7,000-8,000 (harsh). In 2023 the LEAP fleet leaders were at 9,882 and about 4,800. The LEAP-1A kit more than doubles time on wing, matching the CFM56, and is retrofitted at shop visits, adding none. If the Ducted's tests show it trading durability for fuel burn or for the 2041 date, that is Culp's red line and I will flag it.

tests.name: Safety call (advice): the Board's three items and any flag (asks 2 and 3)
tests.threshold: A problem touching safety or durability goes to a cross-functional team, not one person. Say what we know, what we don't, and who owns the gap
tests.numbers: (a) LEAP-1B kit: certification due 1H 2026, a year after my 2025 date. The outcome is not in our record. The public record for 2030-2035 shows no quality event: Boeing builds the 737 at 57 a month and asks to confirm the LEAP-1B allocation, and Airbus certifies CFM first. That is an absence of an event, not a test result. I own the gap, with Boeing and the FAA as the audience. (b) Hot-section plan for the Ducted: owned by the joined supply-chain, engineering and quality team, with Safran (Safran's engineers are not in my sources). Turn on, turn off in hot-and-harsh and dust before any date moves; HPT dust testing from the start of development, as on the RISE compact core; enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make and MRO. It holds 2041 or later. (c) RISE: more than 200 hours of wind tunnel, more than 350 tests with an early durability focus, HPT-blade dust testing from October 2025, and noise tests with Airbus. Nothing after October 2025 is on our record; I own that gap with Safran. Flag: none. No durability failure is in evidence, though nothing tested yet clears one either. The flag condition stands: any test or field failure goes to the cross-functional team before any date moves.

tests.name: Supply load (advice, doctrine): does the grid pay the strain?
tests.threshold: Two or more projects bring $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers; recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain
tests.numbers: The package is three projects (Ducted, Partner Embraer and the live GEnx) carrying one $2B strain. The item net of $4B R&D and strain is +1.36 / -6.00 / +4.05. At Culp's S1 50 / S2 10 / S3 40 it is +1.70 (package -24.95, hold -26.65). At equal weights it is -0.20 (-28.87 against -28.67), which fails. With S1 = S3, it pays while S2 is below 31.1% and clears $1B below 19.6%. The Ducted alone is -0.20 at Culp's weights and -1.63 at equal weights, and pays only with S2 below 8.5%. The weights are Culp's call: no evidence, following Culp.

tests.name: Supply load (advice, doctrine): floor evidence the Board asked for (ask 5)
tests.threshold: Floor evidence that the 9 suppliers at 15 sites behind 80% of shortages carry the LEAP rate with margin, before the strain is taken on
tests.numbers: Rate: the game record shows CFM delivering 2,592 NB engines a year in 2030-2034 (LEAP-1B 1,368 at 57 a month; LEAP-1A 1,224 at 60% of 1,020 A320neo), with no slip or quality event on the record. Margin: not shown. The board models airframe factories, not our suppliers. The latest floor data in our record is from 2025, in colleagues' words, not mine: 80% of shortages from 9 suppliers at 15 sites; LEAP down 13% in Q1 2025 on material inputs; material flow up more than 30% a year later in Q3 2025; 550-600 engineers at supplier sites. On the board's demand, CFM NB engines fall to 1,454-1,966 a year in 2037-2045, 24-44% below the 2,592 peak. The Ducted's production from 2041 lands in that trough (1,643 in 2041, 37% below); its development in 2035-2036 overlaps the peak. That is demand, not the floor. I own the gap. Following doctrine: lean before capital, and kits ahead of the new programme.

tests.name: Supply load (advice): capacity requests alongside a Ducted (ask 6)
tests.threshold: Requested volumes within what the record shows delivered; product and supply only; no number before Safran agrees
tests.numbers: LEAP-1B at today's 57 a month = 1,368 engines a year, the rate on the record for 2030-2034. On the Alt plan Airbus's A320 lines are a ceiling, never above today's rate, and NGSA has first claim. On the board, CFM NB demand never exceeds 2,592 a year after 2036. On the board's demand, supply can carry both requests and a Ducted, but the floor margin is unproven (previous row). The numbers go to Safran first.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign (advice)
tests.threshold: Widebody: prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture. Narrowbody: RISE technology into LEAP while RISE matures; this does not argue against the Open Fan
tests.numbers: GEnx: a live upgrade on a proven architecture, +5 pp widebody from 2042 with no new R&D. Narrowbody: the Open Fan is held and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP. The Ducted should take its hot section from LEAP durability hardware and RISE compact-core work, not a clean sheet (inference).

vetoes.plan: partner_embraer: launch on an Open Fan without a Ducted, with or without lobby_emissions. This is not in Culp's options B or C and does not apply to the package; it is recorded so it is not added later.
vetoes.ground: Dates not backed by real testing, binding ground 1. Partner Embraer counts from 2042 (2035 + 7), but an Open Fan is ready in 2045 at the earliest (launch + 10, not before 2045). The grid credits it anyway: Open Fan + Partner Embraer + Lobby minus Open Fan + Lobby = +1.67 (S1) / 0.00 (S2) / +2.31 (S3), a value that depends on a CFM engine three years before any test could back it. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results. The team rule binds this veto unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: Any public statement, other move, capacity answer to Airbus or product proposal to Boeing that gives a Ducted ready or delivery year before 2041, states 2041 as a promise rather than a floor, or gives any Open Fan entry date. Culp's draft passes ('ready when testing says so, and not before 2041'; RISE 'with no date on it'). This is recorded so the wording holds.
vetoes.ground: Dates not backed by real testing, binding ground 2: a date no test backs. 2041 is the board's development time (2035 + 6), not a test result, so it may be given only as a floor. Note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference. My words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern believing durability-fix results. The team rule binds this veto unless Culp answers it with evidence.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in any combination (option D)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a date veto: the 2045 date passes. Readiness fails, because it is ready in 2045 against NGSA's 2037 entry, 8 years late in every column. Item -20.59 / -10.00 / -24.26; with Lobby -21.59 / -11.00 / -25.26; inside the four-item plan -20.02 / -9.00 / -23.83 against the package. Hold, and keep RISE whole as technology. We failed twice. We got it done.

vetoes.plan: ducted: launch alone (option C), for example if Partner Embraer is struck
vetoes.ground: Advice (supply load, doctrine): the grid does not pay the strain. The item is -0.44 / -6.00 / +1.56: -0.20 at Culp's S1 50 / S2 10 / S3 40 and -1.63 at equal weights. It pays only with S2 below 8.5%. If Partner Embraer falls, I advise hold.

vetoes.plan: ducted + partner_embraer (option B): conditions for the strain and the date, not an objection on dates

LEAP durability kits and the LEAP rate stay first, and the Ducted's long-lead supplier orders wait for floor data showing margin; engineering and test can start at launch. I own the gap. (2) The hot-section durability plan is owned by the cross-functional supply-chain, engineering and quality team, with Safran. It runs turn on, turn off in hot-and-harsh and dust, and holds 2041 or later. (3) 2041 is a floor. If testing moves it later, we report it, and the grid value booked at 2041 falls. ops.would_change_mind_if: Test or field data only, never analysis. (1) A durability or quality event on the LEAP-1B or LEAP-1A fleet on the record, or a LEAP-1B kit outcome showing the fix did not turn the problem off. I would flag the Ducted's hot section and hold its date until the cross-functional team turns the problem on and off in test. (2) Hot-and-harsh or dust test results showing the Ducted's hot section cannot hold durability by 2041. The date then moves later, never earlier, and Culp re-tests the value the grid books at 2041. If the plan needs durability traded for fuel burn or for 2041, that is a red line and I flag it. (3) Floor data showing the 9 suppliers at 15 sites cannot carry the LEAP rate and kits with margin alongside the Ducted's development. Then I advise hold, or gating every long-lead order. Field data showing margin would close the gap. (4) Open Fan: nothing on this board moves 2045 earlier, and NGSA's 2037 entry is on the record, so readiness keeps failing. Only a record with no new narrowbody entering service before 2045 would change that. (5) The column weights are Culp's and Ghai's ground. If S2 carries 31% or more, the grid no longer pays the strain and my supply-load advice turns to hold.
ops.memo:
Turn on, turn off. I recomputed every date.

Ducted, launched now: ready 2041, launch plus 6. Four years after NGSA's 2037 entry, four before a 2045 fps in S3. The board books its value from 2041, no earlier. It passes. But 2041 is the board's development time, not a test result: a floor, not a promise. Partner Embraer counts from 2042 on that engine. Passes. Open Fan: 2045 at the earliest, eight years after NGSA. The date passes; readiness fails. Hold.

One thing the frame missed. Open Fan plus Partner Embraer plus Lobby credits Partner Embraer +1.67 in S1 and +2.31 in S3, from 2042, on an engine not ready before 2045. That fails my date ground. Not proposed; recorded.

The Board's three items. LEAP-1A: tested, certified, in every delivery. LEAP-1B kit: certification due first half 2026; the outcome is not in our record. RISE: more than 350 tests, HPT dust testing from October 2025; nothing later. I own those gaps. No failure is on the record, so no flag. Nothing tested clears one either.

Hot section: a cross-functional team owns it; dust and hot-and-harsh testing before any date moves. No single person makes a safety decision. Not the next generation: less than half the open fan's gain. The reason is physics.

Supply: the record shows the LEAP rate delivered, 2,592 engines a year. Not the margin. Kits first; long-lead orders wait for floor data.

No veto on the package. We find problems before problems find us.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order.

Here's what we know. Airbus has launched its new single-aisle and given its customers a choice of engine, and CFM is on it. We thank them for that. We don't have a birthright on any order, and we'll earn our place on that airplane every day.

So, together with our partners at Safran, we're committing to a new CFM engine for it, a step forward from today's LEAP, and we're offering it to both of our airframer customers. It's ready when testing says so, and not before 2041. We'll prove its durability in test, hot and harsh conditions included, before it enters service. Our customers ask that of us, and we ask it of ourselves. We're also working with Embraer, with Safran, so that engine has a home on more than one airframe.

RISE stays our technology programme with Safran. Testing goes on, and what we learn keeps flowing into the LEAP fleet. We won't put a date on it. It goes into service when an aircraft needs it.

On capacity, we'll work with both airframers, together with Safran, on LEAP today and on what comes next. LEAP durability kits and deliveries come first.

Here's what we don't know: when the next airplane after this one launches, and what it flies with. When we know, you'll know. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW DO WE WIN [CX-0467]. The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. The record moved in 2030. NGSA launched for entry into service in 2037 on code 7, and two rival new narrowbody engines (GTF2, ready 2036, and UltraFan NB, ready 2037) are launched and selected next to us. On the hold path our narrowbody share falls from 76% to 43.4% in 2045, and hold is already -22.89. We don't have a birthright on that next order [CX-0564]. We win by defending the seat the record gives us, paid for in the columns the record supports, without betting the balance sheet. We get paid in dollars, not in percentages [CX-0630].

DECISION
- ducted: launch.
- partner_embraer: launch.
- open_fan, lobby_emissions and genx: hold.
This is option B, the package. Ghai and Ali each recommended it on their own. No colleague's binding test fails, so there are no overrides.

THE TESTS
1. Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0609].
- Package row: -21.53 / -39.48 / -25.59, against hold at -22.89 / -33.48 / -29.64.
- Item: +1.36 / -6.00 / +4.05. The grid charges the full $6B bill ($4B of R&D plus the $2B strain next to the live GEnx).
- With NGSA on the record, S1 shows the launch's own effect: +1.36. Rahul's correction stands: all of that S1 gain is Partner Embraer's (+1.80 / 0.00 / +2.49). The Ducted alone is -0.44 / -6.00 / +1.56, so it's both or neither.
- Cost in S2: the whole $6B bill and no more. Airbus would have to walk away from its own stated aim of "supply certainty, not leverage".
- The bill is committed today. The next round, 2045, comes after the 2041 ready year, so there's no cancel. I carry that risk because it's bounded at the bill and S2 is the column the record argues against.

2. Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. Expected column S1, the record. Weights: S1 60 / S2 10 / S3 30.
- I moved 10 points from S3 to S1, off my frame's 50/10/40 and onto Rahul's reading. Boeing launched nothing, gave no date, and says it would "much rather be a month late than a month early". I defer to the airframer on dates [CX-0205].
- Weighted values (hold / Ducted alone / package):
  - 60/10/30: -25.97 / -26.37 / -24.54. Package item +1.43.
  - My frame's 50/10/40: item +1.70.
  - Equal weights: item -0.20.
  - Record only, 90/10/0: item +0.62.
- S2 break-evens. At my 2:1 ratio of S1 to S3: 27.3% for the item to stay at zero or better, 15.2% for it to clear $1B. With S1 = S3: 31.1% and 19.6%. The Ducted alone needs S2 below 8.5% (S1 = S3), or 3.6% at 2:1.
- The record puts S2 at 10%, for three reasons: Airbus chose code 7, it says it certifies CFM first, and it seeks capacity agreements with us from 2035. It isn't zero: 2035 is the one round Airbus can switch before 2037.
- The package clears my $1B ε by 0.43, so no tie-break is needed. At a 50/20/30 stress blend it falls inside ε (+0.69). That is the line I watch.

3. No birthright [CX-0564, CX-0587]. I read S2 as hard as S3. In S2 the package loses its bill. In S3, Boeing selects all three makers, and P&W and RR take part of the 737 slot CFM holds alone today. There the package is +4.05, the best plan.

4. H3 (Ducted only as a defence). The trigger is on the public record: GTF2 and UltraFan NB were launched in 2030 and selected on NGSA. The column where a rival takes CFM's slot is S3, where the item is +4.05, more than $1B ahead; S1 is a three-way split too. The Ducted is a defensive LEAP-class step with less than half the open fan's fuel-burn gain [CX-0183]. It is never offered or described as the next generation.

5. My 20% line [CX-0217]: rebutted, not struck. It binds RISE, the next-generation engine, and RISE stays the engine of more than 20%. The Ducted answers the line by never being offered as the next engine.

6. Durability line [CX-0208]: held. Ali reports no order trades durability. 2041 is a floor that moves later if tests say so. LEAP kits stay ahead of the new programme.

7. Ali's date test.
- Ducted ready 2041, which is launch + 6. Partner Embraer counts from 2042, on that engine. No value rests on an earlier year.
- The statement says "not before 2041" as a floor, and gives no Open Fan date.
- His recorded veto on Partner Embraer riding on an Open Fan (2042 on a 2045 engine) doesn't apply: there's no Open Fan order.

8. Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- Three projects (the Ducted, Partner Embraer and the live GEnx) carry one $2B strain, and the grid pays for it net.
- The floor margin is not shown. Ali's floor data ends in 2025. The rate delivered (2,592 engines a year) is on the record; the margin is not.
- So I follow doctrine (lean before capital) [CX-0540, CX-0653]. Engineering and test start now. Long-lead supplier orders wait for floor data. Kits and the LEAP rate stay first.

9. H2 and the Open Fan. NGSA enters service in 2037, eight years before any Open Fan could be ready, so every Open Fan row carries the wait.
- Alone: -20.59 / -10.00 / -24.26.
- In the four-item plan: -20.02 / -9.00 / -23.83 against the package, or $20.06B at my weights.
- That is beyond the $2.0B cap and the $15B RISE allowance. Hold, no cancel (H5). RISE stays whole as technology [CX-0214, CX-0174].
- Lobby serves only an Open Fan, so hold.

10. Premium: $0. The package is the best grid plan in S1, in S3 and at my weights. Game total: $0 of $4.0B. RISE allowance unused.

SAFRAN GATE (H7, the CFM parity rule)
- Ducted: a defence on an airframe where rivals are now selected next to CFM, offered to both airframers. That's how CFM serves every critical platform [CX-0185, CX-0587], so consent is assumed as joint practice (inference).
- Partner Embraer: a CFM engine for a third airframer, which serves every airframer. Consent assumed (inference). No Embraer number goes out before terms are agreed with Safran.
- Airbus's capacity-agreement request and Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation go through CFM with Safran, on product and supply only, standard terms, with no number before Safran agrees [CX-0184, CX-0160].
- GEnx is GE alone and is on hold.

THE BOARD'S CONDITIONS
- Weights given (60/10/30), with the expected column S1, not S2.
- Weighted item +1.43, at or above zero; +4.05 in S3, more than $1B.
- Bounded downside: the worst column (S2, -6.00) equals the bill.
- The three safety items, from Ali:
  - LEAP-1B kit outcome: not in our record. The 2030-2035 record shows no quality event, but that is an absence, not a test. Ali owns the gap with Boeing and the FAA.
  - Hot-section plan: owned by the cross-functional supply-chain, engineering and quality team, with Safran. It holds 2041 or later, with hot-and-harsh and dust testing before any date moves.
  - RISE: more than 200 hours of wind tunnel, more than 350 tests and HPT dust testing from October 2025; nothing later. Ali owns that gap with Safran.
- No safety or durability flag is raised. Absence of failure isn't clearance, so any test or field failure goes to the cross-functional team before any date moves [CX-0012, CX-0009].
- My 20% line is rebutted, and no binding objection stands.

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD, DROVE three things: Partner Embraer (Embraer isn't in my record), the supply-load gate (Ali's floor record ends in 2025), and the S2 weight (no precedent).

WHAT CHANGES MY MIND
- Airbus signals a code change or withdraws its capacity request, raising S2 above about 15% at my ratio.
- A test or field failure in the hot section.
- Floor data showing the supply base can't carry LEAP and the kits alongside the Ducted.
- Safran declining.
If Partner Embraer falls, the Ducted falls with it. It ain't that hard [CX-0653].

memo_weighing.cfo:
Weighed heavily. On money I defer to Rahul's tests, and his profit calls land [CX-0910].

What I took:
- His weights, S1 60 / S2 10 / S3 30, as my decision weights. They are the low-case read on the item: +1.43 against +1.70 at my frame's weights.
- His correction that all of the S1 gain is Partner Embraer's, so the package is both or neither.
- His volumes-first pass. S1 rests on the NGSA code-7 selection on the record. Partner Embraer's value rests on that same volume, not on Embraer airframes. S3 counts through the hard-rule-3 carve-out.
- His capex count. $1.00B a year inside the $0.88-1.32B band and the $2.55B room; the 70% payout ($5.95B) whole; no A-range risk.
- His terms condition: capacity answers on standard terms, price to Safran first, no 'competitive' in the text.
- His $0 premium, and his note that holding would have cost $1.43B at these weights.

His binding vetoes are respected. Option C, the Open Fan, Lobby alone, Partner Embraer without the Ducted, and hold with S3 as the expected column: none is ordered. The statement carries no price.

Where I differ: one notch on the booking. He books -26.0. I book -26.3, the 50/20/30 stress blend, which is the line where the package's edge falls inside ε. I guide low, then raise.

His 'what the case leaves out' list goes into my watch list: irreversibility to 2041, a Joint Venture, and Boeing moves outside S3.
memo_weighing.ops:
Weighed on dates and engineering; a thin record elsewhere. His own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering: durability, the test standard and RISE physics. On supply and capacity his record is my description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked that part of his memo against doctrine.

Taken in full:
- His date passes. Ducted 2041 (launch + 6), Partner Embraer 2042, Open Fan 2045. GEnx counts from 2042.
- His reading that 2041 is the board's development time, not a test result: a floor, never a promise. The statement and the moves say exactly that.
- His recorded veto on Partner Embraer riding on an Open Fan, which my frame missed. It isn't ordered.
- His physics confirmation that the Ducted has less than half the open fan's gain. It is never the next generation, and RISE stays the 20% engine.

On safety: no flag. He's candid that no ducted product has been tested and that the LEAP-1B kit outcome isn't in our record. I accepted his structure as the cross-functional answer: the team owns the hot section with Safran; hot-and-harsh and dust testing come before any date moves; dates move later, never earlier. He owns the two evidence gaps.

On supply: he failed his own floor-evidence check. The rate is shown, the margin is not. I didn't treat that as a veto (it's advice, and doctrine). I took his remedy, which matches doctrine (lean before capital): engineering and test start at launch, and long-lead supplier orders wait for floor data. Kits and the LEAP rate stay first.

His supply-load advice is to hold if S2 reaches 31% (S1 = S3). That's consistent with my break-evens.

decision.objective_note:
Introduce the Open Fan (launched and ready by 2050): NOT MET, and it now can't be met. 2035 was the last round in which a launch could be ready by 2050 (2045). NGSA's 2037 entry is on the record, so any Open Fan waits eight years and carries the 35 pp penalty (H2). Meeting the objective would cost $20.02B in S1, $23.83B in S3 and $20.06B at my weights against the package. That is above the cap and the $15B RISE allowance, and I won't stretch the airframer test to dress it up. RISE stays funded as technology with Safran.

Narrowbody share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050: NOT MET on the hold path.
- Hold path: 65.0% in 2040, 43.4% in 2045 (the worst year), 48.0% in 2050.
- The package adds +10 pp from 2041 (Ducted) and +5 pp from 2042 (Partner Embraer). Those points apply on the new types where CFM is fitted: NGSA in S1, plus the fps in S3. The A320neo and 737 slots don't move.
- So the lift to total narrowbody share is smaller than 15 pp. My brief doesn't show the package's share path, so I can't say whether 2045 and 2050 clear 50%. On my rough reading they move toward it (inference). The GM's count decides.

The package was chosen on PV, so no premium is paid for this objective.

Safety and quality. No flag is not the same as clearance, because no ducted product has been tested yet.

Delivery. Our round 1 request is only partly met, and we raise it again. The LEAP rate is shown; the margin at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of shortages is not.
- Release the Ducted's long-lead supplier orders only on floor data that shows margin, and report that data to us before release.
- LEAP durability kits and the LEAP rate stay ahead of the new programme.
- Lean before capital.

The two orders stand or fall together, and the bill is irreversible.
- Record Safran's consent to the Ducted and Partner Embraer as one package in CFM.
- If Partner Embraer falls (Safran declines, or it slips past 2042), the Ducted alone is -0.44 in S1 and -0.40 at 60/10/30, and would not pass our test. Come back to us.
- The next round (2045) falls after the 2041 ready year, so the $6B is committed today with no cancel.

Customers and Safran.
- Answer Airbus's capacity-agreement request and Boeing's LEAP-1B allocation (57 a month) through CFM with Safran. Keep the answers to product and supply, on standard terms, with no number before Safran agrees.
- In the reply to Boeing's sourcing invitation, proven durability is our own standard. Any guarantee, time-on-wing commitment or penalty is a commercial term: it goes to Safran first and is modelled conservatively.
- Give no Embraer number until terms are agreed.

Watch S2 and book low. We accept the -26.3 booking.
- The package's edge falls inside ε at the 50/20/30 stress blend (+0.69). It goes below zero once S2 passes about 27% at the CEO's 2:1 ratio of S1 to S3.
- Report Airbus's engine code and whether the capacity agreements are signed.
- Raise the booking only when the agreements are signed or a Boeing fps is on the record.

RISE. Keep it whole as technology with Safran, with no cancel and the allowance unused.
- We accept the Open Fan objective as unmet, stated in dollars ($20.02B in S1, $23.83B in S3).
- A 2045 launch would be ready in 2055, long after NGSA's 2037 entry. Bring no Open Fan launch to us unless an airframer path appears on the record.

Cost and capital.
- New spend is $1.0B a year against $2.55B of room, the 70% payout stays whole, and the game premium is $0 of $4.0B.

- Next round, report the package's narrowbody share path from the GM's count against the 50% objective.

Public statement: acceptable as drafted. It names no rival and blames no one. It gives the Ducted only as 'not before 2041', a floor, puts no date on RISE, and carries no price.
- Keep the Embraer line free of numbers and dates.
- Never call the Ducted the next generation.
- Keep telling the market what we know and what we don't.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment with Rolls-Royce, on stated terms

Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces. (2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233]. (3) Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' is answered by equal shares, its own modules and the equal-share rule. It is never answered with P&W technology or with cash beyond our $2B share; any cash credit would return to Finance as a capital item. (4) On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward P&W's share, so the commitment needs no new spending. (5) If the Joint Venture forms, the first engine to enter service is GTF2's tested configuration. Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block, after its own durability proof. (6) No Joint Venture engine enters service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decision. No date is given for the Joint Venture.

The offer is on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The same terms apply on NGSA. A rival's price does not move the offer. pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The shortfalls were in our industrial performance: a manufacturing process issue in powder-metal parts, and shop and parts capacity that did not keep up, so engines did not get back to our customers fast enough. Engines flying in hotter, sandier conditions have also seen shorter time on wing than expected. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new-engine test hardware.

We control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch, and we are carrying it through for the customer that selected it. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. If the test data take longer, entry into service waits, and the testing does not. GTF2 is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Any partnership shares risk and investment; it never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules. On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward our share, so the commitment needs no new spending. The same durability rule applies to any Joint Venture engine. Rolls-Royce will speak for its own decisions, and the airframers for their own programmes.

The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr commit. premium_b 0; overrides empty. This is Eddy's proposal, Mitchill's recommendation and my framing lean, and all three agree.

1. THE CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035][PX-0073]. GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA (code 7, includes P&W) enters service in 2037, and an fps launched this round would enter service in 2042 or 2045. A Joint Venture formed this round is ready in 2036 with GTF2 folded in. Every P&W engine on the plan is ready by the entry into service it serves. The margin on NGSA is one year. Eddy's record is the Advantage, which certified about a year late, and mine is operating dates that slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0087]. So I promise readiness at launch + 6 and no entry-into-service date. Durability and full-life parts are conditions, not claims. If the data are late, entry into service moves and the testing does not. Eddy's configuration freeze is written into the package: if the Joint Venture forms, NGSA's first engine is GTF2's tested configuration, and his ground-1 watch item stays live.

2. BINDING VETOES. Mitchill raises none. His cancel objection is advice, and his two conditional ground-3 and ground-4 vetoes are not engaged: equal shares with no cash or technology credit, and the booked number is +0.48 (S1) with no Rolls-Royce commitment, later formation or code-5 protection booked. Eddy raises none; both his grounds pass on A and B. Nothing is struck except by the tests below.

3. GTF2: HOLD, NOT CANCEL.
- An airframer put P&W on the record. That is the visible demand I said we invest on [PX-0109], and we stand by it.
- Cancel against hold is -16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17. That is -15.52 at my weights, -14.82 at Mitchill's and -16.08 at the Board's. It writes off $1.67B to save the last $0.33B and gives up $16.50B of engine value on NGSA in S1.
- It fails Mitchill's round-1 cancel test and the Board's premature-exit test in every column.
- 2035 is the last cancel round, so hold carries GTF2 to readiness for good.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is RTX-wide in my record, and applying it here is inference. Here it argues the same way: we have already won this cycle and would be walking away from it.
- My 2024 reset of a failing fixed-price programme [PX-0064] is no precedent, because this programme is on track and selected.

4. JOINT VENTURE: COMMIT. My record here is Low. This is company doctrine plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback rule directs.
- The trigger is met: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, and the airframe is not yet in service.
- The item is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15 against hold and never below it. It is +0.39 at my weights, +0.22 at Mitchill's, +0.32 at the Board's and +0.11 with S4 at 0.05. Break-even p(S4) is 0.
- It costs nothing: GTF2's $2B covers P&W's $2B share, with no fold write-off.
- Gear and core stay P&W modules with no licence or transfer [P-1233]. Rolls-Royce's technology credit is answered by equal shares, never by P&W technology or cash.
- I note my architecture-loyalty bias. The Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036 only because GTF2 folds in, so the geared architecture comes first [PX-0014].
- Partnerships kept under strain are how we run this business [PX-0038][PX-0037].
- If Rolls-Royce waits, which is likely given its 'once Pratt & Whitney's commitment is on the public record', the commitment stands. A 2045 formation is worth roughly +0.8 to +1.2 only if GTF2's spend still counts toward our share. That is Mitchill's judgement and is not booked. The 2045 withdraw test is written in.

5. WEIGHTS. I moved toward Mitchill after his memo. S4 is lower because Rolls-Royce's wording points to sequencing, not a same-round commitment. S2 is higher because the Airbus Alt plan reverts on an engine slip, GTF2 has one year of margin, and I discount my own dates. Final weights: S1 0.50, S2 0.12, S3 0.20, S4 0.18.

Safety and durability first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- No P&W engine enters service before it is ready and its durability is proven. GTF2 and the Joint Venture engine (with GTF2 folded in) are ready in 2036, against NGSA's 2037: one year of margin.
- Every life-limited part is at full life at entry into service, and no endurance testing is traded for schedule. If the data are late, entry into service moves and the testing does not.
- Eddy's readiness and durability check binds me; I have no override.
- My own operating dates have slipped by one quarter to about two years [PX-0017][PX-0087], so I promise readiness at launch + 6 and no entry-into-service date.

Stand by the customer that selected us. No cancel while a live airframe whose code includes P&W (NGSA, code 7) can still be served by GTF2 in time. That carries in the Board's premature-exit test: the cancel row would have to beat hold in every plausible column, and it beats hold in none. It also applies Mitchill's round-1 cancel test: cancel only if the cancel row beats the hold row at his weights, judged on the remaining $0.33B, not the sunk $1.67B.

Joint Venture: share risk and investment, never our core technology [P-1233].
- P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules, with no licence and no transfer.
- Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' is answered with equal shares of risk and investment, never with P&W technology. Any cash credit beyond our $2B share goes back to Mitchill as a capital item.
- The commitment is public at once.
- On this board GTF2 folds into the Joint Venture, so they are one programme, not two engines aimed at the same airframer (company doctrine, inference).

Book only what is on the record (Mitchill's ground 4; the Board's proof before commitment).
- The booked number is the S1 value, +0.48.
- No Rolls-Royce commitment, 2045 or 2050 formation, Boeing launch or code-5 protection is booked or stated as fact.
- Other columns are weighted, not booked.

The dividend first and foremost [PX-0081], then debt back to pre-ASR levels before buybacks [P-0686][P-0669]. The only spend this round is GTF2's last $0.33B, 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, and the one-time stretch stays in reserve. Never fund an engine by cutting the dividend; Mitchill confirms.

Value, not share [PX-0055][PX-0100]. GTF2 is offered to Airbus and Boeing on standard terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade. No concession to Rolls-Royce to win the Joint Venture. A rival's discount never moves the answer.

Disclosure limits:
- No entry into service earlier than launch + 6 (ready 2036), and no durability claim not yet proven.
- Nothing on an airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062].
- No Rolls-Royce commitment stated as fact.
- The 'learned our lesson' line is replaced by a factual account of the fleet durability work, reviewed by counsel (the Board's recommendation, carried from round 1).
No widebody engine [PX-0027].

The Board's would-veto list, carried in:
(1) gtf2_solo cancel, with or without a commit.
(2) A commit whose case books Rolls-Royce's commitment, a later formation or code-5 protection as certain value.
(3) A commit on terms that put our gear or core into the Joint Venture, or that pay Rolls-Royce's technology credit in P&W technology.
(4) A commit if Eddy finds the Joint Venture engine cannot be ready by NGSA's entry into service, or finds an unresolved parts failure.
(5) Any unresolved Mitchill or Eddy veto, unrebutted red-line flag, or entry in overrides.
(6) Any spend that strains the dividend or takes debt off its pre-ASR path.

Premium cap: doctrine and objective premiums together stay at or under $1B. The Board passes an item that trails hold only as a declared premium of at most $0.5B that serves the objective. I expect premium_b 0, because the commit item is at least 0 at any weights.

If Shane cannot write terms that keep the gear and core out, or flags a fold-in risk to the 2037 entry into service, my fallback is jv_with_rr hold.

WHY HOLD GTF2:
- An airframer put us on the record. That is the visible demand I said I invest on [PX-0109]; we invested, and we stand by it.
- Cancel is below hold in every column (-16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17). It writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B, abandons the customer that selected us, and walks away from a cycle we have already won [PX-0071][P-1347]. I said 'miss a cycle' of RTX's businesses in general; applying it here is inference.
- A live GTF2 also answers a 2035 fps with no new capital (S3, +5.21).
- My 2024 reset of a failing fixed-price programme [PX-0064] is no precedent here: this one is on track and selected.

WHY COMMIT NOW (record Low; this is doctrine plus Neil's cash test and Shane's technical test):
- My trigger is met: a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce.
- On the grid it is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15, never below hold, with no new R&D because GTF2 folds in. If Rolls-Royce waits, the commitment stands, and we can withdraw before formation once the 2045 grid shows the value.
- GTF2 comes first [PX-0014]. It is the reason the Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036, so any Joint Venture engine is built on our geared architecture. I note my own architecture-loyalty bias here.
- Partnerships kept under strain are how this business runs [PX-0038][PX-0037].
- Not booked: Rolls-Royce's commitment, any later formation, any protection against a code-5 switch.

PROVISIONAL WEIGHTS: S1 0.45, S2 0.10, S3 0.25, S4 0.20. Expected column S1 (rivals hold). Expected PV: A +0.66, B +0.23. My instinct puts the next single-aisle around mid-decade [PX-0093]; I discount my own timing views and never speak for an airframer's dates.

OTHER MOVES:
- Public: standard terms on GTF2 to both airframers, no launch discounts.
- Public: the Hot Section kit sold through MRO at value.
- Private: an annual GTF2 programme NPV review to the Finance Committee.
- Private: the GTF2 durability programme, with entry into service conditional on the data.

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE (Neil to check the figures, Shane the readiness, counsel the GTF paragraph):
'Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The fleet durability work goes on: the Hot Section upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new-engine test hardware. We control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch, and we are carrying it through for the customer that selected it. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. If the test data take longer, entry into service waits, and the testing does not. GTF2 is on offer to any new single-aisle on standard terms, with no launch discounts. Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Any partnership shares risk and investment; it never shares our core technology, and Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own. Rolls-Royce will speak for its own decisions, and the airframers for their own programmes. The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.'

tests.numbers:
Rough scale, judgement only:
- In the S1 year table, the discounted gain from 2045 on is about 0.57 of the 2037-2060 total. A level stream over 2045-56 is about 0.37 of one over 2037-56, and over 2050-56 about 0.17.
- Scaled from the +2.15, a 2045 formation is worth roughly +0.8 to +1.2 and a 2050 formation +0.4 to +0.6.
- That holds only if GTF2, by then ready and in service, still folds in with its $2.00B counted toward our share.
- If the board charges a fresh $2.00B share instead (R&D is charged undiscounted), a 2045 formation is roughly -0.8 to -1.2, and a 2050 formation about -1.5.
- So a later formation is worth at least 0 only on the fold-in condition. Once NGSA is in service, the equal-share rule can also cut either way.

The 2045 withdraw test: order withdraw if the 2045 brief's withdraw row is no worse than its hold row in every column weighted at 0.2 or more, or if its weighted value against hold is at least 0. Withdraw also if a condition we commit on has lapsed:
- (a) GTF2's spend no longer counts toward our share;
- (b) the gear and core are not P&W's own modules;
- (c) no live airframe not yet in service carries a code that includes Rolls-Royce, and Rolls-Royce's commitment is not on the record (NGSA will be in service by 2045);
- (d) a technology credit is asked for in cash or in P&W technology.

The withdraw is sealed in the same round as Rolls-Royce's order, so it is our only protection against a formation we do not want.

tests.name: S2 exposure (NGSA to code 5)
tests.threshold: Judgement only. It is not on the grid and is not bookable
tests.numbers:
No order repairs S2. It is -13.87 on both hold rows and -15.69 on both cancel rows, and the commit adds 0 in S2.

My first read is that this is a timing risk: GTF2 has one year of margin, 2036 against 2037. If the durability data slip, it becomes more pervasive, because the Alt plan reverts on an engine slip.

Under code 5, Rolls-Royce is fitted with UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture engine. On a literal reading of the equal-share rule, a formed Joint Venture could carry P&W share on NGSA. But the grid has no S2 + S4 column, and a switch to code 5 would most likely follow a GTF2 slip or quality event that a Joint Venture does not cure. I put $0 on it. The answer is a GTF2 that is ready and proven.

Hold (the last $0.33B): against cancel it keeps +16.17 (S1), +1.82 (S2), +21.53 (S3) and +16.17 (S4). That is 5x to 65x the tranche, against PV 0 for $0.33B put to debt or a buyback.

vetoes.plan: gtf2_solo: cancel, with or without jv_with_rr: commit (options C and D)

CONDITIONAL, not engaged by option A as drafted: jv_with_rr: commit on terms that pay Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology Rolls-Royce brings' in cash beyond equal shares of the $2.00B, or in P&W gear or core technology
