cfo.would_change_mind_if:
(1) Hold to cancel: only if a brief's cancel row beat its hold row. On this grid, that would need extra GTF2 spend above $16.17B in S1 (or $1.82B in S2) to flip even one column. A durability slip that cost us NGSA would still leave cancel $1.82B below hold. Nothing on this grid changes it.

(2) Commit to hold:
- Eddy cannot write terms that keep the gear and core as P&W's own modules, or he flags a fold-in risk to the 2036 readiness or the 2037 entry into service. That is his ground and Calio's stated fallback.
- Rolls-Royce's terms require a technology credit paid in cash beyond equal shares, or in P&W technology. I would then veto on ground 3.
- The case or the statement books Rolls-Royce's commitment, a later formation or code-5 protection. I would then veto on ground 4.
- Evidence before the orders seal that a formation would charge new R&D beyond GTF2's $2.00B. The commit row would then fall below hold in some column.
Weights alone never change the commit, because it is at least hold at any weights.

(3) My outlook, not the order: S2 below about 0.10 makes A's expected PV positive at my weights (break-even 0.098). A public Airbus signal on durability or supply would move S2 the other way.

(4) In 2045: the withdraw test. Withdraw if the 2045 withdraw row is no worse than hold in the columns I weight at 0.2 or more, or if a condition we commit on has lapsed: the fold-in, gear and core, a Rolls-Royce trigger, or no cash or technology credit.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. The worst column on both hold rows is S2, Airbus moving NGSA to code 5, at -13.87. No order on this board repairs it; only a GTF2 that is ready and proven does. My first read is timing, on a one-year margin; if the durability data slip, it is more pervasive.

My weights, S1 to S4: 0.60 / 0.15 / 0.15 / 0.10. Nothing new is on the record from Boeing or Rolls-Royce.

Hold GTF2. A cancel writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B. It is below hold in every column (-16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17), or -14.82 at my weights. 2035 is the last cancel round, and my round-1 test fails it everywhere. The last $0.33B is 5.6% of a $6B envelope. The dividend and the path back to pre-ASR debt are untouched.

Commit to the Joint Venture. NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, so the trigger is met. On the grid the commit is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15, or +0.22 at my weights. It costs nothing: GTF2's $2.00B covers our share, with no fold write-off. Rolls-Royce's 'credit for technology' gets equal shares of risk and investment: no cash beyond our share, and never the gear or core.

I book +0.48, the S1 value: no Rolls-Royce commitment, no later formation, no code-5 protection. A 2045 formation pays only if GTF2's spend still counts toward our share. The 2045 grid decides that, with the withdraw test written in.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: commit, on conditions. If the conditions cannot be written in, my fallback is jv_with_rr: hold.

gtf2_solo HOLD. GTF2 was launched in 2030 and is ready in 2036 (bulletin; brief section 1). NGSA's code 7 includes P&W and enters service in 2037, so GTF2 can serve the customer that selected it. No fleet, quality or supply problem in the brief needs those engineers back on the fleet, so I see no technical case for cancel. I have no evidence of my own on cancelling a programme, so hold is my default, not a view of my own. The cancel test goes to Mitchill and Calio. Grid: cancel against hold is -16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17 (rows 'cancel GTF2' minus 'GTF2: hold', S1 to S4).

jv_with_rr COMMIT. My lever trigger is met because a live airframe not yet in service (NGSA, code 7) includes Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce's own commitment is conditional and is not booked. The technical tests pass. A Joint Venture formed in 2035 is ready in 2036 with GTF2 folded in (rules: 6 years after formation, which would be 2041, or earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along; UltraFan NB, ready 2037, folds in too). 2036 is no later than NGSA's 2037. If Rolls-Royce waits, nothing forms and GTF2 serves NGSA solo. Grid: hold + commit minus hold is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15. There are three conditions (inference; my record has no Joint Venture):
(1) Gear and core. P&W designs, makes and supports them as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence and no transfer [P-1233].
(2) Configuration freeze. If the Joint Venture forms this round, the engine that enters service on NGSA in 2037 is GTF2's tested configuration, and its final-year testing is untouched. Rolls-Royce content comes in on a later block, after its own durability proof.
(3) The same rule for every engine. No Joint Venture engine enters service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life.
Capital, value and the decision itself are Calio's and Mitchill's.

ANSWERS TO CALIO'S ASKS
1. Proposal: as above.

2. GTF2 readiness and durability.
- Ready 2036. NGSA EIS 2037 gives 1 year of margin. An fps launched in 2035 enters service in 2042 (7-year, 6 years of margin) or in 2045 (10-year or Embraer, 9 years of margin). By then GTF2 would have 5 to 8 years of service on NGSA, and that in-service record is the proof Boeing's contract condition asks for.
- Test data: the GTF2 severe-environment data and the life-limited-part results are not in the brief, and the board does not model them. I will not tell the Board there is no surprise coming. My one dated record on this point is the Advantage: certification aimed at mid-2024 came in 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785], and its EIS aim of 2024 slipped about two years.
- One year of margin covers a certification-sized slip, not an EIS-sized one.
- What I bring to the Governance and Public Policy Committee is the plan, not proof: Advantage-level testing (3x the base programme [PX-0084]) at representative severe-environment conditions, and every life-limited part at full life at EIS. The data go to the committee as they exist.
- If the data are late, EIS moves and the testing does not.
- The Airbus Alt plan reverts on an engine slip, so a slip costs us more than NGSA's first year. That is a reason not to overpromise, never a reason to compress.

3. Joint Venture readiness.
- Formed now: ready 2036 with GTF2 folded in. The risk is integration work landing in GTF2's final test year, which is why condition (2) exists. Certification follows GTF2's tested configuration, so the fold-in does not move the 2036 readiness or the 2037 EIS.
- Integrated teams [P-1240]: the team mirrors the engine. Each partner owns its modules end to end, a joint integration and test team works the interfaces, and the GTF2 test team stays intact under P&W through certification.
- The pair is one development: on formation both solo programmes fold in (rules). Before formation, GTF2 and UltraFan NB are separate solo programmes; that is Rolls-Royce's programme, not our engineering load. Rolls-Royce's own account is that a Joint Venture holds only while both partners are on the same new engine [P-1875], and the fold-in gives exactly that.

4. Joint Venture terms. Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' is answered in three ways: equal shares of risk and investment; its own modules, which it designs, makes and supports; and the equal-share rule on NB share. It is never answered in P&W technology. I can write that.
- If Rolls-Royce's terms require a licence or data access to the gear or core, the condition fails. I would then propose withdraw before formation, in 2045 at the latest. Withdraw is not legal this round.
- If Calio already knows the terms cannot hold, propose hold now.

5. Pacing parts and capacity.
- The brief shows no live AOG, powder-metal or MRO problem, and the board does not model parts. My last own-words count is June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, castings +40% [PX-0120][PX-0123][PX-0125]. I have no 2035 count.
- Volumes (brief section 1): P&W delivers 816 NB engines a year through 2036. That falls to 579 in 2037 (-29%) as the A320 lines wind down, then climbs to 976 by 2044 (+69% from 2037). The largest single step is 2040-41, +161 (+24%). The peak is +160 over today (+20%).
- So OE volume transfers from GTF1 to GTF2 before it stacks, and the 2037-40 dip is the window to qualify GTF2 parts capacity before rate. Powder metal came from a capacity ramp [P-1040].
- Fleet spares stay ahead of GTF2 test hardware, and ahead of GTF2 OE when they compete for parts [PX-0123][PX-0080].

6. Engineering load (advice only; there is no strain charge on this board).
- Option B (hold, hold): one programme, GTF2, in its final year.
- Option A (hold, commit): the same load if Rolls-Royce waits. If it commits, still one programme, plus interface work kept off the certification path by condition (2).
- Options C and D: cancel frees engineers, but nothing in the brief needs them.

7. Technical veto check on each option. My two grounds are durability not proven before EIS and parts short of the fleet's needs.
- A: passes both. Conditions (2) and (3) keep ground 1 intact.
- B: passes both.
- C: neither ground is engaged, because a cancel puts no engine into service early. My record is silent on cancel: hold is the default, and the test is Mitchill's and Calio's.
- D: neither ground is engaged. If Rolls-Royce commits, the Joint Venture engine is ready only via UltraFan NB, in 2037, zero margin on NGSA's 2037 EIS (advice only). If it does not commit, P&W has no engine for NGSA at all.
No binding veto on any option.

8. Disclosure readiness check on Calio's draft. It passes.
- 'Due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch' is launch + 6.
- 'It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. If the test data take longer, entry into service waits, and the testing does not' is a condition, not a claim.
- It gives no EIS date and no airframer date.
- 'Fleet spares come ahead of new-engine test hardware' is a commitment I own daily.
- Advice: add 'The same rule applies to any Joint Venture engine.'
- Keep the time-on-wing sentence factual, as I put it in 2023 [PX-0122], with counsel's review. The 'learned our lesson' line is gone, which I support: the gaps were industrial, not the architecture [PX-0120][PX-0111].

tests.name: Readiness and durability by EIS (veto ground 1)
tests.threshold: Binding: each engine's ready year no later than the EIS of the airframe it serves. GTF2 is ready at launch + 6. The Joint Venture engine is ready 6 years after formation, or at the ready year of a folded-in solo programme if that is earlier (rules.md).
tests.numbers: GTF2: launched 2030, ready 2036 (bulletin; brief section 1). NGSA: code 7, EIS 2037, so 2036 <= 2037. fps launched in 2035 (S3 or any): EIS 2042 (7-year) or 2045 (10-year or Embraer), so 2036 <= 2042 and 2036 <= 2045. Joint Venture formed in 2035 (S4): 2035 + 6 = 2041, but with GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) folded in, the engine is ready in 2036, and 2036 <= 2037. If Rolls-Royce waits, no Joint Venture forms and GTF2 serves NGSA solo. Option D (cancel + commit, S4): ready 2037 via UltraFan NB only, so 2037 <= 2037 with zero margin; without Rolls-Royce, P&W has no engine for NGSA.

tests.name: Durability margin for severe-environment testing (advice only, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: About 1 year between ready year and EIS (inference from my own certification slip and the profile's +1.5-2 year derivative slip prior)
tests.numbers: Margin: 1 year on NGSA (2037 - 2036), the minimum; 6 years on a 7-year fps (2042) and 9 years on a 10-year fps (2045). Record: Advantage certification aimed mid-2024, came 2025 (+1 year); Advantage EIS aimed 2024, about +2 years; profile prior +1.5-2 years. One year covers a certification-sized slip, not an EIS-sized one. Thin for 2037. The Airbus Alt plan reverts to base on an engine slip, so a slip costs more than NGSA's first year. Reason to keep the testing whole, not to compress it.

tests.name: Full life at entry into service, test-data status and disclosure
tests.threshold: All life-limited parts at full life at EIS; no public EIS earlier than launch + 6 (2036); no durability claim not yet proven; severe-environment data to the Governance and Public Policy Committee as it exists
tests.numbers: Data status: the GTF2 severe-environment data and life-limited-part results are not in the brief, and the board does not model them. I present the plan (Advantage-level testing, 3x the base programme, at severe-environment conditions; full-life LLPs at EIS), not proof. Calio's draft: 'due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch' (launch + 6); 'will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life'; 'entry into service waits, and the testing does not'. Each is a condition, not a claim. No EIS or airframer date is given. Advice: add 'the same rule applies to any Joint Venture engine'.

tests.name: Pacing parts and capacity (veto ground 2)
tests.threshold: If the brief or bulletin shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, the fleet comes first and an unconditional launch fails; if none is shown, pass and note that the board does not model parts
tests.numbers: No live P&W AOG, quality escape or supply problem in the 2035 bulletin or brief. No launch is ordered this round. Brief section 1 volumes: 816 NB engines a year through 2036; 579 in 2037 (-237, -29%); 636 (2038), 659, 665, 826 (2041, +161, +24%, the largest step), 850, 869, 976 (2044); peak +160 over today (+20%). OE volume transfers from GTF1 to GTF2 before it stacks, and 2037-40 is the window to qualify GTF2 parts capacity before rate (powder metal came from a capacity ramp). Last own-words count, June 2023: 10% of the fleet AOG, about 30 pacing parts, castings +40%. No 2035 count. Fleet spares stay ahead of GTF2 test hardware and GTF2 OE.

tests.name: Contain first
tests.threshold: If a quality escape is in the brief, contain it with a dated recovery before any new commitment
tests.numbers: No quality escape in the 2035 bulletin or brief.

tests.name: Engineering load (advice only; no strain charge on this board)
tests.threshold: One new development at a time; a live GTF2 folds into a formed Joint Venture, so the pair is one programme
tests.numbers: B (hold, hold): one programme, GTF2 in its final year (2035-36). A (hold, commit): the same if Rolls-Royce waits. If Rolls-Royce commits (S4), GTF2 and UltraFan NB fold into one programme, and interface work is kept off GTF2's certification path by the configuration freeze. C and D: cancel frees engineers that no fleet problem in the brief needs. The profile's pairing constraint (no GTF2 and Joint Venture aimed at the same airframer unless the payoff favours the pair) passes: the grid gives commit 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15.

tests.name: Architecture and Joint Venture technical terms
tests.threshold: The next engine extends the GTF; in a Joint Venture, P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence and no transfer (company red line)
tests.numbers: GTF2 is a geared-turbofan derivative, and it is the reason the Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036. Terms I can write: module ownership end to end; Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' answered by equal shares of risk and investment, its own modules and the equal-share rule, never in P&W technology. Teams mirror the modules, with a joint integration and test team at the interfaces. Pass is conditional on these terms in the commitment and the statement. If Rolls-Royce's terms demand gear or core licence or data, withdraw before formation (2045 at the latest).

tests.name: Single aisle
tests.threshold: No widebody engine
tests.numbers: No widebody move is proposed; this board has none for P&W.

tests.name: Joint Venture trigger (lever test, not a veto ground)
tests.threshold: Commit only once Rolls-Royce's commitment is on the record or a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (1, 4, 5 or 7); then state the technical conditions and leave the call to Calio
tests.numbers: NGSA (live, EIS 2037, not yet in service) carries code 7, which includes Rolls-Royce. Rolls-Royce's stance is conditional ('commits once Pratt & Whitney's commitment is on the public record'): not a commitment, and not booked. Grid: 'hold + commit' minus 'hold' = 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15 (S1 to S4).

tests.name: Cancel check (deferred to Mitchill and Calio; my record is silent)
tests.threshold: When cancel is legal, propose hold as the default, report whether GTF2 can still be ready by the EIS of any live airframe whose code includes P&W, and flag the cancel test
tests.numbers: GTF2 ready 2036 against NGSA (code 7, includes P&W) EIS 2037: it can be served. 2035 is the last cancel round. Cancel minus hold = -16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17; cancel + commit minus hold + commit = -16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -1.66. No technical case for cancel: no fleet problem in the brief needs the engineers. Proposed: hold. The test belongs to Mitchill and Calio.

vetoes.plan: Option A: gtf2_solo hold + jv_with_rr commit (my proposal)
vetoes.ground: NOT A VETO. Both grounds pass: GTF2 and the Joint Venture engine are ready in 2036, no later than NGSA's 2037, and no live fleet, quality or supply problem is in the brief. My conditions are the gear and core as P&W modules, no change to GTF2's tested configuration or final-year testing if the Joint Venture forms now, and the full-life rule for any Joint Venture engine. If the final package drops the configuration freeze, or lets a Joint Venture fold-in compress GTF2's final-year testing, I invoke ground 1 at my veto check, and the team rule makes it binding then.

vetoes.plan: Options C and D: gtf2_solo cancel, with or without a Joint Venture commit
vetoes.ground: NOT A VETO. A cancel puts no engine into service before it is ready and draws no parts, so neither of my grounds is engaged. My record is silent on cancel: I propose hold as the default, report that GTF2 can still be ready (2036) for NGSA's code 7 (2037), and flag the cancel test to Mitchill and Calio. Advice only: under D, a Joint Venture formed in S4 is ready only via UltraFan NB in 2037, with zero margin.

vetoes.plan: Watch item for my veto check, not invoked: any order or public statement that gives a GTF2 or Joint Venture engine EIS date, claims GTF2 durability as proven, or compresses the durability programme to hold NGSA's 2037 EIS
vetoes.ground: Ground 1, durability not proven before entry into service. Not invoked now: Calio's draft states durability and full-life parts as conditions of EIS and gives ready 2036 (launch + 6). If such wording or an order appears in the final package, I invoke the veto at my check, and the team rule makes it binding.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
1. GTF2 test data, or a durability finding, that puts readiness after 2036 or leaves no margin to NGSA's 2037 without compressing testing. Then NGSA's EIS for GTF2 moves and the testing does not (ground 1). I would also propose jv_with_rr hold until GTF2 is in service, so no integration work lands on the critical path.
2. Rolls-Royce's terms requiring a licence of, or data access to, P&W's gear or core, or putting Rolls-Royce content into the 2037 NGSA configuration. Then hold now if it is known before sealing, or withdraw before formation (2045 at the latest).
3. A later bulletin showing a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, such as an AOG wave or a powder-metal-type escape. Then contain it with a dated recovery first, and keep fleet spares ahead of GTF2 test hardware and the GTF2 OE ramp (ground 2 on any new launch).
4. Evidence that the GTF2 production ramp (579 in 2037 to 976 in 2044) would run on capacity not qualified before rate. Then the ramp waits for qualification.
5. On cancel: only a technical failure that GTF2 cannot be ready for any live P&W code would give me a view. Absent that, hold, and the cancel test is Mitchill's and Calio's.
ops.memo:
Bad number first: S2. If Airbus moves NGSA to code 5, we're at minus 13.87, and no order on this board fixes it. What keeps us on NGSA is a GTF2 that's ready and proven. The Alt plan reverts on an engine slip, so a slip costs us more than a year.

Proposal: GTF2 hold, Joint Venture commit, on conditions.

GTF2 is ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037. One year of margin. That's the least I want; the Advantage certified about a year late. I don't have GTF2 severe-environment data, the board doesn't model it, and I won't tell you there's no surprise coming. Advantage-level testing, every life-limited part at full life at entry into service. If the data are late, the date moves, not the testing.

Cancel: no technical case, and no fleet problem in the brief. Hold; the cancel test is Neil's.

Joint Venture: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce. With GTF2 folded in it's ready 2036. Terms: we design, make and support the gear and core as our own modules, no licence, no transfer. The 2037 engine is GTF2's tested configuration; Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block after its own proof. If we can't write that, hold.

Parts: no live fleet or quality problem in the brief. We go from 816 engines to 579 in 2037, then 976 by 2044. Qualify capacity before rate; spares first.

No veto. My record is one event, June 2023; where it's silent, this is seat doctrine.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment with Rolls-Royce, on stated terms
other_moves.detail: Pratt & Whitney puts its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce on the public record. The terms: (1) The partners share risk and investment equally. Each designs, makes and supports its own modules end to end, and a joint integration and test team works the interfaces. (2) P&W designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules under its own type data, with no licence, no data access and no transfer [P-1233]. (3) Rolls-Royce's 'credit for the technology it brings' is answered by equal shares, its own modules and the equal-share rule. It is never answered with P&W technology or with cash beyond our $2B share; any cash credit would return to Finance as a capital item. (4) On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward P&W's share, so the commitment needs no new spending. (5) If the Joint Venture forms, the first engine to enter service is GTF2's tested configuration. Rolls-Royce content comes on a later block, after its own durability proof. (6) No Joint Venture engine enters service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. Rolls-Royce speaks for its own decision. No date is given for the Joint Venture.

other_moves.move: GTF2 proposal to Boeing's next single-aisle and to Airbus on standard terms; no launch-style discounts
other_moves.detail: This answers Boeing's public invitation to all three engine makers. GTF2 is ready six years from its 2030 launch, in 2036. Its durability will be proven before entry into service, which Boeing has made a contract condition. The offer is on standard commercial terms, with no launch discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055][PX-0100]. The same terms apply on NGSA. A rival's price does not move the offer. Nothing is said on either airframer's dates or rates [PX-0062].

other_moves.move: GTF fleet durability: Hot Section kit sold through MRO at value; fleet spares ahead of new-engine hardware
other_moves.detail: The GTF Hot Section durability upgrade stays on offer to operators through our MRO network at value. It is sold, not given away, and it is not tied to any airframe campaign [PX-0088][PX-0100]. decision.public_statement:
Bad news first. The GTF has not always given our customers the time on wing they paid for, and we own that. The shortfalls were in our industrial performance: a manufacturing process issue in powder-metal parts, and shop and parts capacity that did not keep up, so engines did not get back to our customers fast enough. Engines flying in hotter, sandier conditions have also seen shorter time on wing than expected. The fleet work goes on. The Hot Section durability upgrade is offered to GTF operators through our MRO network, and fleet spares come ahead of new-engine test hardware.

We control what we can control. GTF2, launched in 2030, is due to be ready in 2036, six years from launch, and we are carrying it through for the customer that selected it. It will not enter service until its durability is proven and every life-limited part has full life. If the test data take longer, entry into service waits, and the testing does not. GTF2 is on offer to any new single-aisle, Boeing's included, on standard terms, with no launch discounts.

Today Pratt & Whitney puts on the record its commitment to a Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Any partnership shares risk and investment; it never shares our core technology. Pratt & Whitney designs, makes and supports the gear and the core as its own modules. On the terms we commit to, the GTF2 programme already under way counts toward our share, so the commitment needs no new spending. The same durability rule applies to any Joint Venture engine. Rolls-Royce will speak for its own decisions, and the airframers for their own programmes.

The dividend comes first, and this plan needs no change to it or to our path on debt. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: gtf2_solo hold; jv_with_rr commit. premium_b 0; overrides empty. This is Eddy's proposal, Mitchill's recommendation and my framing lean, and all three agree.

1. THE CONSTRAINT FIRST [PX-0035][PX-0073]. GTF2 is ready in 2036. NGSA (code 7, includes P&W) enters service in 2037, and an fps launched this round would enter service in 2042 or 2045. A Joint Venture formed this round is ready in 2036 with GTF2 folded in. Every P&W engine on the plan is ready by the entry into service it serves. The margin on NGSA is one year. Eddy's record is the Advantage, which certified about a year late, and mine is operating dates that slipped by one quarter to two years [PX-0017][PX-0087]. So I promise readiness at launch + 6 and no entry-into-service date. Durability and full-life parts are conditions, not claims. If the data are late, entry into service moves and the testing does not. Eddy's configuration freeze is written into the package: if the Joint Venture forms, NGSA's first engine is GTF2's tested configuration, and his ground-1 watch item stays live.

2. BINDING VETOES. Mitchill raises none. His cancel objection is advice, and his two conditional ground-3 and ground-4 vetoes are not engaged: equal shares with no cash or technology credit, and the booked number is +0.48 (S1) with no Rolls-Royce commitment, later formation or code-5 protection booked. Eddy raises none; both his grounds pass on A and B. Nothing is struck except by the tests below.

3. GTF2: HOLD, NOT CANCEL.
- An airframer put P&W on the record. That is the visible demand I said we invest on [PX-0109], and we stand by it.
- Cancel against hold is -16.17 / -1.82 / -21.53 / -16.17. That is -15.52 at my weights, -14.82 at Mitchill's and -16.08 at the Board's. It writes off $1.67B to save the last $0.33B and gives up $16.50B of engine value on NGSA in S1.
- It fails Mitchill's round-1 cancel test and the Board's premature-exit test in every column.
- 2035 is the last cancel round, so hold carries GTF2 to readiness for good.
- 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is RTX-wide in my record, and applying it here is inference. Here it argues the same way: we have already won this cycle and would be walking away from it.
- My 2024 reset of a failing fixed-price programme [PX-0064] is no precedent, because this programme is on track and selected.

4. JOINT VENTURE: COMMIT. My record here is Low. This is company doctrine plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, as my fallback rule directs.
- The trigger is met: NGSA's code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, and the airframe is not yet in service.
- The item is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.15 against hold and never below it. It is +0.39 at my weights, +0.22 at Mitchill's, +0.32 at the Board's and +0.11 with S4 at 0.05. Break-even p(S4) is 0.
- It costs nothing: GTF2's $2B covers P&W's $2B share, with no fold write-off.
- Gear and core stay P&W modules with no licence or transfer [P-1233]. Rolls-Royce's technology credit is answered by equal shares, never by P&W technology or cash.
- I note my architecture-loyalty bias. The Joint Venture engine is ready in 2036 only because GTF2 folds in, so the geared architecture comes first [PX-0014].
- Partnerships kept under strain are how we run this business [PX-0038][PX-0037].
- If Rolls-Royce waits, which is likely given its 'once Pratt & Whitney's commitment is on the public record', the commitment stands. A 2045 formation is worth roughly +0.8 to +1.2 only if GTF2's spend still counts toward our share. That is Mitchill's judgement and is not booked. The 2045 withdraw test is written in.

5. WEIGHTS. I moved toward Mitchill after his memo. S4 is lower because Rolls-Royce's wording points to sequencing, not a same-round commitment. S2 is higher because the Airbus Alt plan reverts on an engine slip, GTF2 has one year of margin, and I discount my own dates. Final weights: S1 0.50, S2 0.12, S3 0.20, S4 0.18.
- Expected PV: A +0.09, B -0.30, C -15.82, D -12.82.
- Worst column on A and B: S2 at -13.87, which no order repairs. The answer to S2 is a GTF2 that is ready and proven.
- A is the best row at any weights, because it weakly dominates B. No doctrine or objective premium is needed.

6. TIE-BREAKS. The fleet comes first: spares stay ahead of GTF2 test hardware and OE [PX-0080]. A rival's price does not move the answer: the offer is on standard terms only [PX-0055].

7. DIVIDEND. GTF2's final $0.33B is 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, and the commit adds $0. The dividend and the pre-ASR debt path are untouched, and the one-time stretch stays in reserve [PX-0081][P-0686][P-0669].

8. DISCLOSURE. The 'learned our lesson' line is gone, replaced by a factual account of the industrial shortfalls in my 2023 words [PX-0023][PX-0029] and Eddy's [PX-0120][PX-0122]. That paragraph goes to counsel before release. The statement includes Eddy's 'same rule for any Joint Venture engine' line and Mitchill's conditional 'no new spending' wording. It gives no entry-into-service date beyond ready at launch + 6, no airframer date, and no Rolls-Royce commitment as fact.

memo_weighing.cfo: Weighted heavily. I trust Neil's cash numbers over my own dates. His arithmetic confirms my frame: cancel writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B and fails in every column; the commit costs $0 net of GTF2; the envelope is 5.6%; the dividend and debt are untouched. He books +0.48 (S1). I adopted three things from him: (1) a lower S4 weight (0.18, from my 0.20), on his reading that Rolls-Royce's 'once Pratt & Whitney's commitment is on the public record' points to sequencing; (2) a higher S2 weight (0.12, from my 0.10), on the one-year margin and the Alt-plan reversion; (3) his 2045 withdraw test and his conditional 'no new spending' wording. His two conditional vetoes, ground 3 on cash or technology credit and ground 4 on booking upside, are respected in the terms and the statement, so neither is engaged. His cancel objection is advice; I took it. At his weights the plan's expected PV is -0.75, so I record that the capitalise objective is met on the booked number but at risk in expectation. That changes the outlook, not the order.
memo_weighing.ops: Weighted as binding on readiness and parts, and as the source of the engine orders, which he proposed: hold and commit. His seat rests on one own-words event (June 2023, Low), and he says so. Where his record is silent (cancel, the Joint Venture) his memo is seat doctrine, and I treat it that way. His readiness check is exact against the rules: GTF2 2036 against NGSA 2037 and fps 2042 or 2045; the Joint Venture 2036 with GTF2 folded in; option D only via UltraFan in 2037 at zero margin. His candour that the GTF2 severe-environment data are not in hand, and that one year covers a certification slip but not an EIS slip, is the strongest input to my S2 weight. I adopted all three of his conditions: gear and core as P&W modules; the configuration freeze on the first NGSA engine; the full-life rule for any Joint Venture engine. I also took his capacity point (qualify GTF2 parts in the 2037-40 dip before rate) and his advice to add the Joint Venture durability line to the statement. No veto is raised. His ground-1 watch item stays live, and the statement gives no EIS date and claims no proven durability.

recommendations.text: Take the open door out of the public Joint Venture terms. Term (3) says Rolls-Royce's technology credit is 'never' paid in P&W technology or in cash beyond the $2B share, then adds that 'any cash credit would return to Finance as a capital item'. Published, the second clause reads as an invitation to negotiate. Keep 'never' as the public floor and move the Finance routing into the private record, as Mitchill advises.

Bring the 2045 Joint Venture decision to the Finance Committee before the orders seal, even if the ExCo plans to hold.
- The commitment is public and standing, and Rolls-Royce's wording points to it committing in 2045. A 2045 'hold' would then let the Joint Venture form, and a hold never reaches this Board.
- The rules do not say whether a GTF2 that is ready and in service still folds in at a later formation with its $2.00B counted toward P&W's share. Mitchill's judgement is that a 2045 formation is worth about +0.8 to +1.2 if it does, and about -0.8 to -1.2 if a fresh $2B share is charged.
- Show the 2045 withdraw row beside the hold row under Mitchill's written test.
- The Board would approve a withdraw whose weighted item value is at least 0 (Premature exit).

Durability before entry into service on a one-year margin.
- Eddy states that the GTF2 severe-environment data and life-limited-part results are not yet in hand, and that the committee will see the plan, not proof. The Advantage certified about a year late.
- The Governance and Public Policy Committee should receive the data as they arrive, and a readiness report before GTF2 is declared ready in 2036.
- Keep the configuration freeze: any Joint Venture integration stays off GTF2's certification path.
- If the data are late, entry into service moves and the testing does not. Airbus's Alt plan reverts on an engine slip, so a slip costs more than a year of NGSA.

Add GTF2's readiness for NGSA, and the S2 exposure (Airbus moving NGSA to code 5: -13.87 against +0.48 booked), to the top enterprise risks shared with the Audit Committee and the full Board.

- No order on this board repairs S2. Only a GTF2 that is ready and proven does.

The Board welcomes the first annual GTF2 whole-programme NPV review.
- Keep +0.48 as the booked figure.
- Label the Do Nothing comparison (+14.50 / +0.15 / +19.86 / +14.50) as derived (the cancel row plus the $1.67B write-off) and weighted, not booked.

Disclosure check: the statement passes.

Keep the dividend whole and debt on its path back to pre-ASR levels. GTF2's final $0.33B is 5.6% of the roughly $6B envelope, the commit adds nothing new, and the one-time envelope stretch stays unused and in reserve. Any GTF2 testing overrun, or any cash term in the Joint Venture, returns to Finance as a capital item.

rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION
Orders: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (the live Solo continues), `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This is my framing proposal, unchanged. McCabe and Watson recommend the same orders, and the Board lists it as would-approve. The commit is the only Board item.

1. GRID ROWS (S1-S6, $B ΔPV)
- Submitted row, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': +10.10 / -4.26 / +18.48 / +12.38 / +10.01 / +10.01.
- The same row with the item at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold': +10.10 / -4.26 / +18.48 / +10.10 / +10.01 / +10.01.
- Item value: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00.
- Worst column: 0.00, against a $4B bill. The row's own worst column, -4.26 in S2, is the live Solo's exposure, not the commit's, and it sits inside the Solo's $8B bill.

2. WEIGHTS AND EXPECTED GAIN
- Weights A, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.55, S2 0.10, S3 0.05, S4 0.10, S5 0.12, S6 0.08.
- The selection is already made (NGSA, code 7, on the record), so these weights cover rivals' moves, not a selection.
- S4 sits at 0.10 because P&W orders sealed, before our commitment is public, and its record says 'not committing today'.
- Expected gain of the commit:
  - +0.23 on A;
  - +0.38 uniform;
  - +0.23 on my S2-heavy set;
  - +0.68 S4-heavy;
  - +0.11 on McCabe's guide-low set M (S4 0.05).
- It is never below 0 on any weights. The expected row is +9.29 on A, against +9.07 for hold.

3. ROWS TESTED AND STRUCK
Each item is measured against its matching row without it.
- Cancel UltraFan NB:
  - item value -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -16.38 / -16.38 / -16.38; -15.36 on A;
  - worst -24.76, against a $5.71B write-off ($8B x 5/7);
  - it gives up $18.67B of narrowbody value in S1 (McCabe), and it loses even in S2;
  - red line: NGSA, a live airframe not yet in service, flies it. Struck.
- Cancel + commit, against hold + commit: -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -4.00 / -16.38 / -16.38. Struck.
- Trent 1000 upgrade:
  - -6.03 in S1-S4 and -5.88 in S5-S6; -6.00 on A;
  - worst -6.03 against a $2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks on it;
  - red line: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (to 2037). McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding). Struck.
- UltraFan WB:
  - -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6; -8.59 on A;
  - worst -9.00 against a $4B bill;
  - no Re-engine is on the record, it overlaps the Solo without both being selected, and it is far above the $1B cap. McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding). Struck.
- Combinations against hold: commit + upgrade -5.77 on A; commit + UltraFan WB -8.36.
- The best plan inside the red lines is hold + commit, which weakly dominates hold. Premium $0.

4. TESTS
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: an airframe already flies our engine (NGSA, code 7). The commit is no new launch and spends nothing new.
- Partner test: P&W's own commitment is not on the record, but NGSA's code 7 names P&W beside us. That meets the Board's reading of the partner test. This is doctrine (teams.md and the Board), not my record, which is Low on Joint Venture terms.
- Profitable or not at all: the commit needs an expected gain above 0, and +0.23 passes. The Board wants a narrowbody item at 0 or better with no premium: passes.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: passes.
  - Differentiated: 'we are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072].
  - Large market: NGSA.
  - Viable business: our narrowbody money falls from $8.0B to $5.7B in S4, and the 2050 share stays at 27.6%.
  - Synergy: gearbox sizing, and partner MRO.
- Sure to deliver [RX-0124]: Watson confirms the Solo ready in 2037, the full seven years. That is zero margin against NGSA's 2037 EIS: a note, not compression. If the Joint Venture forms this round, its engine is ready in 2037 through the folded Solo; without the fold it would be 2041 (formation + 6). Nothing counts on GTF2's 2036.
- No options management [RX-0051]: a live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine (under code 7, RR's slot takes UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture engine). The commitment stands only while that holds, and it gets a decision at the 2045 round.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]:
  - the remaining Solo spend is $2.29B, about $1.14B a year to 2037;
  - that is £0.84-0.85bn a year at 1.34-1.36 $/£, £1.68-1.71bn in all, and 16-17% of the FY2028 free cash flow target;
  - the commit adds no cash. If the Joint Venture forms this round, the £1.68-1.71bn is not spent.
- Widebody: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 on every held row, 5.2 pp above the line.

5. WHY THE ORDER OF STEPS CHANGED
- Round 1 said 'we commit when our partner does'. P&W says it will consider a Joint Venture once a partner's commitment is on the record. Two partners each waiting form nothing.
- Airbus has now put both of us on NGSA. That is the alignment Rolls-Royce lacked at IAE [R-0318].
- So we move first on what we control [RX-0094]. Partnership remains a preference, not a need [RX-0118], and there's no change of strategy [RX-0098].
- The test is binary. The table is set. If P&W comes to it, the Joint Venture forms. If not, we fly alone and lose nothing.

6. THE STANDING COMMITMENT (not priced on the grid; McCabe's case, adopted)
- A 2045 formation would save no cash, because all $8B is spent by then.
- It would write off $4B already spent and equalise our share with P&W's. That share effect is unpriced.
- The rules allow a withdraw before the Joint Venture forms. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so at the 2045 round we decide on that round's grid:
  - keep the commitment if the formation row beats hold and a live airframe can use the engine in time;
  - otherwise order `withdraw` in that round.
- The downside stays in our hands.

7. VETOES AND RED LINES
- McCabe co-signs the commit. Her condition is met: standard terms, with no concession in any move. Her binding withholdings on the upgrade and UltraFan WB cover orders that were not submitted. No balance-sheet veto is triggered.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. None of his three conditional grounds applies to the final text:
  - no Joint Venture date, and no UltraFan entry into service before 2037;
  - nothing counts on the Joint Venture engine before 2037, and there is no joint design change on the folded engine before entry into service;
  - the partner-shop support plan stays ours and is live before entry into service.
- The red-line flags (cancel, upgrade, UltraFan WB) are struck: none is ordered. `overrides` is empty.

8. DOCTRINE AND RECORD
The partner-first ordering, the column weights and the 2045 review are doctrine and inference (teams.md, profile.md §9, the Board), not my record. On cash I take McCabe's test as my evidence; on readiness and support, Watson's.

- Her co-signature on the commit is the condition I needed.
- She confirms weights A. I note her guide-low set M (+0.11) and keep A for the record.
- Her condition on terms is met: standard, win-win terms, with no concession anywhere in the package.
- I adopt her standing-commitment case as the 2045 plan. That includes her rule: if a fold of a ready Solo charges our $4B share on top of the $8B, the review becomes a firm withdraw.
- Her binding withholdings on the upgrade (-6.00; worst -6.03 against $2B) and UltraFan WB (-8.59; worst -9.00 against $4B) match my red lines. Neither is ordered.
- I take her S2 point. This is the last round in which Airbus can drop us before NGSA's EIS, and nothing on the grid hedges it. A cancel only makes S2 worse (-2.02).
- Capex is £0.84-0.85bn a year from free cash flow, inside a flat envelope. No balance-sheet veto is triggered.
- She offers little counterweight beyond the numbers, as expected, and the numbers agree with the proposal.
memo_weighing.ops:
I took Watson's memo as the evidence on readiness, strain, capacity and support. He invokes no Civil veto.
- Zero margin against NGSA 2037 is recorded as a note. The schedule is the full seven years, not compressed.
- I adopt his planning date for the Joint Venture engine: 2037 through the folded Solo, 2041 without it. GTF2's 2036 is not counted.
- His three conditional grounds shaped the final text:
  - no Joint Venture date, and no entry into service before 2037;
  - the folded engine keeps its own test programme, with no joint design change before entry into service;
  - the partner-shop plan stays ours and is live before entry into service; a partner's shops add capacity only after.
- He confirms $0 strain in every column for the Solo plus the commit.
- His capacity advice (gearbox, castings and forgings; about 1,040 narrowbody engines a year from 2046) goes into the internal support plan. The Boeing proposal carries the same support condition.
- Widebody's low point is 55.2%. Time on wing inside the envelope is the lever, not a programme.

recommendations.text: Take the partner in the right order: we would approve `jv_with_pw: commit` this round. NGSA's code 7 already names Pratt & Whitney beside us, and P&W has said it will consider a Joint Venture once a partner's commitment is on the record. The commit costs nothing in five columns and is worth +2.28 in S4. If the Joint Venture forms, it narrows our narrowbody money from $8.0B to $5.7B. Bring it with McCabe's co-signature and Watson's confirmation that the Joint Venture engine is ready by 2037 through the folded Solo, with no compressed maturity. Update the public wording from 'we commit when our partner does' to 'we have committed, on terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings'. If the ExCo prefers to keep its round-1 word and wait, hold is never vetoed. Say so plainly, because a deadlock in which each partner waits for the other forms nothing.

Plan now to review the standing commitment at the 2045 round. It stands until withdrawn. By 2045 both solo engines are ready (GTF2 2036, UltraFan 2037), so a P&W commit then would form a Joint Venture on terms the grid does not price today. McCabe should state that case and its bill in this package. In 2045 the ExCo should bring us either the formation with its grid row, or a withdraw if that row is below hold or no live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine in time. A withdraw in 2045 still comes before formation, so this downside stays in our hands.

The risk that matters this round is S2, Airbus moving NGSA to code 6. The hold row falls from +10.10 in S1 to -4.26 in S2, a swing of $14.36B. Nothing on the grid hedges it, and a cancel makes it $2.02B worse. Our defence is maturity and durability, not a cancel. Pace testing to the full seven years. Prove durability before entry into service, since Airbus certifies 'further makers as their engines mature'. Report Watson's ready year against NGSA's 2037 EIS, and his support gates, to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee every round. If maturity slips, tell Airbus early.

Answer Boeing's engine-sourcing invitation as a public other move, at no new spend. Offer a proposal on standard terms, with durability proven before entry into service, and give no dates. UltraFan ready in 2037 can meet any fps launched in 2035 or later (EIS 2042 at the earliest), and Boeing names code 7 if P&W and Rolls-Royce can be ready. A second airframe on the same engine is the growth story; it needs no launch from us.

No widebody programme this round, and plan the next one with the strain in mind. The widebody franchise test is not triggered. Trent holds 58% to 2041 and 55.2% in 2042-2050 on every hold row, the 2.8 pp loss being the GEnx upgrade's. No Re-engine is on the record. Keep the Trent durability and time-on-wing work inside the R&D envelope. From 2037 the Solo is ready and the $5B strain can no longer be removed, so any later Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB must carry its bill plus $5B. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, bring us the full row, within $3B of premium in all and $1B for UltraFan WB.

State the objectives plainly in `rationale`, as last round:
- Narrowbody entry: met (29.7% in 2045, 27.6% in 2050).
- Widebody: met (55.2% at the low point).
- Bounded narrowbody risk: no longer attainable on any row. The figure is $8.0B today and $5.7B at best, whether through a Joint Venture fold or a cancel, and the cancel loses everything else.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0 strain, and kept only by holding every widebody item.
We accept the bounded-risk breach because an airframe selected us, and we do not ask the ExCo to buy it back at any price.

frame.question:
So, the 2035 question, in cash and quality of earnings [RX-0054]. The narrowbody bet is made. UltraFan NB was launched in 2030 because Airbus selected us: code 7 on NGSA, entry into service 2037. About $5.7B is spent and $2.3B is still to go, to 2037. Today's position is ΔPV +10.10. Frankly, this round is not about adding activity. It is about protecting the programme an airframe flies, and finding out whether anything improves the cash without risking the downside.

There is one candidate: `jv_with_pw: commit`, with the Solo continuing. Against hold it is 0.00 in five columns and +2.28 in S4. If Pratt & Whitney commits in the same round, our narrowbody money falls from $8.0B to $5.7B. Everything else on the grid loses money in every column: the cancel, the Trent 1000 upgrade and UltraFan WB.

So the questions are these:
- Do we put our Joint Venture commitment on the record first, now that NGSA's code 7 puts Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce on the same aircraft?
- Or do we keep the round-1 wording, 'we commit when our partner does', and hold?

"We won't do anything not profitable" [RX-0058]. "We don't commit that easily" [RX-0124].

DRAFT PUBLIC STATEMENT
"So, plainly. UltraFan is in development for a new single-aisle, with entry into service no earlier than 2037. Durability will be proven, and support and MRO in place through partner shops, before entry into service. Our preference is partnership. Rolls-Royce has committed to the Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. We have offered UltraFan to every airframer on standard terms. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically."

EXPECTED SCENARIO AND PREDICTIONS (initial, private)
- S1 is the most likely column.
- NGSA keeps code 7: about 0.90.
- Boeing launches fps this round: about 0.35-0.45. If it does, the 10-year variant is likelier (headroom), on code 7, since P&W and RR are ready by its entry into service. That is upside the grid does not price.
- P&W commits this round: about 0.10.
- 787 Re-engine: about 0.12; both Re-engines: about 0.08.

OBJECTIVES
- Narrowbody entry: met.
- Widebody: met at 55.2%.
- Bounded risk: not attainable on any row ($8.0B; $5.7B only if the Joint Venture forms). We accept that because an airframe selected us.
- Widebody never starved: met at $0, and kept only by holding every widebody item.

tests.name: Hurdle (co-signature): jv_with_pw commit, Solo at hold
tests.threshold: The expected gain over hold must be above 0. P&W's commitment must also be on the public record (team rule: partner first). The Board's round-1 recommendation widened that condition to 'P&W's commitment, or a live airframe's code that includes P&W'. The board has no hurdle input and runs at a 10% WACC. The bars are team doctrine (inference).

tests.name: Hurdle (co-signature): t1000_upgrade launch, alone or beside the commit
tests.threshold: The row must beat hold, or the CEO must declare the gap as a premium within $3B. Separately, no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (company red line; flagged, not my ground).
tests.numbers:
Row 'UltraFan NB: hold + T1000 upgrade' minus hold: -6.03 in S1-S4 and -5.88 in S5-S6. Expected gain:
- -6.00 on A, -5.98 uniform, -6.01 S2-heavy, -6.01 S4-heavy.
Beside the commit (row 'hold + commit to JV + T1000 upgrade' minus 'hold + commit to JV') it is the same: -6.03 / -5.88. The combined plan against hold is -5.77 on A. It never beats hold, and the premium of about $6.0B is above the $3B cap. UltraFan NB is in development to 2037: red line.

tests.name: Hurdle (co-signature): ultrafan_wb launch, alone or beside the commit
tests.threshold: The row must beat hold, or the CEO must declare the gap as a premium within $3B (the Board caps an UltraFan WB premium at $1B). A Re-engine must be on the public record.
tests.numbers:
Row 'UltraFan NB: hold + UltraFan WB' minus hold: -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6. Expected gain:
- -8.59 on A, -8.32 uniform, -8.69 S2-heavy, -8.69 S4-heavy.
Beside the commit it is the same against the commit row. The combined plan against hold is -8.36 on A. The shortfall is far above the $1B cap. No 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. It would overlap the UltraFan NB Solo without both being selected (red line, flagged).

tests.name: Unselected downside / worst column against own bill: recommended orders (Solo hold + jv_with_pw commit)
tests.threshold: State the worst column of every row. No item may lose more than its own bill in any plausible column.
tests.numbers:
Commit: worst 0.00 (S1, S2, S3, S5, S6) against its $4B bill. Plan row 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': +10.10 / -4.26 / +18.48 / +12.38 / +10.01 / +10.01.
- Its worst column is S2 (-4.26 against the status quo). That is the live Solo's exposure, not the commit's, and it sits inside the Solo's $8B bill.
- S2 swings $14.36B from S1, and nothing on the grid hedges it.
- On the rules, Airbus can change NGSA's code only until its 2037 EIS, and the next round is 2045. So this is the last round in which S2 can occur (inference).

tests.name: Worst column against own bill: rejected items
tests.threshold: No item may lose more than its own bill in any plausible column.
tests.numbers:
Cancel: -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -16.38 / -16.38 / -16.38. Worst -24.76 (S3) against a $5.71B write-off. Beside the commit: -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -4.00 / -16.38 / -16.38 against the commit row (-14.12 on A).
- Write-off arithmetic: $8B x 5/7 = $5.71B, booked in 2035. It saves only the remaining $2.29B.
- What it gives up (derived from the grid): the hold row is engine value less the $8.00B R&D; the cancel row is engine value of -0.57 (the GEnx widebody loss both rows carry) less the $5.71B.
- So it gives up $18.67B of narrowbody value in S1 and S4-S6 and $27.05B in S3. Even in S2 it gives up $4.31B, because the hold row keeps 6.4% of narrowbody engines in 2050.
Upgrade: worst -6.03 against $2B, because the $5B strain is stacked on it. UltraFan WB: worst -9.00 against $4B. Cancel + upgrade: worst -25.79. Cancel + UltraFan WB: worst -28.76.

tests.name: Standing-commitment case (off the grid)
tests.threshold: Any downside the grid does not price must be stated and must stay in our hands (inference).
tests.numbers:
A 2045 formation, read from the rules (inference):
- Cash and bill: UltraFan is ready in 2037 with all $8B spent. A fold counts $4B as our Joint Venture share and writes off $4B already spent. No new cash goes out and nothing is saved: narrowbody money stays at $8.0B, against $5.7B for a 2035 formation. I plan to our $4B share as the ceiling.
- Shares: our share is equalised with P&W's. In S4 this round, the nearest analogue, equalisation leaves our 2050 share at 27.6%. I cannot see P&W's 2045 share, so that effect is unpriced: 0 at best, a loss on our narrowbody share from 2045 at worst.
- Readiness: the Joint Venture engine is ready at formation, because both folded engines are already ready.
- Control: the Joint Venture forms only in a round in which both are committed. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so the withdraw must be ordered in the 2045 round itself, on that round's grid, before we see P&W's order. Ordered that way, it keeps the downside in our hands.
- Upside: if NGSA ever left RR off, a formed Joint Venture could share P&W's slot. That is unpriced, and I book none of it.

tests.name: Capex a year in GBP
tests.threshold: For information only; my evidence sets no threshold.
tests.numbers:
Remaining Solo spend:
- $8B x 2/7 = $2.29B over 2035-2036, to the 2037 ready year: $1.14B a year.
- About £0.84bn a year at 1.36 $/£ and £0.85bn at 1.34 (the effective rate from 2028), or £1.68-1.71bn in all.
- That is 22-23% of FY2026 FCF guidance (£3.6-3.8bn) and 16-17% of the FY2028 target (£5.0-5.3bn). These are the latest figures on the record: no 2035 free cash flow figure exists, and my evidence ends in 2025.
Commit: no new spend. If the Joint Venture forms this round, the $5.71B already spent covers our $4B share, and the remaining $2.29B (£1.68-1.71bn) is not spent. For the record: the upgrade ($2B over 3 years) and UltraFan WB ($4B over 6 years) each run at about £0.49-0.50bn a year.

tests.name: Flat R&D envelope (advice)

tests.numbers: Solo + commit: $0 strain in every column (objective table, row 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV'). A narrowbody commit beside the narrowbody Solo is no overlap. The upgrade or UltraFan WB would add $5B in every column; that charge is already in their rows. From 2037 the Solo is ready and can no longer be cancelled, so any later widebody programme carries the $5B for good. The £0.84-0.85bn a year is redeployed inside a broadly flat gross R&D envelope, not added.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Delivered numbers and an announced customer would change my view.
- **The commit below hold in any column:** if the CEO's final orders or a corrected grid show the commit below hold anywhere this round, I withdraw my co-signature, and we hold at a cost of +0.23 (A).
- **Fold costs new money:** if the GM's rules show that a fold of a ready Solo charges our $4B share on top of the $8B already spent, I still co-sign this round, because nothing forms without P&W. But the 2045 withdraw then becomes a firm plan, not a review.
- **The 2045 grid:** if the 2045 grid shows formation below hold, or no live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine in time, we order the withdraw in that round. If it shows formation above hold, the commitment stands.
- **Watson's veto:** if a Civil veto stands against the final orders, the commit goes back to hold. That is his ground, not mine, and I would say so.
- **A Re-engine on the record:** I re-test UltraFan WB or the upgrade, A350 first, one programme at a time. From 2037 each must carry its bill plus the $5B strain for good, inside the $3B premium cap ($1B for UltraFan WB).
- **The weights:** none of my votes turns on them. Only a column below 0 for the commit would change them.
cfo.memo:
We've always said safety, then the balance sheet. The narrowbody bet is made, so this round I test what protects the cash.

Joint Venture commit, Solo at hold: I co-sign. Against hold it is 0.00 in five columns and +2.28 in S4. On weights A, which I confirm, that is +0.23; +0.38 uniform; +0.11 on my guide-low case. Its worst column is 0.00 against a $4B bill. P&W's own commitment is not on the record; NGSA's code 7 meets the Board's partner test, and the order of steps is Tufan's call.

If P&W commits this round, our narrowbody money falls from $8.0B to $5.7B: about £1.7bn saved. The S4 row already carries the write-off and the equalised share. After this round that saving is gone: by 2045 all $8B is spent, so a formation saves nothing. We review it at the 2045 round and order the withdraw in that round if its row is below hold.

The Solo's remaining $2.29B runs at about £0.85bn a year to 2037, 16-17% of the FY2028 free cash flow target: from cash, inside a flat R&D envelope, no equity, no borrowing.

I withhold my signature on the Trent 1000 upgrade (-6.00; worst -6.03 against $2B) and UltraFan WB (-8.59; worst -9.00 against $4B). The cancel breaks a hard rule and loses up to $24.76B against a $5.71B write-off.

My record is silent on the Joint Venture; the bars are team doctrine. That's how you should hold it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS (UltraFan NB Solo)
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready (launch + 7) no later than the EIS of each live airframe that selects it. Zero margin passes, with a note. A fail is advice, not a veto.
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030, ready 2037 (2030 + 7, the full seven years, not compressed). The bulletin shows it in development, ready 2037: no slip on the record. NGSA: launched 2030, EIS 2037, code 7, so margin 0. That is a pass with a note, not a fail and not a veto ground. fps is not launched. If launched in 2035: 7-year EIS 2042 (+5), 10-year or via Embraer EIS 2045 (+8). S3 (fps 10-year, code 5): ready 2037 against 2045, +8. Durability: both airframers make proven durability before EIS a condition, and Airbus certifies 'further makers as their engines mature'. Zero margin means the test schedule never bends to Airbus's date. If maturity slips, we tell Airbus early [R-0970]. S2 (code 6, hold row -4.26) is the column that hurts, and maturity is the only defence against it.

tests.name: Ready by EIS (Joint Venture engine, if it forms in 2035)
tests.threshold: Joint Venture engine ready at formation + 6, or earlier only with a folded Solo that is further along. It must be ready by the selecting airframe's EIS.
tests.numbers: It forms only if P&W also commits this round (S4). Formation + 6 = 2041, which on its own would miss NGSA 2037 by 4 years. Our live Solo folds in and is further along (ready 2037), so the Joint Venture engine is ready 2037: margin 0 against NGSA 2037, +5 against a 2035 fps 7-year (2042), +8 against a 2035 fps 10-year (2045). GTF2 (2030 + 6 = 2036) may fold too. If the bulletin then shows 2036, that is P&W's full six years and not compressed. But I plan on 2037, our folded UltraFan, and nothing counts on 2036 before the bulletin shows it. The grid confirms the fit: in S4 RR keeps 27.6% of NB engines in 2050. If P&W does not commit, nothing forms (0.00 in S1-S3, S5, S6). A two-maker engine formed two years before EIS does not compress maturity, on one condition (inference): the folded engine keeps its own test schedule to EIS, and joint design content (for example a P&W gearbox) waits for its own testing schedule after it. IAE lesson [R-0318]: here both partners are on the same new aircraft.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No disclosed EIS or ready date earlier than launch + 7 (UltraFan NB: 2037), launch + 6 (UltraFan WB), or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (or the earlier ready date the bulletin shows for a folded Solo). Applies to the statement, the public other moves and anything the rationale counts on.
tests.numbers: Draft statement: 'entry into service no earlier than 2037' = 2030 + 7. It gives no Joint Venture date and nothing on NGSA's or the fps dates. 'Durability will be proven, and support and MRO in place through partner shops, before entry into service.' The draft public other moves (Boeing answer, support plan, standard terms, Trent time on wing) carry no dates. The rationale must use 2037 for any Joint Venture engine (or 2041 = formation + 6 without a fold), never 2036 before the bulletin shows it. I re-check the final text at step 4.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale, so a support plan through partner shops must be in place before any narrowbody EIS (inference)
tests.numbers: The plan of record has been a public other move since round 1 and went live on NGSA's 2030 selection: a partner-shop network on the Singapore Joint Venture model, repair technology qualified in those shops, a spare-engine pool and an early-years intervention team. Internal gates: agreements in the trigger year (2030), capacity qualified by 2036, support live before the first EIS (2037). The board reports no gate status, and nothing on the record shows a slip. I report the gates as the plan, not as a test result. The draft statement keeps support through partner shops before EIS. If the Joint Venture forms, the partner's shops add capacity after EIS and never replace our plan before 2037 (inference). Boeing proposal: it must carry the same condition, with support through partner shops in place before fps EIS and sized for a second airframe, and no dates.

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: A narrowbody project (UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture) beside a widebody project (UltraFan WB or the Trent 1000 upgrade) costs a one-off $5B of strain. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (seat and company rule, inference).
tests.numbers: Recommended orders: the Solo (NB) plus a Joint Venture commit (NB), with no widebody project. Strain is $0 in all six columns (brief objective table), and the commit's item value is 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00. Trent 1000 upgrade: $5B strain in all six columns. Item value -6.03 in S1-S4 and -5.88 in S5-S6, the same beside the commit. A 2035 launch overlaps UltraFan NB development for 2 years (2035-2037) and breaks the red line. UltraFan WB: $5B strain in all six columns. Item value -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6. It overlaps for 2035-2037 with no Re-engine and is not selected: red line. From 2037 the Solo is ready and can no longer be cancelled, so any later widebody programme carries the $5B for good (brief §2). History: resources for 3 of 4 engines in 2014 [R-0929]; three programmes in parallel was 'unprecedented' in 2016 [R-1127].

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief. The board sets no engine capacity limit, so the result is not applicable unless the brief reports a constraint. A narrowbody ramp needs partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity (advice).
tests.numbers: Brief §1 hold row. The commit row is the same, and S4 keeps 27.6% in 2050. NB engines: 7 (2037), 23 (2038), 80 (2039), 254 (2040), 478 (2041), 692 (2042), 1,035 (2045), 1,040 a year from 2046 to 2060. WB engines: 197 a year to 2041, 188 from 2042. RR's total is about 1,228 engines a year from 2046, against 197 today and my midterm widebody OE ramp of 300-350. In S3 the NB share rises to 45.6% in 2050, a larger ramp. The brief reports no constraint. Advice: place gearbox, castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers (GBP 685M of GBP 2.5B in 2023), and build MRO through partner shops. For widebody shop-visit load I use my figure of 1,100-1,200 a year, not the 1,400-1,500 definition. A Joint Venture could ease the 'gearbox sizing' constraint (dashboard §3, inference).

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection
tests.numbers: Hold and commit rows, every column: 58.0% in 2040, 55.2% in 2045, 55.2% in 2050. The low point, 55.2%, is 5.2 pp above the line. The 2.8 pp step from 2042 is the GEnx upgrade. The upgrade would give 60.0% in 2050, which is not needed. UltraFan WB would give 64.8% in S5-S6 only, with no Re-engine on the record. Time on wing is the lever, inside the envelope rather than as a programme: longer-life HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000, and life-limited part extensions.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: UltraFan technology feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values never adjusted.
tests.numbers: UltraFan NB development and demonstrator technology keep feeding Trent time on wing [RX-0295]. This is not priced and the grid is not adjusted. Holding the widebody programmes does not stop the Trent durability work inside the flat R&D envelope.

vetoes.plan: CEO's proposal: ultrafan_nb_solo hold, jv_with_pw commit, ultrafan_wb hold, t1000_upgrade hold, with the draft statement
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. No compressed maturity: the Solo is ready in 2037 at the full seven years, and a 2035 Joint Venture is ready in 2037 on the folded Solo. No early date: the draft says 'no earlier than 2037' and gives no Joint Venture date. Support is through partner shops before EIS. The commit is not my ground: Solo against the Joint Venture is the CEO's call. Note, not a veto: zero margin against NGSA 2037.

vetoes.plan: jv_with_pw: commit, final orders and statement at step 4
vetoes.ground: Conditional. I would invoke the binding Civil veto only if one of these holds. (a) The statement or a public other move discloses any Joint Venture ready or EIS date, or an UltraFan EIS before 2037. (b) The statement, the rationale or an other move counts on the Joint Venture engine before 2037 (for example on GTF2's 2036 before the bulletin shows it). It would also hold if they count on a joint design change to the folded engine before EIS. (c) The partner-shop support plan is dropped, or is replaced by the partner's network, before EIS. The team rule makes it binding. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

vetoes.ground: Not a Civil veto ground. It breaks a company red line: no Trent 1000 upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (UltraFan NB to 2037). It adds $5B of strain in every column. Item value -6.03 in S1-S4 and -5.88 in S5-S6, beyond its $2B bill. If submitted I flag it at step 4 as a red-line breach, and the CEO strikes it.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb: launch, alone or beside the commit
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil veto ground. It is a red-line breach: UltraFan WB beside the UltraFan NB Solo, not both selected, with no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. It adds $5B of strain. Item value -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6. Flag it at step 4; the CEO strikes it.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_nb_solo: cancel, in any combination
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It is advice from the operating seat: it orphans a programme that is ready by its airframe's 2037 EIS, along with the support plan already live. Item value -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -16.38 / -16.38 / -16.38. Beside the commit: -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -4.00 / -16.38 / -16.38. Cancel discipline is the CEO's and the Board's red line.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Any of these would change my view:
(1) Test or durability evidence that UltraFan NB slips past 2037. With zero margin against NGSA, we tell Airbus early and never squeeze testing [R-0970].
(2) Formation terms that open a design change on the folded engine (for example swapping in P&W's gearbox) before EIS. That is compressed maturity, and I would invoke the binding Civil veto.
(3) A final statement, other move or rationale with a Joint Venture date, an UltraFan EIS before 2037, or no partner-shop support before EIS: binding veto.
(4) A 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record. That brings UltraFan WB or the upgrade back, one at a time, now always carrying the $5B strain. After 2037 the upgrade no longer breaks the in-development red line.
(5) At the 2045 review: a P&W commit then forms a Joint Venture beside engines already in service. I re-test its ready year (formation + 6 = 2051 without a fold) against live airframes' EIS.
(6) Named airline commitments for UltraFan on NGSA [RX-0297].
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: Civil tests, 2035.

Readiness. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, the full seven years from the 2030 launch, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service. Zero margin, not compression: a pass, with the note. My gates stand: partner-shop agreements from the trigger year, capacity qualified by 2036, support live before the first entry into service. Airbus certifies makers as their engines mature, so maturity is our defence in S2. If testing slips, we tell Airbus early.

Joint Venture. Formed this round, it folds our Solo: ready 2037, not 2041. If GTF2 folds too, the bulletin may show 2036; I don't plan on it. No compression, provided the folded engine keeps its test schedule to entry into service. No Joint Venture date in public. Solo against the Joint Venture is your call; I see no Civil ground against the commit.

Strain. The commit beside the Solo adds $0 in every column. The upgrade (-6.03) and UltraFan WB (-9.00) each add $5B and break our red lines; from 2037 that strain can't be removed. Hold them.

Widebody. 55.2% at the low point, 5.2 points above the line. Time on wing, inside the envelope, is the lever.

Capacity. Narrowbody engines rise from 7 in 2037 to 1,040 a year by 2046: partner shops and high-performing suppliers, sized before entry into service. Boeing's proposal carries the same condition.

Statement: no early date, support before entry into service. I concur. We're pacing that program properly.

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. UltraFan is in development for a new single-aisle on the full seven years: entry into service no earlier than 2037. Durability will be proven, and support and MRO will be in place through partner shops, before entry into service. Testing does not bend to anyone's date. Our preference is partnership; it is not a need. Airbus has put Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney on the same aircraft, so we have moved first. Rolls-Royce has committed to the Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney, on standard terms that credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. There's no change of strategy. We have answered Boeing's invitation: UltraFan, on standard terms, with durability proven before entry into service. No widebody UltraFan until a Re-engine is on the table. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
Orders: `ultrafan_nb_solo: hold` (the live Solo continues), `jv_with_pw: commit`, `ultrafan_wb: hold`, `t1000_upgrade: hold`. This is my framing proposal, unchanged. McCabe and Watson recommend the same orders, and the Board lists it as would-approve. The commit is the only Board item.

1. GRID ROWS (S1-S6, $B ΔPV)
- Submitted row, 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV': +10.10 / -4.26 / +18.48 / +12.38 / +10.01 / +10.01.
- The same row with the item at hold, 'UltraFan NB: hold': +10.10 / -4.26 / +18.48 / +10.10 / +10.01 / +10.01.
- Item value: 0.00 / 0.00 / 0.00 / +2.28 / 0.00 / 0.00.
- Worst column: 0.00, against a $4B bill. The row's own worst column, -4.26 in S2, is the live Solo's exposure, not the commit's, and it sits inside the Solo's $8B bill.

2. WEIGHTS AND EXPECTED GAIN
- Weights A, confirmed by McCabe: S1 0.55, S2 0.10, S3 0.05, S4 0.10, S5 0.12, S6 0.08.
- The selection is already made (NGSA, code 7, on the record), so these weights cover rivals' moves, not a selection.
- S4 sits at 0.10 because P&W orders sealed, before our commitment is public, and its record says 'not committing today'.
- Expected gain of the commit:
  - +0.23 on A;
  - +0.38 uniform;
  - +0.23 on my S2-heavy set;
  - +0.68 S4-heavy;
  - +0.11 on McCabe's guide-low set M (S4 0.05).
- It is never below 0 on any weights. The expected row is +9.29 on A, against +9.07 for hold.

3. ROWS TESTED AND STRUCK
Each item is measured against its matching row without it.
- Cancel UltraFan NB:
  - item value -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -16.38 / -16.38 / -16.38; -15.36 on A;
  - worst -24.76, against a $5.71B write-off ($8B x 5/7);
  - it gives up $18.67B of narrowbody value in S1 (McCabe), and it loses even in S2;
  - red line: NGSA, a live airframe not yet in service, flies it. Struck.
- Cancel + commit, against hold + commit: -16.38 / -2.02 / -24.76 / -4.00 / -16.38 / -16.38. Struck.
- Trent 1000 upgrade:
  - -6.03 in S1-S4 and -5.88 in S5-S6; -6.00 on A;
  - worst -6.03 against a $2B bill, because the $5B strain stacks on it;
  - red line: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (to 2037). McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding). Struck.
- UltraFan WB:
  - -9.00 in S1-S4 and -6.96 in S5-S6; -8.59 on A;
  - worst -9.00 against a $4B bill;
  - no Re-engine is on the record, it overlaps the Solo without both being selected, and it is far above the $1B cap. McCabe withholds her co-signature (binding). Struck.
- Combinations against hold: commit + upgrade -5.77 on A; commit + UltraFan WB -8.36.
- The best plan inside the red lines is hold + commit, which weakly dominates hold. Premium $0.

4. TESTS
- Airframers first [RX-0058]: an airframe already flies our engine (NGSA, code 7). The commit is no new launch and spends nothing new.
- Partner test: P&W's own commitment is not on the record, but NGSA's code 7 names P&W beside us. That meets the Board's reading of the partner test. This is doctrine (teams.md and the Board), not my record, which is Low on Joint Venture terms.
- Profitable or not at all: the commit needs an expected gain above 0, and +0.23 passes. The Board wants a narrowbody item at 0 or better with no premium: passes.
- Four-part gate [RX-0030]: passes.
  - Differentiated: 'we are actually bringing a technology' [RX-0072].
  - Large market: NGSA.
  - Viable business: our narrowbody money falls from $8.0B to $5.7B in S4, and the 2050 share stays at 27.6%.
  - Synergy: gearbox sizing, and partner MRO.
- Sure to deliver [RX-0124]: Watson confirms the Solo ready in 2037, the full seven years. That is zero margin against NGSA's 2037 EIS: a note, not compression. If the Joint Venture forms this round, its engine is ready in 2037 through the folded Solo; without the fold it would be 2041 (formation + 6). Nothing counts on GTF2's 2036.
- No options management [RX-0051]: a live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine (under code 7, RR's slot takes UltraFan NB or the Joint Venture engine). The commitment stands only while that holds, and it gets a decision at the 2045 round.
- Cash as an input [RX-0042]:
  - the remaining Solo spend is $2.29B, about $1.14B a year to 2037;
  - that is £0.84-0.85bn a year at 1.34-1.36 $/£, £1.68-1.71bn in all, and 16-17% of the FY2028 free cash flow target;
  - the commit adds no cash. If the Joint Venture forms this round, the £1.68-1.71bn is not spent.
- Widebody: 58.0% in 2040 and 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 on every held row, 5.2 pp above the line.

5. WHY THE ORDER OF STEPS CHANGED
- Round 1 said 'we commit when our partner does'. P&W says it will consider a Joint Venture once a partner's commitment is on the record. Two partners each waiting form nothing.
- Airbus has now put both of us on NGSA. That is the alignment Rolls-Royce lacked at IAE [R-0318].
- So we move first on what we control [RX-0094]. Partnership remains a preference, not a need [RX-0118], and there's no change of strategy [RX-0098].
- The test is binary. The table is set. If P&W comes to it, the Joint Venture forms. If not, we fly alone and lose nothing.

6. THE STANDING COMMITMENT (not priced on the grid; McCabe's case, adopted)
- A 2045 formation would save no cash, because all $8B is spent by then.
- It would write off $4B already spent and equalise our share with P&W's. That share effect is unpriced.
- The rules allow a withdraw before the Joint Venture forms. Orders are sealed and simultaneous, so at the 2045 round we decide on that round's grid:
  - keep the commitment if the formation row beats hold and a live airframe can use the engine in time;
  - otherwise order `withdraw` in that round.
- The downside stays in our hands.

7. VETOES AND RED LINES
- McCabe co-signs the commit. Her condition is met: standard terms, with no concession in any move. Her binding withholdings on the upgrade and UltraFan WB cover orders that were not submitted. No balance-sheet veto is triggered.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. None of his three conditional grounds applies to the final text:
  - no Joint Venture date, and no UltraFan entry into service before 2037;
  - nothing counts on the Joint Venture engine before 2037, and there is no joint design change on the folded engine before entry into service;
  - the partner-shop support plan stays ours and is live before entry into service.
- The red-line flags (cancel, upgrade, UltraFan WB) are struck: none is ordered. `overrides` is empty.

8. DOCTRINE AND RECORD
The partner-first ordering, the column weights and the 2045 review are doctrine and inference (teams.md, profile.md §9, the Board), not my record. On cash I take McCabe's test as my evidence; on readiness and support, Watson's.
