- Her co-signature on the commit is the condition I needed.
- She confirms weights A. I note her guide-low set M (+0.11) and keep A for the record.
- Her condition on terms is met: standard, win-win terms, with no concession anywhere in the package.
- I adopt her standing-commitment case as the 2045 plan. That includes her rule: if a fold of a ready Solo charges our $4B share on top of the $8B, the review becomes a firm withdraw.
- Her binding withholdings on the upgrade (-6.00; worst -6.03 against $2B) and UltraFan WB (-8.59; worst -9.00 against $4B) match my red lines. Neither is ordered.
- I take her S2 point. This is the last round in which Airbus can drop us before NGSA's EIS, and nothing on the grid hedges it. A cancel only makes S2 worse (-2.02).
- Capex is £0.84-0.85bn a year from free cash flow, inside a flat envelope. No balance-sheet veto is triggered.
- She offers little counterweight beyond the numbers, as expected, and the numbers agree with the proposal.
memo_weighing.ops:
I took Watson's memo as the evidence on readiness, strain, capacity and support. He invokes no Civil veto.
- Zero margin against NGSA 2037 is recorded as a note. The schedule is the full seven years, not compressed.
- I adopt his planning date for the Joint Venture engine: 2037 through the folded Solo, 2041 without it. GTF2's 2036 is not counted.
- His three conditional grounds shaped the final text:
  - no Joint Venture date, and no entry into service before 2037;
  - the folded engine keeps its own test programme, with no joint design change before entry into service;
  - the partner-shop plan stays ours and is live before entry into service; a partner's shops add capacity only after.
- He confirms $0 strain in every column for the Solo plus the commit.
- His capacity advice (gearbox, castings and forgings; about 1,040 narrowbody engines a year from 2046) goes into the internal support plan. The Boeing proposal carries the same support condition.
- Widebody's low point is 55.2%. Time on wing inside the envelope is the lever, not a programme.

The folded engine keeps its own test programme to EIS, and partner-shop support stays ours and is live before EIS. No binding Civil veto stands. (3) Profit over share: I checked the item value against the brief. Row 'UltraFan NB: hold + commit to JV' minus 'UltraFan NB: hold' is S1 0.00 / S2 0.00 / S3 0.00 / S4 +2.28 / S5 0.00 / S6 0.00. That gives +0.23 on McCabe's confirmed weights A, +0.11 on her guide-low set M and +0.38 uniform. It is at least 0 on any weights, with no premium. (4) Declared premium: $0. This is a narrowbody item, and the plan weakly dominates hold. (5) Reasonable worst case: the worst column is 0.00 against its -$4B bill. The row's -4.26 in S2 is the live Solo's exposure and sits inside that programme's bill. (6) One big programme at a time: a narrowbody commitment beside the narrowbody Solo with no widebody item adds $0 strain in every column (objective table). (7) Partner alignment: P&W's own commitment is not on the record, but NGSA's code 7 (RR, P&W, CFM) is a live airframe's code that includes P&W, and the weighted value is at least 0. (8) Balance sheet and position weakening: not applicable. The commit spends no new cash, and McCabe invokes no balance-sheet veto. (9) Disclosure: passes, with no early date and no airframer dates. The standing commitment's off-grid 2045 case (no cash saved, $4B of sunk spend written off, shares equalised) stays in our hands through a withdraw ordered in that sealed round (rules line 74). That is a recommendation, not a ground.

recommendations.text: The standing commitment needs a real decision at the 2045 round, not a default. The calendar runs 2030, 2035, 2045, 2050, and orders are sealed. If P&W answers our public commitment in 2045, the Joint Venture forms in that round unless we withdraw in the same sealed orders. So keeping the commitment in 2045 is a decision to accept formation. Bring us the 2045 grid row 'commit to JV' against hold, column by column, with its worst column against the $4B bill. Order `withdraw` if that row is below hold, if a fold of the ready UltraFan charges our $4B share on top of the $8B already spent, or if no live airframe can use the Joint Venture engine in time. McCabe should price the share equalisation, which is unpriced today, from P&W's 2045 share on the bulletin.

Hold the formation terms to two conditions, and report on them if the Joint Venture forms. First, the folded UltraFan keeps its own test programme through to EIS. No P&W gearbox or other joint design change goes onto it before EIS: that would compress maturity, and Watson would veto it. Second, the terms stay standard and credit our technology, with no concession to P&W or to any airframer to buy share. Our support plan through partner shops stays ours before EIS. The partner's shops add capacity only after it.

S2 is the risk that matters, and this is the last round in which Airbus can move NGSA off code 7 before its 2037 EIS. The hold row swings from +10.10 to -4.26, and nothing on the grid hedges it. Our defence is maturity and durability. Report Watson's ready year against NGSA 2037, and his gates (capacity qualified by 2036, support live before EIS), to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee at every round. If testing slips, tell Airbus early, and never bend the schedule to its date.

Answering Boeing's sourcing invitation is right: standard terms, no launch discount, durability proven before EIS, no dates. Keep the support plan for a second airframe sized before any fps EIS. Gearbox, castings and forgings should go to high-performing suppliers ahead of a ramp to about 1,040 narrowbody engines a year by 2046.

Widebody watch for 2045. The franchise test is not triggered: 55.2% at the low point, and no Re-engine on the record. From 2037 the Solo is ready and cannot be cancelled, so any later Trent 1000 upgrade or UltraFan WB carries its bill plus the $5B strain for good. If a 787 or A350 Re-engine reaches the bulletin, bring us one row only, A350 first. Show its item value and worst column against its own bill. The premium is capped at $3B in all and $1B for UltraFan WB. Keep Trent time-on-wing work inside a flat R&D envelope until then.

Keep the public statement this disciplined at the 2045 round. Give no ready or EIS date for any Joint Venture engine, even after formation, unless it is formation plus six years or the bulletin's own date for a folded engine. Say nothing on NGSA's or fps dates. Restate that the bounded-risk line locks at $8.0B after this round unless the Joint Venture forms now. We accept that breach because an airframe selected us.

board_review.note: We approve the Joint Venture commitment. Product safety is, and always must be, our most important priority, and nothing here bends it. UltraFan keeps its full seven years, and support is in place through partner shops before entry into service. The commitment costs nothing in five columns, is worth +2.28 in S4 and cannot fall below hold. McCabe co-signs it, Watson raises no Civil ground, and NGSA's code 7 puts Pratt & Whitney beside us on the public record. That is the alignment we lacked at IAE. Two partners each waiting would form nothing. A standing commitment is still a commitment, though, and we do not want to underestimate the risks. At 2045 we expect a decision on that round's grid: formation, or a withdraw in the same sealed round. The discipline holds: one programme at a time, a flat envelope, no widebody programme without a Re-engine. Then comes the growth story, a second airframe on the same engine.
